messages.subject: visualizing Wishart and lkj_corr priors
messages.subject_clean: visualizing Wishart and lkj_corr priors
messages.body_plain:
I am aware of the paper by Andrew and colleagues on visualizing variance covariance matrix priors, but I wanted to make up a simpler example for visualizing what it means to have a prior on a 2x2 variance covariance matrix or a correlaton matrix. Would people agree that this is a reasonable way to do this for a Wishart prior:

## R code:
library(MCMCpack)
draw <- rwish(3, matrix(c(1,.3,.3,1),2,2))

nsim<-1000
store22<-store21<-store12<-store11<-rep(NA,nsim)

for(i in 1:nsim){
draw <- rwish(3, matrix(c(1,0.9,0.9,1),2,2))
store11[i]<-draw[1,1]
store12[i]<-draw[1,2]
store21[i]<-draw[2,1]
store22[i]<-draw[2,2]
}

library(MASS)

variances<-as.matrix(data.frame(store11,store22))
bivn.kde<-kde2d(variances[,1],variances[,2],n=nsim)
persp(bivn.kde,phi=10,theta=0,shade=0.2,border=NA,
      main="Simulated variances' joint distribution")

My Stan related question is: I want to have something simple like this for lkj_corr(2.0), lkj_corr(0.5), and lkj_corr(2.0). Does this make sense:

## Stan and R code:
omegamodel<- '
parameters {
corr_matrix[2] Omega;
}
model {
// vary the parameter: set it to 0.5, 1.0, 2.0
// to see the shape change
Omega ~ lkj_corr(1.0);
}
'

library(rstan)
set_cppo("fast")

fit <- stan(model_code = omegamodel,
            iter = 500, chains = 2)

print(fit)

fit2<-as.matrix(fit)

offdiags<-fit2[,c(2,3)]

bivn.kde<-kde2d(offdiags[,1],offdiags[,2],
                n=500)
persp(bivn.kde,phi=10,theta=0,shade=0.2,border=NA,
      main="Simulated lkj_corr joint distribution")

--
Shravan Vasishth
Professor for Psycholinguistics und Neurolinguistics
Department of Linguistics
University of Potsdam, Germany
http://www.ling.uni-potsdam.de/~vasishth

messages.body_plain:
The (2 x 2) case for correlation only has one free
parameter --- the correlation rho_{1,2}.

The LKJ priors are only on correlation matrices.
We then build up covariance priors by scaling
with independent priors on the scale of each dimension.

No problem drawing from lkj_corr as you do, but you can
skip the MCMC approach and just code an independent-draw MC
approach in Stan by using lkj_corr_rng in the generated quantities
block.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
That's a bug in PyStan.  I'm not sure if it originates in
Stan or not.  I'd run your models and see, but I don't know
how to handle the JSON-formatted data.

What should happen is that the error should be caught and the sample
rejected.  You still might not be able to fit the model, but
an overflow in digamma() shouldn't cause the sampler to die.

However we fix Stan, you need a better model.  The
computational problem is a symptom of a problem in the model ---
what Andrew calls the "folk theorem".  In this case, there are
two issues with the model:  (a) no priors on the parameters to
the beta distribution, and (b) the beta distribution doesn't fit
the data.  With a prior, you should be able to get a (bad)
fit computationally.

- Bob

Thanks for all the help, the response has been well beyond what I could have hoped. I have a very naive question. How would I specify a prior on the alpha and beta parameters? My understanding is that the lower and upper keywords specify hard constraints (or as close as is allowed given numerical precision issues). Do I specify a prior by sampling the alpha and beta parameters from a distribution defined by a hyperparameter?

I'm looking through the manual for any mention of priors and coming up with nothing. My thinking would be (using a normal prior for both parameters for simplicity's sake):

data {
   ...
   real prior_mu;
   real prior_sigma;
}

parameters {
   real alpha;
   real beta;
}

model {
   alpha ~ normal(prior_mu, prior_sigma)
   beta ~ normal(prior_mu, prior_sigma)
   for (i in 1:N) {
      y[i] ~ beta(alpha, beta);
   }
}

This model compiles and runs but I have little confidence that it's doing what I think it is from a theoretical standpoint.

messages.body_plain:
On 1/1/14, 9:31 PM, Filip Krynicki wrote:
> Thanks for all the help, the response has been well beyond what I could have hoped.

We take bugs seriously, and diagnosing them often involves
us having to dive into the particulars of the models.

We're also interested in bringing more people up to speed in
Bayesian modeling and want to understand where new users have
problems.

> I have a very naive question. How
> would I specify a prior on the alpha and beta parameters? My understanding is that the lower and upper keywords specify
> hard constraints (or as close as is allowed given numerical precision issues).

They restrict alpha and beta to the constrained ranges (both > 0 in this case,
modulo arithmetic underflow, which can make them 0).  Then you get a uniform
prior over that range, which is improper in this case because

   INTEGRAL_0^infinity const dx = infinity

> Do I specify a prior by sampling the
> alpha and beta parameters from a distribution defined by a hyperparameter?

Yes, but the sampling statements don't actually do sampling.  So
you don't actually sample alpha and beta from their priors, per se,
though that's the generative story of your model.  In Stan, sampling
statements just add terms to the log probability function.

> I'm looking through the manual for any mention of priors and coming up with nothing.

They're all over the place in the manual.  In the
very first example there's a beta prior on theta.

We're assuming a fair degree of background in Bayesian
stats, though there's a chapter near the end of the manual
on Bayesian data analysis that recapitulates the initial
chapter(s) of Gelman et al.'s book of the same name.

> My thinking would be (using a
> normal prior for both parameters for simplicity's sake):
>
> data {
>     ...
>     real prior_mu;
>     real prior_sigma;
> }
>
> parameters {
>     real alpha;
>     real beta;
> }
>
> model {
>     alpha ~ normal(prior_mu, prior_sigma)
>     beta ~ normal(prior_mu, prior_sigma)
>     for (i in 1:N) {
>        y[i] ~ beta(alpha, beta);
>     }
> }
>
> This model compiles and runs but I have little confidence that it's doing what I think it is from a theoretical standpoint.

This is OK, theoretically at least.  The prior is
technically a normal truncated to the constrained values.

A more typical prior might be an exponential or lognormal, if you
put it direclty on alpha and beta.   But it's more typical to do
what we discuss in section 17.1 of the manual, which specifically discusses
priors for the beta distribution in terms of a reparameterization
in terms of the mean (alpha / (alpha + beta)) and
total prior count (alpha + beta).  There we use a Pareto prior following
Gelman et al.'s Bayesian Data Analysis, but a lognormal or
exponential (or more geneally gamma) would also make sense.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
On Wednesday, January 1, 2014 1:47:03 AM UTC-5, Shravan Vasishth wrote:
> My Stan related question is: I want to have something simple like this for lkj_corr(2.0), lkj_corr(0.5), and lkj_corr(2.0). Does this make sense:

It is possible but a bit inefficient to use Stan for this. Attached is a .R file that randomly draws from the LKJ distribution (quickly).

When the shape parameter is not equal to 1, then the correlations do not all have the same marginal distribution, unless you do a symmetric permutation of the rows and columns of the correlation matrix. But a marginal correlation is a red herring anyway.

In my opinion, the thing to visualize is "effective independence" --- which is the determinant of the correlation matrix raised to the power of 1/K or equivalently the geometric mean of the eigenvalues --- as K and the shape parameter varies. So, something like

source("lkj.R")
stopifnot(require(parallel))

K <- 2:22
eta <- seq(from = 0, to = 5, length.out = 21)
eg <- expand.grid(K = K, eta = eta)

ei_lkj <- function(K, eta, SIMS = 1000) {
  mean(replicate(SIMS,
                 exp(2 * mean(log(diag(rcorvine(K, eta, cholesky = TRUE)))))) )
}

theta_lkj <- mcmapply(ei_lkj, K = eg$K, eta = eg$eta, mc.cores = detectCores())

par(mar = c(5,4,1,1) + .1)
image(K, eta, matrix(theta_lkj, length(K), length(eta)), las = 1)
contour(K, eta, matrix(theta_lkj, length(K), length(eta)), las = 1)

yields

If you do something similar for the Wishart or inverse Wishart distribution with identity scale matrix and use the cov2cor() function in R to obtain the implied covariance matrix, you can see how effective independence varies with K and the degrees of freedom. A lot of people use the inverse Wishart distribution with degrees of freedom equal to K + 1 in order to get marginally uniform correlations and end up with low effective independence values.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
The key is that sampling statements, like x ~ foo(theta), don't
actually set the value of x.  Instead, they increment
the total model log probability with log foo(x|theta).
This means x must already be set.

We say it right in the introduction of the manual, but I fear that people
don't read any of the manual, but rather read the
R getting started guide and then they work by analogy to BUGS,
which then leads them astray as in this example.

We initialize local integer values to 0, so that when Quresh did this:

    model {
      int Z[R];   // declare latent variable indicating occupancy status of site.
      real mu_p[R,J];
      psi ~ uniform(0,1);
      p ~ uniform(0,1);
     //loop over all sites R
     for (r in 1:R) {

       Z[r] ~ bernoulli(psi);   *** PROBLEM HERE, Z[r] not set ***

       for (j in 1:J) {

         mu_p[r,j] <- Z[r]*p;   *** PROBLEM:  mu_p[r,j] can be 0 ***

         Y[r,j] ~ bernoulli(mu_p[r,j]);
       }
     }

rather than getting an error message, it just behaves unexpectedly, because
each of the Z[r] is set to 0.

Usually, you can solve this problem the way Jiqiang suggests,
by moving the local variable into a parameter.

But for integers, you need to marginalize them out of the log
probability function.  We discuss how to do this in the manual.

Quresh's model also brings up another issue with inits for local
variables.   For real-valued local variables, we initialize to NaN.
There's no equivalent for integer values, and I think we're
initializing to 0 (I'd have to check the generated code).

One thing we could do is try to catch uses of variables
before they're ever set.  I'm adding an issue for that:

   https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/477

I assigned myself, but don't know when I'll be able to
get around to it.

Also, it's not necessary to set variables BUGS-style by defining
locals for whole loops.  The for loop over j could be replaced
with a single vectorized statement with no locals:

    Y[r] ~ bernoulli(Z * p);

at least if Z were defined as a vector rather than as an array.

- Bob

On 1/3/14, 5:44 PM, Quresh Latif wrote:
> Thanks for your responses. To be honest, I do not have a strong programming background or deep knowledge of Bayesian
> statistics, so a lot of what's in the manual went over my head. For example, I'm not yet clear on what is meant by
> "...increment the total model log probability with log foo(x|theta)."

Stan just defines the log probability function for p(data,parameters),
which is proporitional to the posterior p(params|data) given Bayes's rule.

 > and why this means that "x must already be set."

Stan is more like a programming language than like BUGS.  So it's
just like in R --- if you use a variable in R, it must already be set.

You can't write an R program that looks like this:

    Z <- rep(0,R);

    for (r in 1:R)

      Z[r] <- rbinom(1,1,psi[r]);

because psi hasn't been set to any value at the point you
execute the rbinom(1,1,psi[r]) expression.

> But, I will look back at the manual and continue working on my understanding.
> One thing I want to be clear on: if I do marginilize 'Z' out of the log probability function, will this model work

Yes, it should.

> I need an alternative that does not involve explicitly defining 'Z'?

Hmm.  I fyou marginalize out Z, you won't have an explicit Z.
For instance, if b is discrete and has two possible values, 0 and 1,
then to marginalize b out of p(a,b), you have

   p(a) = SUM_(b in {0,1}) p(a,b)

        = p(a,0) + p(a,1)

So b doesn't appear in the final expression for p(a).

> You mentioned that local integer parameter values
> are initialized at 0, which would definitely not work with this model, because when a species is observed at a site, Z
> must equal 1 at that site. So, the question is, will marginilization of Z as described in the manual take care of this
> problem, or is this model simply a no-go in the current version of STAN?

Yes, it should work.  But it'll require some algebra and
won't look at all like the model you have now.

> Thanks again for all your help.

Here's the critical bit where you need to marginalize Z[r] out:

   Z[r] ~ bernoulli(psi[r]);     // define latent variable indicating occupancy status of site.

   for (j in 1:J) {

     mu_p[r,j] <- Z[r]*p[r,j];

     Y[r,j] ~ bernoulli(mu_p[r,j]);
   }

If Z[r] = 1, which happens with probability psi[r], you get:

   for (j in 1:J) {

     mu_p[r,j] <- 1 * p[r,j];

     Y[r,j] ~ bernoulli(mu_p[r,j]);
   }

or equivalently

   for (j in 1:J)

     Y[r,j] ~ bernoulli(p[r,j]);

which can be vectorized in Stan along with the probability psi[r]
to produce log probability

   log(psi[r]) + bernoulli_log(Y[r], p[r]);

Now if Z[r] = 0, which happens with probability 1 - psi[r], you get:

   for (j in 1:J)

     Y[r,j] ~ bernoulli(0);

This can be vectorized to log probability

    log1m(psi[r]) + bernoulli_log(Y[r],0);

where log1m(u) =def= log(1 - u), but it's faster and more aritmetically stable.

So writing out the marginalized probability in full, you have:

   increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(log(psi[r]) + bernoulli_log(Y[r], p[r]),
                                  log1m(psi[r]) + bernoulli_log(Y[r], 0)));

where  log_sum_exp(u,v) = log(exp(u) + exp(v)), but is also faster and more stable.

Next, we recognize that

   bernoulli_log(Y[r],0) = 0 if all Y[r,j] = 0
                         = -infinity otherwise,

Because exp(-infinity) = 0, you can just reduce this whole thing to
a much more efficient form as:

    if (sum(Y[r]) == J)
      increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(log(psi[r]) + bernoulli_log(Y[r], p[r]),
                                     log1m(psi[r]));
    else
      increment_log_prob(log(psi[r]) + bernoulli_log(Y[r], p[r]);

It's ugly, but it should be much much faster than actually sampling
a discrete Z[r].

You could make it even faster by pulling out an indicator for sum(Y[r]) == J
in the transformed data block so you don't have to keep redundantly calculating
the sum.

You should check my work on the algebra, too!

- Bob

Happy new year stan teams & users!

Just wanted to follow up on this thread. I noticed that there is a new message in the dev version of stan that provides info about the time it takes to evaluate the gradient - cool! This is really helpful, thanks for adding this.

I did notice that the value printed is quite different than my previous attempts based on timing only the model block, by more than a factor of two (model block eval: ~1.9s; gradient eval: ~4.7s). I am pretty sure this is what we expect, because to evaluate the gradient, I think we evaluate the model block as well as do some other computations. From what I understand about NUTS, the gradient needs to be evaluated each time my position changes (so for every leapfrog step) - is this correct?

Also, when trying to figure out timing previously, I noticed that the time it takes to evaluate the model block decreases over the first ~5-10 evals, and then remains somewhat more constant. Perhaps this happens as a result of starting at initial conditions that make computation a little harder? I am wondering if the printed gradient timing may be larger than what it will be for most of the evals if it is evaluated so early on. Any thoughts?

Thanks again for all your hard work on stan, and for maintaining an awesome users list!

Andria

messages.body_plain:
The timing estimate is very, very crude and really just to give users and idea of the order of magnitude their
code will take to run (i.e. is this going to take a few seconds to run or a few days?).  In particular, it ignores
overhead but also warmup so it's not unreasonable for it to overestimate simple models but underestimate
complex models.

The behavior you're seeing is entirely expected during warmup, where the chain needs to move far to get
from the tail into the typical set.  Once in the typical set it tends to move in much shorter trajectories.

I can't really say how much more, as it would really depend on the details of the model, but for some models it could be significant, particularly if the system is under memory pressure.

messages.body_plain:
Thanks again for your quick responses. Good to know about the crudeness and memory allocation. I'm really not looking for an exact timing either, just trying to get at the order of magnitude.

Some of my models seem to be on the scale of weeks to months so I'm trying to
1) speed up my code (I'm not a programmer, but have gotten lots of great tips from everyone answering questions on the list), and
2) determine what size of problem is realistic in terms of being able to get a large enough effective sample size from the posterior. I don't think I can run the model I want on the domain I would like, but can scale back to something doable by using a subdomain, aggregating, or changing my assumptions for now.

The challenge is that the difference between the *crude* lower and upper timing bounds is so wide that my estimates are sometimes not that helpful (I jokingly say a run could be done NOW, NEVER, or some time in between). They are more helpful when the order of the *crude* lower bound estimate is much larger than my tolerance.

messages.body_plain:
Another uncertainty in the estimates is that the warmup iterations
often tend to take longer than the sampling iterations.  I've
found it can be as much as a factor of 3 in models we've
been playing with.

Also, the report is for the number of time it takes to do 10
leapfrog steps (and yes, each of those does a log prob and
gradient calc).  The tree depth we report as treedepth__ is
actually the depth - 1, at least as computer scientists measure
depth.   Another twist is that we may throw away some leapfrog
steps due to the NUTS condition, though that usually doesn't
happen very often.

Also, you might want to evaluate how quickly your model
converges, not only to the high mass volume of the posterior,
but also in terms of the adaptation parameters.  You don't
need to warmup for longer than that.

Also, you should tune how long you run to the number of effective
samples you need.  Our defaults of 1000 warmup and 1000 sampling
iterations are usually way more than we need.  We'd talked about
scaling the default back to 200 and 200, but never seem to have
done that.  So I'd start small and only increase the number of warmup
iterations if you haven't converged (both in terms of parameter estimates
entering the high-mass volumeof the posterior and the adaptation parameters)
and only increase the number of sampling iterations if you need more effective
samples.

How many effective samples you need will depend on what you're doing.
If you're evaluating tail probabilities (such as 99.9% intervals), you'll need a lot.
If you're evaluating 90% intervals, you'll need less.  If you're evaluating
posterior variance, even fewer.  If you're evaluating just posterior means,
you don't need that many at all (as in 20 or so should probably be enough).

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Yeah, timing difficult models can be really hard.  There are two big complications:

1) Warmup, which is hugely affected by the initial conditions.

2) Position-dependent curvature.

(1) is really hard to estimate and can be anywhere from much faster than sampling to much slower.
(2) makes estimating timing hard, because the NUTS tree might be huge in one region of parameter space
but small in another.

If you've been able to converge then you can get a reasonable estimate of timing once you've reached a few
effective samples.  That should extrapolate pretty accurately and allow you to estimate the number of chains
or days/weeks/years you'll need.

If you're still having problems with warmup there is, unfortunately, not much principle strategy in estimating
the timing.

Hi all,

First, I want to express my appreciation for all the work that has gone into developing Stan -- it is remarkably user-friendly and flexible, and has a great community.

This post is similar in nature to that of Avi Feller on 12/30/13, but I thought it wouldn't hurt to start a new thread. I've been working on problems in function-on-scalar regression -- basically, subject-level responses are smooth functions observed on a dense grid, predictors are scalars, and coefficients are smooth functions. Coefficient functions are estimated using a B-spline basis, so estimation and inference focuses on the B-spline coefficients. I'm attaching an R file that simulates such a dataset, poses a Bayesian estimation model using RStan, and estimates the spline coefficients. This is a pretty simplified version of the model in Goldsmith & Kitago "Assessing Systematic Effects of Stroke on Motor Control Using Hierarchical Function-on-Scalar Regression", in case the attachedl code isn't particularly clear.

The issue that I'm running into is related to computation time. Direct comparisons between Stan 1.3 and 2.1 are difficult (I'm running on two different machines to keep from having to repeatedly reinstall different versions), but my best guess is that for the same effective sample sizes 2.1 is taking between 10 and 20 times longer than 1.3. Moreover, the difference seems to get worse as the number of iterations increases. For more complex models, the difference can be much more substantial.

Any thoughts about how to speed up the code in general would be appreciated, but in particular I'm wondering if there is some explanation for the surprising increase in computation time for the same effective sample sizes.

Thanks for any insights the group can provide, and happy new year!

Best,

Jeff

messages.body_plain:
The LDLT changes were never in 1.3.  This is most likely due to the changes in the sampler code, e.g., adaptation, acceptance rate, etc.

Looking at the model I don't think the LDLT changes would make a big difference here as the covariance matrices are pretty small.

Finally, Jeff, your model would probably be faster if you did something like the following:

transformed data {
...
cholesky_factor_cov{Kt] chol_inv_CovMat;
chol_inv_CovMat <- cholesky_decompose(inverse(CovMat));
}

model {
...
// Prior for spline coefficients for beta
for (pcur in 1:p) {
(beta[pcur])' ~ multi_normal_chol(mu_beta, beta_sig[pcur] * chol_inv_CovMat);
}
...
}

and drop the transformed parameters.

Also, drop all of the ~uniform calls, they are redundant and just slow things down.  If you want to restrict the range of these variables, change their definitions.  Or, even better, put proper priors on them as I suspect Andrew will chime in here saying any minute now.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] prediction/simulation/causal analysis
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] prediction/simulation/causal analysis
messages.body_plain:
[This is really for Andrew as corresponding author of the Gelman and Pardoe 2007 paper http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/published/ape17.pdf--hereafter G&P--mentioned in previous messages, but I figured there might be some value to keeping it on list.]

G&P advocates doing average predictive comparisons for a focal variable u, with v representing all other variables, by computing a weighted average of predicted differences across the space of u x u, in practice all possible increasing combinations of u values (e.g., equations 2 & 5).  It refers to these as "transitions" from u(1) to u(2) (p. 32) and weights them according to the likelihood of the transition (p. 37).

Following the causal effects literature, e.g., Pearl's ftp://ftp.cs.ucla.edu/pub/stat_ser/r379.pdf, I've been doing something different, and wonder if I'm missing something.  The approach there is to create u(1) and u(2) by direct manipulation, e.g., u(1) = observed u - 1/2 and u(2) = observed u + 1/2.
In that case rather than evaluate an n x n grid of u(1) x u(2) values one has only n pairs to evaluate, or n x 2.  n is the number of observations.

The G&P approach seems odd for several reasons, with 3 being my main concern:
The things referred to as transitions do not refer to actual transitions in the real (or counterfactual) world in which u changed from u(1) to u(2).
In complicated situations some u values might be incompatible with some v values, so that no outcome could be predicted for some u, v combinations.  As a practical matter one could work around this, but it suggests the oddity of considering all u values for each case.
As the paper points out, effects are not generally linear in u(1)-u(2).    But it looks as if the weighting scheme is effectively averaging [E(y|u(1)) - E(y|u(2)] / [u(1)-u(2)].  The result apparently is to be interpreted as the predicted difference of a unit change in u, but it is actually coming from a linearized version of differences over varying scales.  This might be of some interest if u were subject to real transitions with the assumed distribution, but that interpretation seems inappropriate in most settings (repeating point 1).
It's more work to compute over n x n than n x 2, especially when the n x n computation also involves coming up with some weighting function.

In contrast, with the Pearl approach, taking the points in order:
The change from u(1) to u(2) correspond to hypothetical states of the world, sometimes to possible experimental manipulations.
The counterfactual levels of u must be consistent with the observed v.
The effects correspond to a fixed change in u.
less work.

What am I missing?

I realize that "predicted differences" is an attempt to avoid the claim that the differences are causal, but I don't see why that important interpretive issue bears on the different expectations being taken in G&P vs Pearl.

Thanks.

Ross Boylan

P.S. What I'm doing differs in other ways, mostly in that I do not have ready access to E(y|u, v) (while I do have ready access to simulated values of y given u and v) , from the paper's setup, but that's a different issue.

On 12/27/2013 1:39 PM, Andrew Gelman wrote:

>
> On Dec 27, 2013, at 9:22 PM, Ross Boylan wrote:
>
> > On Fri, 2013-12-27 at 17:18 +0100, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> > > Ross:
> > > I think you can just draw one simulation of the outcome for each parameter value, so you can do that in the "predictive quantities" block or whatever it is called, right?  But maybe there is something I'm missing here.
> > If all I wanted was an estimate of the mean effect, I think doing one
> > simulation per parameter set would suffice, but I don't think that gives
> > me the uncertainty I need.
>
> Ahh, I see what you are saying.  In this case, I suspect that two random draws of new data per simulation of the parameters would suffice.
> >
> > Concretely, I can simulate draws from a count distribution, and compare
> > the average counts between the high and low scenarios.  But the
> > variability in the outcome arises partly from variability in the
> > parameters and partly from the variability induced by the random process
> > for a given set of parameters (mechanically, the last part corresponds
> > to the simulation given parameter values).  I only want the former.
> > Since I'm taking means for my sample of individuals (or subsets of them)
> > I thought the simulation induced variability would be trivial (since I'm
> > taking the mean of many simulated values), but some testing showed it is
> > not.
> >
> > A more mechanical problem is that I'm estimating each model separately
> > (e.g., A->B, A+B->C, ...) but I need to combine them all at the end.  So
> > I can't do predictions within a single model estimation.
> >
> > In a perfect world I would estimate all the models jointly, and thus
> > avoid assuming the coefficients between models were independent, but
> > estimating them singly was hard enough.
> >
> > A final mechanical issue is that the prediction is not based on the data
> > used to fit the model, but a modified version of that data.
> >
> > > Also, I assume you've seen this paper:
> > > http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/published/ape17.pdf
> > > A
> > I hadn't.  Thank you for the reference.
> >
> > I looked around in the 3rd edition of BDA but didn't find much; my
> > impression is the 2nd edition had a bit more, though I haven't checked
> > it.
>
> No, the place we discuss this is in my book with Jennifer Hill.  But the treatment in the paper with Pardoe is more comprehensive.
>
> >
> > Ross
> >
> > P.S. Fortunately I've been able to speed up the R code, though the
> > post-analysis is still much slower than the model estimation, which
> > seems off.  It took about 900 CPU hours to evaluate 2000 sets of
> > coefficients with 400 simulations for each.
>
> With only 2 each it should be faster!
>
> >  In contrast, I think
> > fitting all the models took only a handful of CPU hours.
> >
> > >
> > > On Dec 27, 2013, at 12:07 AM, Ross Boylan wrote:
> > >
> > > > This is a question about interpreting stan models, not estimating them.
> > > > I don't think it's really stan-specific, but I thought I'd see if anyone
> > > > has suggestions.  I am trying to compute effects, defined as the average
> > > > change in outcomes.  The problem is that for each set of coefficients I
> > > > have to draw repeated simulations, and it's taking forever.  Is there a
> > > > better way?
> > > >
> > > > I want to find the average causal effect of some variable for my sample:
> > > > define the effect, delta, to be mean(B | low) - mean(B | high).
> > > > B is an outcome; the mean is across members of the sample; low and high
> > > > are versions of the data with some variable A manipulated to take on low
> > > > or high values (e.g., observed - 1/2 and observed + 1/2).
> > > > The distribution of B depends on covariates X through a model with
> > > > parameters b.  A is one of the covariates.
> > > >
> > > > I want the  posterior distribution of delta, or at least the mean and
> > > > standard deviation of that distribution.
> > > >
> > > > Given the posterior distribution of b, estimated with stan, one can draw
> > > > b(i), the i'th simulated set of coefficients, and compute delta(i) if
> > > > the model is straightforward.
> > > >
> > > > If not, one can simulate outcomes B for each set of coefficients, giving
> > > > delta(i, j) where i is the i'th set of coefficients and j indexes
> > > > simulated outcomes for those coefficients.  One can estimate delta(i)
> > > > with the mean over j of the delta(i, j).
> > > >
> > > > There are 2 reasons the direct computation of delta(i) does not seem
> > > > feasible for me.  The main one is that I am working in a multi-stage
> > > > model, in which A->B->C->D, A causes B, B causes C, and so on.  There
> > > > are also control variables, and earlier variables can have direct as
> > > > well as indirect effects on later ones.  This means that one set of
> > > > coefficients for the A->B model create a distribution of B's, and each
> > > > distribution of B's implies a different set of downstream estimates.
> > > > This seems to leave me with numerical integration as the only reasonable
> > > > strategy.
> > > >
> > > > The minor problem is that computing the expected outcome for each
> > > > individual, given all the covariates and a set of parameter values, is
> > > > not always straightforward because the models may have truncation,
> > > > censoring, or mixtures.
> > > >
> > > > At the moment B is a count; C is multinomial; and D is binary.
> > > >
> > > > I'm thinking of capturing the predicted means directly when feasible.
> > > > This should increase precision, but does not eliminate the need to draw
> > > > repeatedly for each parameter set.
> > > >
> > > > Ross Boylan

With respect to using the Cholesky formulation, I'm happy to play around with it and see if it speeds things up. As a heads-up, there seems to be a typo in the compiled Stan model highlighted in red below:
152:         try { stan::math::check_choelsky_factor(function__,chol_inv_CovMat,"chol_inv_CovMat"); } catch (std::domain_error& e) { throw std::domain_error(std::string("Invalid value of chol_inv_CovMat: ") + std::string(e.what())); };
This looks like a pretty easy fix, but in case you hadn't run into the error in the past I thought I'd point it out. Also, thanks for the tip regarding removing the uniform priors -- I know the specification is redundant, but liked to keep it there to remind myself exactly what is going on. I'll take it out and see if there's a noticeable difference in speed.

With respect to where the change in speed is coming from (multivariate normal code or changes in the sampler code), I guess I'll hold out hope that bug fixes in 2.2.0 can at least help speed things up. As I mentioned, this is a pretty simplified version of the model to illustrate the issues -- in more realistic scenarios the computation time has gone from a few minutes to at least many hours.

Thanks again for your input, and for all the effort done by the Stan development team on this really impressive project. Best,

Jeff

messages.body_plain:
There was a bit of slowdown in the underlying code in the
move from 1.3 to a more general framework in 2.0.   That
should be a pretty constant slowdown of less than a factor
of 1.5.

Then there was a big slowdown (we measured a factor of 1.5 to 2 times
on the BUGS models) in the move in 2.1 of a target acceptance rate of
0.8 from 0.65.   The upside is a reduction in bias in mean estimates
and better variance estimates for hierarchical models (and other models
with varying posterior scales).

Given that it's not the multivariate implementation, I'd suggest
going back to a target acceptance rate of 0.65.  The command-line option
is "adapt delta=0.65" to do that.  If you're using RStan, I don't know
what it is.

***BUT***, as Michael keeps stressing, you need to make sure this doesn't bias your
results.  Do the 1.3 and 2.1 version get the same posterior means, std deviation
and 90% intervals?  If so, you should be OK with a reduced target acceptance rate.

- Bob

messages.subject: Differences between optimizing() and sampling() for IRT model
messages.subject_clean: Differences between optimizing() and sampling() for IRT model
messages.body_plain:
Hello and thanks in advance for helping,

I'm trying to understand differences in results from the same model and data between sampling (NUTS) and optimizing (BFGS). If there are any additional comments or suggestions regarding the attached model or anything else they are more than welcome.

irt_test.stan is a simple IRT model set up for long data. The model is of the form resp ~ alpha * (theta_p - beta_i) where we have person p's ability theta_p, item i's difficulty beta_i, and a global discrimination parameter (equal across all items) alpha.

test_data.Rdat is some simulated data. theta ~ N(0,1), beta ~N(0,1), alpha = 1.3, complete data from 500 persons and 25 items.

Then in R, compile the model, then sample from the posterior and optimize:

load("test_data.Rdat") #list of named objects, called testData

testModel <- stan(file = "irt_test.stan", iter = 1, chains = 1, data = testData)

outSample <- stan(fit = testModel, data = testData, pars = c("alpha", "beta", "theta"), iter = 800, warmup = 400, chains = 2)

outOptim <- optimizing(testModel@stanmodel, data = testData, hessian = T)

I understand that sampling and finding the posterior mode are two different things. I just didn't expect them to be this different. The indeterminacy in IRT can be solved with priors (as discussed by Bob Carpenter here <https://groups.google.com/d/msg/stan-users/U_F1p7YSiro/yl84TruKD7UJ>). With Bob's suggested priors, from sampling I get

lp__ = -5994.2
posterior of alpha  mean = 1.22, sd = .0475
sd across posterior means of theta = 0.947

which is close to the simulated scale (although that was a population and this is a sample), and expected by the theta ~ normal(0,1) prior. But with optimizing(), the scale is vastly different:

lp__ = -5461.13
alpha = 18.60, se = .3439    note: the se here is from sqrt(diag(solve(-outOptim$hessian))), comments?
sd across posterior means of theta = 0.089

There is a balancing act going on here, as the population distribution of theta gets tightened, the discrimination increases. Using either method produces similar predicted probabilities of correct response. Here consider the interaction of the last person and the first item (as they are next to each other in the output):

>  1.2230185 * (0.5044867 - 1.649123) #posterior means from stan()
[1] -1.399911 #which is 19.78%

> 18.6019238 * (0.0357181 -  0.112928) #posterior modes from optimizing()
[1] -1.436253 #which is 19.21%

Why is optimizing() finding a scale so far away from the identifying theta ~ normal(0,1) prior? Why is lp__ different? It seems that if the posterior mode is where optimizing() says it is, then why isn't stan() sampling anywhere near it? What is going on here?

Thank you,
-Quinn

Using: R 3.0.2 and rstan 2.1.0

messages.body_plain:
1.  In general, there's no reason to expect the
mode to be near the high-mass probability region
unless there is a large amount of data.

2.  The log prob calculations for the sampling
model includes the Jacobian term exp(alpha),
or in the more standard model, SUM_i exp(alpha[i]).

3.  Your IRT model is non-standard in that alpha is
typically an item-level parameter, not a single
variable.  So where you have:

parameters {
   real theta[N];
   real beta[I];
   real <lower=0> alpha;
}

model {
  row_vector[NN] diff_local;

  theta ~ normal(0, 1);
  beta ~ normal(0, 10);
  alpha ~ lognormal(0, 1);

  for (n in 1:NN) {
     diff_local[n] <- theta[id[n]] - beta[item[n]];
   }

   resp ~ bernoulli_logit(alpha * diff_local);

}

I would've expected to see the declaration as

   real<lower=0> alpha[I];

and then this line as:

     diff_local[n] <- alpha[item[n]] * (theta[id[n]] - beta[item[n]]);

As is, it's providing an overall scale, which I'm not
sure is going to be well identified and may be the source
of the issue you're seeing.

- Bob

Jeff

messages.body_plain:
Looking more closely at your model, one issue
is that you need to constrain the parameters to their
support.

You have:

parameters {
	matrix[p,Kt] beta;	             // matrix of fixed effect spline coefficients
	real<lower=0> y_sig;             // regression variance
	vector<lower=0>[p] beta_sig;     // tuning parameter
}

and then in the model:

	y_sig ~ uniform(0,50);

	// Prior for variance components controlling smoothness in beta
	for(pcur in 1:p) {
		beta_sig[pcur] ~ uniform(0,50);
	}

You need to add upper=50 to the declaration for y_sig and beta_sig, as in:

    real<lower=0,upper=50> y_sig;

Do you expect the posterior to range over this whole range of 0 to 50?  If
not, tightening the interval should help sampling speed.

Your call to stan looks like this:

PFSR.fit = stan(model_name="PFSR", model_code = pfsrcode,
                  data=dat, iter = 10000, warmup = 4000,
                  control = list(adapt_delta = .65),
                  chains = 1, verbose = FALSE)

I'd recommend more chains of fewer iterations, which can be run in parallel.

How long does it take the model to converge?  And how many effective samples
do you need?

The issue we're going to have with debugging is that the person who
undertands the samplers the best doesn't run R.  I'm running the models
now to see if I can see what's going on.

- Bob

> much more substantial.

messages.body_plain:
Ideally, we'd be able to provide an ongoing estimate
of the remaining time until completion.

The problem I see with the current estimate is that it
gives you time for 10 leapfrog steps, but we
don't know how many leapfrog steps are going to be needed.
At the upper limit, maybe 1000 and at the lower limit, 1.
So it doesn't really give you an idea of how long the
runs are going to be.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Might this be an identifiability issue?

What do the posterior intervals look like in the sampled
results?  Are the optimized results in the 95% intervals?

Are the differences for the individual items similar?
I'd look at a scatterplot of (theta[id[n]] - beta[item[n]])
in both models and see if they're similar.

The scales chosen are going to affect the optimization
results, so again, I want to stress that there's really no
reason to expect them to be the same.  The sampling results
are the ones that make sense from a Bayesian perspective.

- Bob

On 1/4/14, 6:20 PM, qlathrop wrote:
> Thanks for the quick response. In regards to (3), I see the same type of behavior with the usual 2-parameter model
> (model is attached, and using the same data as before):
>
> For sampling(), the posterior means of alpha_i range from 0.9 to 1.6,  sd across posterior means of theta = 0.95, lp__
> -5985.4
> For optimizing(), the posterior means of alpha_i range from 2.9 to 5.6,  sd across posterior means of theta = 0.35, lp__
> -5523.4
>
> -Quinn
>
>
> On Saturday, January 4, 2014 7:02:10 AM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>
>     1.  In general, there's no reason to expect the
>     mode to be near the high-mass probability region
>     unless there is a large amount of data.
>
>     2.  The log prob calculations for the sampling
>     model includes the Jacobian term exp(alpha),
>     or in the more standard model, SUM_i exp(alpha[i]).
>
>     3.  Your IRT model is non-standard in that alpha is
>     typically an item-level parameter, not a single
>     variable.  So where you have:
>
>     parameters {
>         real theta[N];
>         real beta[I];
>         real <lower=0> alpha;
>     }
>
>
>     model {
>        row_vector[NN] diff_local;
>
>        theta ~ normal(0, 1);
>        beta ~ normal(0, 10);
>        alpha ~ lognormal(0, 1);
>
>        for (n in 1:NN) {
>           diff_local[n] <- theta[id[n]] - beta[item[n]];
>         }
>
>         resp ~ bernoulli_logit(alpha * diff_local);
>
>     }
>
>     I would've expected to see the declaration as
>
>         real<lower=0> alpha[I];
>
>     and then this line as:
>
>           diff_local[n] <- alpha[item[n]] * (theta[id[n]] - beta[item[n]]);
>
>     As is, it's providing an overall scale, which I'm not
>     sure is going to be well identified and may be the source
>     of the issue you're seeing.
>
>     - Bob

messages.body_plain:
Thanks for the suggestions to improve speed in the model by constraining the range of support for some of the parameters and to run more chains in parallel. I think that will be broadly useful across a lot of models.

Since I was running comparisons on two systems and getting very different results, I found a third machine to try things out on. This was a clean install of Stan 2.1 (rather than upgrading from 1.3 to 2.1), and most of the issues have gone away -- computation times are now different by the modest 50% or so that was expected all along. My guess is that in upgrading from 1.3 to 2.1 I did something wrong enough to slow things down immensely but not so wrong that it completely broke everything. My apologies for not checking this more carefully before posting, and thank you for all the input along the way.

Best,

Jeff

Ack!  The problem is in RStan 2.1, not in the core
Stan samplers.

For this example, RStan is about 10 times slower than
CmdStan for version 2.1.

Time for 1000 warmup, 1000 sampling iterations with seed=1234
and target acceptance of 0.8 (new default in 2.1):

CmdStan:  40 seconds  ( 26s warmup,  14s sampling)
RStan:   404 seconds  (230s warmup, 175s sampling)

We'll look into what's going on and hopefully roll out a patch
for RStan ASAP (assuming it's not something that Jeff Goldsmith
and/or I did wrong in our config, in which case, we'll roll
out some better instructions).

- Bob

P.S.  I'll follow up on stan-dev list with the model and
       data in separate files.

installed improperly.  I carefully RTFM this time.  No idea

> in both models and see if they're similar.
>
> The scales chosen are going to affect the optimization
> results, so again, I want to stress that there's really no
> reason to expect them to be the same.  The sampling results
> are the ones that make sense from a Bayesian perspective.
>

>

> >
> >     1.  In general, there's no reason to expect the

> >     parameters {
> >         real theta[N];
> >         real beta[I];
> >         real <lower=0> alpha;

messages.subject: Re: occupancy model using RStan giving funky results
messages.subject_clean: occupancy model using RStan giving funky results
messages.body_plain:
I followed Bob's example and used his formulation (see post entitled "Simple occupancy model...") to analyze simulated data with true parameter values (psi, p, no. sites, no. visits) set to levels in this post. It worked great! The complete code for simulating the data, setting up the model in R, and the results are below. I will work on incorporating covariates and post the result here as well in case anyone is interested.

Incidentally, there is some material in the Link and Barker book (Bayesian Inference with Ecological Applications) on complete data likelihoods versus observed data likelihoods that seems relevant to the difference between how occupancy models are typically compiled in BUGS (i.e., the Royle and Kery formulation) versus how they need to be compiled in STAN. It appears to me that STAN requires us to use the observed data likelihood, which is actually the original formulation provided by MacKenzie (2002) for use with maximum likelihood estimation. By going to the observed data likelihood (i.e., not explicitly sampling the posterior for 'Z'), one loses some of the major advantages for shifting from the maximum likelihood to Bayesian framework when running occupancy models. For example, I have been working with multi-species occupancy models (see Dorazio and Royle 2005) from which I am interested in estimating species richness for individual sites. Doing so is easy having estimated 'Z'. I can just add up Z across species to get an estimate of species richness. I imagine there is a way to get at species richness from estimates of occupancy probabilities, but doing so would take some additional thought and would probably be more complicated.

Regardless, appreciate all the assistance and the availability of this new tool.

Working code and results in R (no covariates (yet)):

library(rstan)
set_cppo("fast")  # for best running speed

# Set values for simulating data
p <- 0.7   #Values for p at intercept (mean of covariate values)
psi <- 0.5 #Values for psi at intercept (mean of covariate value(s))

n.site <- 240 #no. sites

n.visit <- 2 #no. visits (will try n.visit<-c(5,10,20,40) for n.site = 30 and p = 0.1 later)

# Functions for simulating data
expit <-
  function(x){
    exp(x)/(1+exp(x))
  }

logit <-
  function(x){
    log(x/(1-x))
  }
Dat.sim <- function(p,psi,n.sts,n.vsts) {
  Y <- matrix(NA,nrow=n.sts,ncol=n.vsts)
  for(ii in 1:nrow(Y)) {
    z<-rbinom(1,1,psi)
    Y[ii,]<-rbinom(n.vsts,1,z*p)
  }
  Dat<-list(Y=Y,psi=psi,p=p)
  return(Dat)
}

# Simulate data
dat <- Dat.sim(p,psi,n.site,n.visit)
R <- nrow(dat$Y)
J <- ncol(dat$Y)
Data <- list(Y=dat$Y,R=R,J=J)

# Set initial values for HMC sampling

inits <- function()
  list(psi=runif(1),p=runif(1))

#Define which parameters to save.
parameters <- c("psi","p")

# Model code
mod_occupancy_simple <- '
data {
int<lower=0> R; // number of sites
int<lower=0> J; // number of visits
int<lower=0,upper=J> Y[R,J]; // detection-nondetection data
}
parameters {
real<lower=0,upper=1> psi;
real<lower=0,upper=1> p;
}

model {
// local variables to avoid recomputing log(psi) and log(1-psi)
real log_psi;
real log1m_psi;
log_psi <- log(psi);
log1m_psi <- log1m(psi);
// priors

psi ~ uniform(0,1);
p ~ uniform(0,1);

// likelihood

messages.body_plain:
Glad you got it to work and thanks for sharing your model.

I only see one place you could make things more efficient:

   for (r in 1:R) {
     psi[r] <- inv_logit(B0 + B_x1*x1[r] + B_x2*x2[r]);
     for (j in 1:J) p[r,j] <- inv_logit(A0 + A_x1*x1[r]);
   }

It's counter-intuitive, but it would help if you made
a B_x1_times_x1 vector and so on.

The first one would be to declare a new transformed parameter

   vector[R] B_x1_times_x1;

and then define it as

   B_x1_times_x1 <- B_x1 * x1;

and then replace the use of B_x1*x1[r] with B_x1_times_x1[r].
You can do the same thing with the other products.

Next, you can use bernoulli_logit_log, which is defined by:

   bernoulli_logit_log(u, q) = bernoulli_log(u, inverse_logit(q))

Then you don't have to define p, you can just define

    for (j in 1:J) logit_p[r,j] <- A0 + A_x1*x1[r];

And then you can vectorize this to:

    logit_p[r] <- A0 + A_x1 * x1;

It's also more arithmetically stable doing it this way.

- Bob

vectorize it or rewrite it to be more efficient.

The simplest approach would be to just put a function waic() in rstan that looks in the output for the variable "log_lik" and, if such a variable exists, calculates Waic.  A more comprehensive approach would allow tagging of the Stan model so that certain lines of code would be identified with the loglikelihood so that "log_lik" would get calculated automatically.

> By the way:  in calculating Waic, we do want to use the full loglik (including the normalizing factor); this gets done automatically when we use increment_log_prob in Stan. If we did it using tagging, we'd just have to be sure to remember to include those factors.

Cody and Z,

Sorry to hear that the command line version isn't working. I'm currently at a conference without a good connection to a development Windows machine, so I'll try to troubleshoot without being able to verify.

First off, I'm assuming you've installed Rtools. If not, I don't have any experience with other toolchains, so you'll have to fill me in on what you're using.

@Cody, can you try that with "make -j2 bin/stanc.exe". There is a chance that the targets without .exe might not work properly.

Just in case you're wondering about the details, we use make for builds and it's not really natural to write cross-platform makefiles. At one point, we were able to use the same target under Windows and *nix, but the target may have drifted over time.

@Z, can you provide:
- version of g++
- the full output
- Windows version (mostly interested in the bitness)

I see the original error and I've only seen that on 32-bit Windows machines when the executables are compiled with the g++ shipped with Rtools on a 32-bit windows. But that doesn't rule out the possibility that the error could be encountered in some other way.

I'll apologize in advance if we don't reply immediately. We're contending with most of the Stan developers sitting in one physical location, an interesting conference, and spotty internet.

Daniel

PS. @Z, you can address me as Daniel. And I'm not a doctor.

messages.body_plain:
Z,

First thing you need to do is type:
    make clean-all

That will clear all the artifacts (this one doesn't need BIT=32, but you can add that for consistency if you want.)

For every call to make on a 32-bit machine, you have to add BIT=32. In other words, this line is incorrect:
    >make bin/stanc.exe

You have two options

1.  Build bin/stanc.exe first.
    >make bin/stanc.exe BIT=32

(the BIT=32 can come before or after the target)

Then, you can run:
    > make BIT=32 src/models/basic_distributions/normal.exe

2. Just build the model and it'll automatically build the appropriate bin/stanc.exe. That is:
    > make BIT=32 src/models/basic_distributions/normal.exe

The error you are seeing is that the Stan compiler is being build with a 64-bit option. On the g++ line, it looks like "-m64". On a 32-bit Windows machine, that executable isn't compatible and the result is the weird characters being printed.

If that doesn't fix your problems, we'll need to dive in a little more, but I'm pretty confident that will fix your problem. It'll be slow compiling, but there isn't much if you've got limited memory.

Daniel

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] censored multivariate normal
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] censored multivariate normal
messages.body_plain:
Thanks for your positive attention to my question. I am encountering the estimation issue of IRT models similar to multivariate probit model, which can be expressed like

y1* = link(theta-mu1) + e1 for item one, where y1* is latent continuous variable, link() is a linking function (linear or nonlinear), theta is a random variable following N(0,1), mu1 is an intercept, and e1 is error term following N(0,sig). In the same manner, y2* = link(theta-mu2) + e2 is for second item, and so on.

Now, for example, the observable responses are y1 = 1, y2=0, y3=0,…, yn=1, which are determined if y1*>=0, y2*<0, y3*<0,…, yn*>0. Additionally, the model assumes the error terms are correlated with parameterized covariance matrix due to the experimental design. Therefore, I have to estimate theta, mu, and a covariance matrix of error term. However, to calculate the multivariate cumulative normal probability is a horrible drag and impractical. So, as far as I know, the best answer may regard the problem in the perspective of censoring mechanism. That is, the y* samples can be drawn from truncated multivariate normal distribution.

By the way, I have tried the JAGS to run this model by using one of its function called dinterval. So, the y* may be sampled from truncated multivariate normal dist (I’m not sure if it indeed works or not). However, I did not get satisfactory parameter recovery in a simulation study.

Hope above description is clear enough for you.

We added a generated quantities block that makes it easier

We discuss this in the manual, but the only example is a
complex one for Gaussian processes in section 16.4.

referring to.)

messages.body_plain:
Hi Keith,

Just based on your response, it seems like you're not specifying the model correctly.

In Stan, the sampling statements don't actually draw random variables from a distribution. You're specifying a joint model over all the parameters. If that doesn't make sense, try rereading chapter 1 of the manual.

Have you taken a look at the IRT models in the Stan repository? Maybe you can start there.

Daniel

On Tue, Jan 7, 2014 at 7:39 AM, Keith Lau <genw...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Thanks for your positive attention to my question. I am encountering the estimation issue of IRT models similar to multivariate probit model, which can be expressed like

> y1* = link(theta-mu1) + e1 for item one, where y1* is latent continuous variable, link() is a linking function (linear or nonlinear), theta is a random variable following N(0,1), mu1 is an intercept, and e1 is error term following N(0,sig). Like same manner, y2* = link(theta-mu2) + e2 is for second item, and so on.
>

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] estimating run time upper limit?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] estimating run time upper limit?
messages.body_plain:
In this discussion of runtime one thing that is important to remember is that there are two relatively orthogonal things that determine how long it takes Stan to produce a given number of effective samples.

1. Sampling efficiency.  If your posterior has highly variable curvature, is poorly initialized, etc, it will be hard for the sampling algorithm to move around efficiently.  This will typically manifest as either poor movement in certain parts of the space (aka, "sticking") or very long NUTS trajectories (large values of the treedepth parameter).

In the case of sticking, Rhat will be high and the number of effective samples will be low because it will be hard to explore the posterior well.  It may appear that models are running "very fast" in this case, running through a large number of iterations in very short periods of this.  This is because "bad" trajectories can be quickly rejected, but the quality of the samples will be terrible.

In the case of long trajectories, iterations will take a huge amount of computation time because a large number of gradient evaluations will be necessary for each iteration.  (Potentially thousands...)  To add insult to injury, it's also possible that these iterations still aren't moving that much and the quality of these samples will range from poor to so-so.

Sampling efficiency can be improved by changing your model (i.e., changing the posterior your sampling from).  Things like reparameterizing things (e.g., the "Matt trick"), tightening priors, simplifying models, marginalizing over parameters instead of sampling them, ensuring appropriate bounds are declared on parameters, etc.

2. Efficient model specification.  I.E., writing your models so that it's efficient to evaluate the gradient.  This is a little tricky (in part because we keep optimizing parts of Stan, so the "best" way to do something things changes) but basically, it means trying to minimize the number of operations that's required to compute the posterior.  Things like using vectorized distributions, caching and reusing computations, expressing things in terms of matrix-vector operations instead of scalar operations, etc all help make the same model faster.  When Stan prints out "Gradient evaluation took 4.060000e+00 seconds", it's referring to this.

By the way, Andria, your strategy of looking at results as they're being produced is a good one.  It would be great if we could adjust bin/print to work without the footer data.

Cheers,
Marcus

   make foo.cpp

That will pass the Stan file through bin/stanc, the Stan parser and code generator. Inside the foo.cpp file, you want to look and edit the ```log_prob(...)` function. If you make any changes and want to compile the edited model, you'll just type:

messages.body_plain:
Hi, a few thoughts:

0.  The type of variable (discrete or continuous) of u is important.  You talk about u - 1/2 or u + 1/2, but if u is discrete, this will not be possible.  So in general we need to think about comparisons of u based on its distribution.
1.  We tried to be clear that these are predictive comparisons, not causal comparisons,  The analogy is to regression coefficients, not to causal estimates.  I think both of these are useful goals, and I agree they should not be confused.
2.  Yes, the issue of dependence of u and v is a concern.  I think this actually is handled in our method, note the terms p(u|v) so that we are including the u's conditional on the v.
3.  It would be possible to do things on nonlinear scales.  For my applications I wanted to understand the models in terms of changes in probabilities.  But it depends on one's applied goals.
4.  Unfortunately we have not yet programmed a general implementation of our method, indeed if you look carefully there are various open choices for example in the level of smoothing that is used in the averaging.

Regarding the Pearl approach, I haven't looked at it but from your description it seems like it is answering a different question, which I think would make it more useful in some settings and less useful in others.

A

P.S.  I'm cc-ing Aki because he is interested in this topic.

>
> G&P advocates doing average predictive comparisons for a focal variable u, with v representing all other variables, by computing a weighted average of predicted differences across the space of u x u, in practice all possible increasing combinations of u values (e.g., equations 2 & 5).  It refers to these as "transitions" from u(1) to u(2) (p. 32) and weights them according to the likelihood of the transition (p. 37).
>
> Following the causal effects literature, e.g., Pearl's ftp://ftp.cs.ucla.edu/pub/stat_ser/r379.pdf, I've been doing something different, and wonder if I'm missing something.  The approach there is to create u(1) and u(2) by direct manipulation, e.g., u(1) = observed u - 1/2 and u(2) = observed u + 1/2.
> In that case rather than evaluate an n x n grid of u(1) x u(2) values one has only n pairs to evaluate, or n x 2.  n is the number of observations.
>
> The G&P approach seems odd for several reasons, with 3 being my main concern:
> The things referred to as transitions do not refer to actual transitions in the real (or counterfactual) world in which u changed from u(1) to u(2).
> In complicated situations some u values might be incompatible with some v values, so that no outcome could be predicted for some u, v combinations.  As a practical matter one could work around this, but it suggests the oddity of considering all u values for each case.
> As the paper points out, effects are not generally linear in u(1)-u(2).    But it looks as if the weighting scheme is effectively averaging [E(y|u(1)) - E(y|u(2)] / [u(1)-u(2)].  The result apparently is to be interpreted as the predicted difference of a unit change in u, but it is actually coming from a linearized version of differences over varying scales.  This might be of some interest if u were subject to real transitions with the assumed distribution, but that interpretation seems inappropriate in most settings (repeating point 1).
> It's more work to compute over n x n than n x 2, especially when the n x n computation also involves coming up with some weighting function.
>
> In contrast, with the Pearl approach, taking the points in order:
> The change from u(1) to u(2) correspond to hypothetical states of the world, sometimes to possible experimental manipulations.
> The counterfactual levels of u must be consistent with the observed v.
> The effects correspond to a fixed change in u.
> less work.
>
> What am I missing?
>
> I realize that "predicted differences" is an attempt to avoid the claim that the differences are causal, but I don't see why that important interpretive issue bears on the different expectations being taken in G&P vs Pearl.
>
> Thanks.
>

> > > > > b(i), the i'th simulated set of coefficients, and compute delta(i) if
> > > > > the model is straightforward.
> > > > >
> > > > > If not, one can simulate outcomes B for each set of coefficients, giving
> > > > > delta(i, j) where i is the i'th set of coefficients and j indexes
> > > > > simulated outcomes for those coefficients.  One can estimate delta(i)
> > > > > with the mean over j of the delta(i, j).
> > > > >
> > > > > There are 2 reasons the direct computation of delta(i) does not seem
> > > > > feasible for me.  The main one is that I am working in a multi-stage
> > > > > model, in which A->B->C->D, A causes B, B causes C, and so on.  There
> > > > > are also control variables, and earlier variables can have direct as
> > > > > well as indirect effects on later ones.  This means that one set of
> > > > > coefficients for the A->B model create a distribution of B's, and each
> > > > > distribution of B's implies a different set of downstream estimates.
> > > > > This seems to leave me with numerical integration as the only reasonable
> > > > > strategy.
> > > > >
> > > > > The minor problem is that computing the expected outcome for each
> > > > > individual, given all the covariates and a set of parameter values, is
> > > > > not always straightforward because the models may have truncation,
> > > > > censoring, or mixtures.
> > > > >
> > > > > At the moment B is a count; C is multinomial; and D is binary.
> > > > >
> > > > > I'm thinking of capturing the predicted means directly when feasible.
> > > > > This should increase precision, but does not eliminate the need to draw
> > > > > repeatedly for each parameter set.
> > > > >
> > > > > Ross Boylan

Daniel,

I think things have changed with how the generated models work now.  log_prob_grad is a static function which explicitly uses the autodiff variable type to call the (generated) log_prob function.  I'm not sure when this change was made exactly or why, but it makes it much more complicated for a user (like Andria) to implement a custom model and gradients in C++.  The instructions used to be as simple as "gut and reimplement log_prob and overload log_prob_grad in your generated model."

Andria,

You need to implement a template specialization of the function log_prob_grad for your specific model as well as changing your models log_prob function.  To do this you don't need to modify util.hpp, but rather you just need to write your own version of log_prob_grad in the generated C++ file but restricted to M being your specific model class.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.body_plain:
We can't use R code directly for two reasons:  (1) we need
functions to be templated independently on all the arguments
that can be parameters (preferably all non-int parameters);
(2) the licenses are not compatible, and due to licensing issues.

Our example distributions are all very complicated because they're
all vectorized.  But if you don't care about the speed boost
of vectorization, you can just implement it for single arguments
following the way any other function in Stan is implemented.
For instance, look at binomial_coefficient_log() or atan2(),
which are binary functions and a lot simpler than looking
at the probability functions.

You should also look at the following for instructions on how
to make the function visible to the Stan modeling language:

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/wiki/Contributing-New-Functions-to-Stan

In order to get something into Stan itself, we require unit tests
and documentation and bounds checks on the function.  We can help with
that if you don't have time to do it, but no promises on when we'll
get to it.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
You can define constraints on your parameters,
but I don't understand what you're trying to say about
y and y*.  Is y* a parameter?

We have truncation in the language in the same way
as BUGS/JAGS, but you need to make sure the constraint
on your variables match the truncation in order for
sampling to be at all efficient.

We do not have anything built in for truncated multivariates
(which you'd need to define censoring).

There's a chapter in the manual on censored and truncated
data models.

- Bob

keskiviikko, 8. tammikuuta 2014 18.19.10 UTC+2 Andrew Gelman kirjoitti:
> Hi, a few thoughts:
>
> 0.  The type of variable (discrete or continuous) of u is important.  You talk about u - 1/2 or u + 1/2, but if u is discrete, this will not be possible.  So in general we need to think about comparisons of u based on its distribution.
> 1.  We tried to be clear that these are predictive comparisons, not causal comparisons,  The analogy is to regression coefficients, not to causal estimates.  I think both of these are useful goals, and I agree they should not be confused.
> 2.  Yes, the issue of dependence of u and v is a concern.  I think this actually is handled in our method, note the terms p(u|v) so that we are including the u's conditional on the v.
> 3.  It would be possible to do things on nonlinear scales.  For my applications I wanted to understand the models in terms of changes in probabilities.  But it depends on one's applied goals.
> 4.  Unfortunately we have not yet programmed a general implementation of our method, indeed if you look carefully there are various open choices for example in the level of smoothing that is used in the averaging.
>
> Regarding the Pearl approach, I haven't looked at it but from your description it seems like it is answering a different question, which I think would make it more useful in some settings and less useful in others.
>
> A
>
> P.S.  I'm cc-ing Aki because he is interested in this topic.

>
> On Jan 4, 2014, at 1:16 AM, Ross Boylan wrote:
>
> > [This is really for Andrew as corresponding author of the Gelman and Pardoe 2007 paper http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/published/ape17.pdf--hereafter G&P--mentioned in previous messages, but I figured there might be some value to keeping it on list.]
> >
> > G&P advocates doing average predictive comparisons for a focal variable u, with v representing all other variables, by computing a weighted average of predicted differences across the space of u x u, in practice all possible increasing combinations of u values (e.g., equations 2 & 5).  It refers to these as "transitions" from u(1) to u(2) (p. 32) and weights them according to the likelihood of the transition (p. 37).
> >
> > Following the causal effects literature, e.g., Pearl's ftp://ftp.cs.ucla.edu/pub/stat_ser/r379.pdf, I've been doing something different, and wonder if I'm missing something.  The approach there is to create u(1) and u(2) by direct manipulation, e.g., u(1) = observed u - 1/2 and u(2) = observed u + 1/2.
> > In that case rather than evaluate an n x n grid of u(1) x u(2) values one has only n pairs to evaluate, or n x 2.  n is the number of observations.
> >
> > The G&P approach seems odd for several reasons, with 3 being my main concern:
> > The things referred to as transitions do not refer to actual transitions in the real (or counterfactual) world in which u changed from u(1) to u(2).
> > In complicated situations some u values might be incompatible with some v values, so that no outcome could be predicted for some u, v combinations.  As a practical matter one could work around this, but it suggests the oddity of considering all u values for each case.
> > As the paper points out, effects are not generally linear in u(1)-u(2).    But it looks as if the weighting scheme is effectively averaging [E(y|u(1)) - E(y|u(2)] / [u(1)-u(2)].  The result apparently is to be interpreted as the predicted difference of a unit change in u, but it is actually coming from a linearized version of differences over varying scales.  This might be of some interest if u were subject to real transitions with the assumed distribution, but that interpretation seems inappropriate in most settings (repeating point 1).
> > It's more work to compute over n x n than n x 2, especially when the n x n computation also involves coming up with some weighting function.
> >
> > In contrast, with the Pearl approach, taking the points in order:
> > The change from u(1) to u(2) correspond to hypothetical states of the world, sometimes to possible experimental manipulations.
> > The counterfactual levels of u must be consistent with the observed v.
> > The effects correspond to a fixed change in u.
> > less work.
> >
> > What am I missing?
> >
> > I realize that "predicted differences" is an attempt to avoid the claim that the differences are causal, but I don't see why that important interpretive issue bears on the different expectations being taken in G&P vs Pearl.
> >
> > Thanks.
> >
> > Ross Boylan
> >
> > P.S. What I'm doing differs in other ways, mostly in that I do not have ready access to E(y|u, v) (while I do have ready access to simulated values of y given u and v) , from the paper's setup, but that's a different issue.
> >
> > On 12/27/2013 1:39 PM, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> > > On Dec 27, 2013, at 9:22 PM, Ross Boylan wrote:
> > >
> > > > On Fri, 2013-12-27 at 17:18 +0100, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> > > > > Ross:
> > > > > I think you can just draw one simulation of the outcome for each parameter value, so you can do that in the "predictive quantities" block or whatever it is called, right?  But maybe there is something I'm missing here.
> > > > If all I wanted was an estimate of the mean effect, I think doing one
> > > > simulation per parameter set would suffice, but I don't think that gives
> > > > me the uncertainty I need.
> > > Ahh, I see what you are saying.  In this case, I suspect that two random draws of new data per simulation of the parameters would suffice.
> > > > Concretely, I can simulate draws from a count distribution, and compare
> > > > the average counts between the high and low scenarios.  But the
> > > > variability in the outcome arises partly from variability in the
> > > > parameters and partly from the variability induced by the random process
> > > > for a given set of parameters (mechanically, the last part corresponds
> > > > to the simulation given parameter values).  I only want the former.
> > > > Since I'm taking means for my sample of individuals (or subsets of them)
> > > > I thought the simulation induced variability would be trivial (since I'm
> > > > taking the mean of many simulated values), but some testing showed it is
> > > > not.
> > > >
> > > > A more mechanical problem is that I'm estimating each model separately
> > > > (e.g., A->B, A+B->C, ...) but I need to combine them all at the end.  So
> > > > I can't do predictions within a single model estimation.
> > > >
> > > > In a perfect world I would estimate all the models jointly, and thus
> > > > avoid assuming the coefficients between models were independent, but
> > > > estimating them singly was hard enough.
> > > >
> > > > A final mechanical issue is that the prediction is not based on the data
> > > > used to fit the model, but a modified version of that data.
> > > >
> > > > > Also, I assume you've seen this paper:
> > > > > http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/published/ape17.pdf
> > > > > A
> > > > I hadn't.  Thank you for the reference.
> > > >
> > > > I looked around in the 3rd edition of BDA but didn't find much; my
> > > > impression is the 2nd edition had a bit more, though I haven't checked
> > > > it.
> > > No, the place we discuss this is in my book with Jennifer Hill.  But the treatment in the paper with Pardoe is more comprehensive.
> > >
> > > > Ross
> > > >
> > > > P.S. Fortunately I've been able to speed up the R code, though the
> > > > post-analysis is still much slower than the model estimation, which
> > > > seems off.  It took about 900 CPU hours to evaluate 2000 sets of
> > > > coefficients with 400 simulations for each.
> > > With only 2 each it should be faster!
> > >
> > > >  In contrast, I think
> > > > fitting all the models took only a handful of CPU hours.
> > > >
> > > > > On Dec 27, 2013, at 12:07 AM, Ross Boylan wrote:
> > > > >
> > > > > > This is a question about interpreting stan models, not estimating them.
> > > > > > I don't think it's really stan-specific, but I thought I'd see if anyone
> > > > > > has suggestions.  I am trying to compute effects, defined as the average
> > > > > > change in outcomes.  The problem is that for each set of coefficients I
> > > > > > have to draw repeated simulations, and it's taking forever.  Is there a
> > > > > > better way?
> > > > > >
> > > > > > I want to find the average causal effect of some variable for my sample:
> > > > > > define the effect, delta, to be mean(B | low) - mean(B | high).
> > > > > > B is an outcome; the mean is across members of the sample; low and high
> > > > > > are versions of the data with some variable A manipulated to take on low
> > > > > > or high values (e.g., observed - 1/2 and observed + 1/2).
> > > > > > The distribution of B depends on covariates X through a model with
> > > > > > parameters b.  A is one of the covariates.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > I want the  posterior distribution of delta, or at least the mean and
> > > > > > standard deviation of that distribution.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Given the posterior distribution of b, estimated with stan, one can draw
> > > > > > b(i), the i'th simulated set of coefficients, and compute delta(i) if
> > > > > > the model is straightforward.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > If not, one can simulate outcomes B for each set of coefficients, giving
> > > > > > delta(i, j) where i is the i'th set of coefficients and j indexes
> > > > > > simulated outcomes for those coefficients.  One can estimate delta(i)
> > > > > > with the mean over j of the delta(i, j).
> > > > > >
> > > > > > There are 2 reasons the direct computation of delta(i) does not seem
> > > > > > feasible for me.  The main one is that I am working in a multi-stage
> > > > > > model, in which A->B->C->D, A causes B, B causes C, and so on.  There
> > > > > > are also control variables, and earlier variables can have direct as
> > > > > > well as indirect effects on later ones.  This means that one set of
> > > > > > coefficients for the A->B model create a distribution of B's, and each
> > > > > > distribution of B's implies a different set of downstream estimates.
> > > > > > This seems to leave me with numerical integration as the only reasonable
> > > > > > strategy.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > The minor problem is that computing the expected outcome for each
> > > > > > individual, given all the covariates and a set of parameter values, is
> > > > > > not always straightforward because the models may have truncation,
> > > > > > censoring, or mixtures.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > At the moment B is a count; C is multinomial; and D is binary.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > I'm thinking of capturing the predicted means directly when feasible.
> > > > > > This should increase precision, but does not eliminate the need to draw
> > > > > > repeatedly for each parameter set.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Ross Boylan
