messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] estimating run time upper limit?
messages.body_plain:
Thanks Marcus for the advice. I am noticing a decrease in runtime as I continue to refine both my model and code, so these tips are really helpful.

It would be great to be able to more easily work with the 'intermediate' output files.

Also, just wanted to point out a super-small typo in the manual. On page 70, in the code never lies section. Documentation is spelled docuementation. Maybe it's been fixed already, but in case it hasn't... Aside from this typo, the new manual is great :) .

Andria

On Tuesday, January 7, 2014 4:07:54 PM UTC-8, Marcus wrote:
> In this discussion of runtime one thing that is important to remember is that there are two relatively orthogonal things that determine how long it takes Stan to produce a given number of effective samples.
>
> 1. Sampling efficiency.  If your posterior has highly variable curvature, is poorly initialized, etc, it will be hard for the sampling algorithm to move around efficiently.  This will typically manifest as either poor movement in certain parts of the space (aka, "sticking") or very long NUTS trajectories (large values of the treedepth parameter).
>
> In the case of sticking, Rhat will be high and the number of effective samples will be low because it will be hard to explore the posterior well.  It may appear that models are running "very fast" in this case, running through a large number of iterations in very short periods of this.  This is because "bad" trajectories can be quickly rejected, but the quality of the samples will be terrible.
>
> In the case of long trajectories, iterations will take a huge amount of computation time because a large number of gradient evaluations will be necessary for each iteration.  (Potentially thousands...)  To add insult to injury, it's also possible that these iterations still aren't moving that much and the quality of these samples will range from poor to so-so.
>
> Sampling efficiency can be improved by changing your model (i.e., changing the posterior your sampling from).  Things like reparameterizing things (e.g., the "Matt trick"), tightening priors, simplifying models, marginalizing over parameters instead of sampling them, ensuring appropriate bounds are declared on parameters, etc.
>
> 2. Efficient model specification.  I.E., writing your models so that it's efficient to evaluate the gradient.  This is a little tricky (in part because we keep optimizing parts of Stan, so the "best" way to do something things changes) but basically, it means trying to minimize the number of operations that's required to compute the posterior.  Things like using vectorized distributions, caching and reusing computations, expressing things in terms of matrix-vector operations instead of scalar operations, etc all help make the same model faster.  When Stan prints out "Gradient evaluation took 4.060000e+00 seconds", it's referring to this.
>
> By the way, Andria, your strategy of looking at results as they're being produced is a good one.  It would be great if we could adjust bin/print to work without the footer data.
>
> Cheers,
> Marcus
>
>
> On Tue, Jan 7, 2014 at 4:21 PM, Andria Dawson <andria...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > Thanks for all the info, comments, and advice.
> >
> > As for the gradient timing info that is printed out, I was a bit confused about the statement '1000 transitions using 10 leapfrog steps', but found the first line which seems to give the time for a single gradient eval helpful. Is 'transition' referring to an iteration?
> >
> > For reference, the printed warning I get for one of my models is:
> > Gradient evaluation took 4.060000e+00 seconds
> > 1000 transitions using 10 leapfrog steps per transition would take 4.060000e+04 seconds.
> > Adjust your expectations accordingly!
> >
> >
> > For what it's worth, I'll share the following, which may or may not be useful to others.
> >
> > Because timing is so variable, and some of the models I run can take a while, I figure out a reasonable warmup, and then set num_samples to something fairly high. Since the output is written to file often (every iteration maybe?), I can check and analyze my results before the run is finished. To do this I just have to edit the csv add the 'Elapsed Time' footer (with fake timing info) and update num_samples in the header to the appropriate value.  Then I can use the read_stan_csv function in R. Sometimes I get what I need well before my program is finished executing, in which case I can just kill it.
> >
> > Also, I wanted to note that my model is not slow because it's implemented in Stan (or because it uses NUTS). The models that are slow for me are relatively complex models. Smaller-scale versions of the slowest model I run were previously implemented using a combination of R & C++ using an MCMC approach, and this was also slow because it was difficult to get things to move, even with much effort spent trying to tune the model. I want to make sure no one is deterred from using Stan because of my comments :) .
> >
> >
> > On Saturday, January 4, 2014 9:52:32 AM UTC-8, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> > > > Ideally, we'd be able to provide an ongoing estimate
> > > > of the remaining time until completion.
> > >
> > > Doable; add it to the list.
> > >
> > > > The problem I see with the current estimate is that it
> > > > gives you time for 10 leapfrog steps, but we
> > > > don't know how many leapfrog steps are going to be needed.
> > > > At the upper limit, maybe 1000 and at the lower limit, 1.
> > > > So it doesn't really give you an idea of how long the
> > > > runs are going to be.
> > >
> > > Sure, but again the warning was never intended to be taken
> > > that precisely.  It's original intention was to prevent people
> > > from spinning of runs that would take weeks without any
> > > warning.

messages.subject: Adaptation Fails in RStan 2.1.0, but Functions OK in RStan 2.0.1
messages.subject_clean: Adaptation Fails in RStan 2.1.0, but Functions OK in RStan 2.0.1
messages.body_plain:
Immediately after Stan 2.0.1 was released I built up an adaptive phylogenetic evolution model, following a paper by Butler and King. The Butler and King model relies on having a known phylogenetic tree with branch lengths (cut times between sucessive nodes). I wrote some code to integrate over uncertainty in the size of these branch lengths, +/- 350 years. Each newly proposed tree was checked for internal consistency (no child node older than a parent) using Stan's positive_ordered vecotor type. The modeled appeared to function well, recovering parameters on constructed data.

I updated RStan upon receiving an email suggesting I rerun anything run under Stan 2.0.1, as there was a bug in the code.

In RStan 2.1.0 adaptation fails, in that at every iteration a proposed positive_ordered vector violates constraints and is rejected (that happens with up to 5,000 iters of warmup).

Is there any way I can reset Rstan 2.1.0 to have the exact same warm up specs as Rstan 2.0.1? If not, is the bug in Stan 2.0.1 bad enough that samples from a non-hierarchical model would  be too biased to warrant publication?

messages.body_plain:
On 1/10/14, 9:54 AM, Aki Vehtari wrote:
> Hi,
>
> Do you have any useful estimate when MStan (Matlab/Octave interface) might be available?

When we find a volunteer who knows MATLAB and wants to do it :-)

> Or how should I proceed if I would like to help implement that?

There are two ways to create an interface.

1.  Process-level wrapper
Just write code in MATLAB to dump the data in a format we can read,
call Stan in a separate process(es) to write samples out, then write
code to read back in the results into MATLAB and ideally do some posterior
analysis.

2.  In-memory wrapper
This is what we've done for PyStan and RStan.  It's a lot more work,
but potentially much faster and definitely more flexible (e.g., it
makes it easy to expose the log prob functions and gradients/Hessians.
MATLAB has a package (whose name I forget) that makes that possible.

One of the things we're going to try to do over the next 12 months
is clean up the underlying C++ code to make approach (2) easier
and more consistent across our interfaces.  Right now, everything
that's in stan/gm/command.hpp needs to be reimplemented in each
interface.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
On 1/10/14, 6:51 AM, Cody Ross wrote:
>   Immediately after Stan 2.0.1 was released I built up an adaptive phylogenetic evolution model, following a paper by
> Butler and King. The Butler and King model relies on having a known phylogenetic tree with branch lengths (cut times
> between sucessive nodes). I wrote some code to integrate over uncertainty in the size of these branch lengths, +/- 350
> years. Each newly proposed tree was checked for internal consistency (no child node older than a parent) using Stan's
> positive_ordered vecotor type. The modeled appeared to function well, recovering parameters on constructed data.

Glad to hear it.

> I updated RStan upon receiving an email suggesting I rerun anything run under Stan 2.0.1, as there was a bug in the code.
>
> In RStan 2.1.0 adaptation fails, in that at every iteration a proposed positive_ordered vector violates constraints and
> is rejected (that happens with up to 5,000 iters of warmup).

As part of the 2.1.0 release, we fixed another bug that caused
step size to be initialized from init=0 rather than from the
user-specified init or random inits.  It's not possible to recreate
the 2.0.1 behavior exactly because it was a bug in the way init was
being done.

If the model worked in 2.0.1, it should work in 2.1.0 with init=0.
This also sets the initial parameter values to 0 on the unconstrained
scale.

But if it only works with init=0 and not other inits, then
there may be a problem in the model specification.  If the positive_ordered
vector is a parameter, the only way it should be able to violate constraints
would be due to overflow or underflow.

> Is there any way I can reset Rstan 2.1.0 to have the exact same warm up specs as Rstan 2.0.1? If not, is the bug in Stan
> 2.0.1 bad enough that samples from a non-hierarchical model would  be too biased to warrant publication?

I'll leave that one for Andrew --- he's the one who found the bug.

- Bob

On 1/10/14, 5:13 AM, Keith Lau wrote:
> In binary data, we assume there a continuous latent variable y* that decide whether observable categorical response y
> will be 1 or 0. Thus, y* is parameter, while y is known data.

> Take y = 1 for example, we only know that the y* is below 0.

> In Stan manual, there are two methods to deal with this problem. The first one is to constrain the region of y*, the
> other is to calculate the univariate cumulative probability.

You always need to declare a variable with constraints such that
the support of the function is unconstrained (i.e., on all of R^n).

multivariate cumulative distributions, nor do we have a very

I think Bob is saying we can have the same inits by setting init=0, so it makes sense to try that first.  Otherwise, if all you have are the Stan 2.0.1 runs, you have a couple options.  One option is to take them as is.  I don't think the inferences are _too_ horrible; in the bivaraiate normal case, we were getting a sd of 0.96 instead of 1.0, and according to Mike B., the bivariate case happens to be the worst case of that bug.  Another option would be to take the draws from the Stan 2.0.1 runs, consider them as a correct summary of the posterior distribution, and do some posterior predictive checks.  But really I wouldn't feel so comfortable until it's running in 2.1--I agree with Bob that it sounds like there could be a problem with the model (Bob is invoking the Folk Theorem here, I believe).

The positive_ordered vector is a transformed parameter. It is a the sum of  the MLE values of linguistic divergence dates plus or minus some random deviation. It is the case that introducing uncertainty this way can lead to proposals in which child nodes are older than parent nodes. I was using positive_ordered as a check, to ensure than any such proposals were rejected.

The sensitivity analysis I ran with the model using simulated data was decently thorough - the model recovered appropriate parameters in each of 10 cases of simulated data, and WAIC preferred the more complex model only when simulated data were created using a model in which adaptive evolution depended on the ecological regime investigated with the more complex model.

messages.subject_clean: Handling Uncertainty/Measurement Error in Stan
messages.body_plain:
I've generated some sample panel data with multivariate normal returns for 10 groups of 10 random variables each, such that there is correlation between groups but no correlation within groups (the only thing that is observed is the 100 random variables and which group they belong to). I then used Stan to perform cross-sectional regressions at each period of time to estimate the group means (this is an approach used in finance). The result of this is an array of the distribution of each group' returns in each period of time.

If I were Gibbs sampling, I could use these simulated distributions to estimate a mean or covariance matrix of the groups' returns. Alternately, I could do a time-series regression of each of the variables against their respect group. Alternately, I could subtract the original returns for the variables minus their respective groups and then perform any analysis on the residuals.

Would it be possible to handle the second part of the analysis in Stan as an alternative to Gibbs? There's a section on measurement error in the manual, but I already have information about how the measurement error for these variables presents itself. I don't need to simulate anything else.

messages.body_plain:
That's precisely what I'm doing. I'm generating fake data and fitting a model and checking to see if it reconstructs the parameters...What I'm saying is that I'm getting some output from Stan (using the fake data) that's a distribution for some parameters and can I use that distribution (and others) in Stan in another separate Stan estimation/fit (again where the data was fake). In a Gibbs sampling approach, I can just add extra steps to each iteration that use the distributions I simulate during the Gibbs sampler.

More detail that may not be all that necessary:
I'm testing fitting some finance asset pricing models with Stan, particularly for use in portfolio management. There's a few papers out there that fit traditional asset pricing models with a hierarchical Bayesian approach, but they focus on the means and variances. The important thing for portfolio management is not just the means and variances, but also the correlations between different securities. Factor models are a common approach to dealing with the large number of correlations to be estimated.

If I fit a hierarchical model of the form:

y ~ N(a[s], sigma^2) where s is an indicator for industry and sigma is an idiosyncratic variance

then it will ignore the correlations. Alternately, a common factor model like:

y ~ N(a[s] + b * x_mkt, sigma^2) where x_mkt is the return on the market

is essentially using the aggregate to predict the underlying, which you have criticized on your blog. I can reformulate this in terms of a structured multivariate normal distribution, but it doesn't easily scale for more sophisticated distributions that are common in finance.

So my first step is to fit a cross-sectional factor model or fundamental factor model (it's from an old paper by Barr Rosenberg), which is a regression cross-sectionally in each period of time using the parameters of some factors. You do that each period in time and then the coefficients to that regression would be like the returns to different factors. You can then forecast the returns and use the factor return forecasts to generate forecasts for the stocks. So for instance, I might regress the stock returns for a period against the price earnings ratio for each stock and an indicator for each industry. The coefficients then represent the returns to a P/E factor and industry factors.

I've already done the above in Stan (excluding the P/E variable) using a hierarchical approach. The result is that each period there is a simulated distribution for the industry/factor return for that period.

Suppose I take the mean of the distribution of returns in each period. This is like treating factor returns like they are known, which means I can apply any type of analysis I want in Stan.The approach I'm using is like regressing

y ~ N(a[s] + b * x[s], sigma^2) where x[s] is the time series of industry returns

so that if you simulate from the posterior predictive of the x's, then the y's will be properly correlated. It's also bottom-up, avoiding the issue mentioned above. It's flexible in that I can separately fit the x's to incorporate things like time-varying means, variances, and fat tails only on the factors.

However, by assuming those are just returns instead of a distribution, I'm losing the information about the estimation error. I can incorporate them just fine in a Gibbs Sampling approach since I have the simulated returns in each iteration and can just add extra steps to perform any additional analysis. I'm just not sure if I can do it in Stan.

messages.subject: Intel MKL libraries: nearly 2x speedup for logistic model
messages.subject_clean: Intel MKL libraries: nearly 2x speedup for logistic model
messages.body_plain:
I've seen some speculation on the list that using the Intel MKL libraries to compile Stan and Eigen might speed up sampling, but no confirmation. I just got MKL working and thought I'd pass along my results.

To test I ran the stan/src/models/speed/logistic model with following sampling setup:
>  sample
>      num_samples = 100000
>      num_warmup = 100000
>      thin = 1000
>  random
>    seed = 1

Here's the results from a vanilla (g++) run:
>   Elapsed Time: 23.43 seconds (Warm-up)
>                 36.5 seconds (Sampling)
>                 59.93 seconds (Total)

And here's the results for MKL (using icc to compile and linking in the appropriate libraries):
>   Elapsed Time: 14.33 seconds (Warm-up)
>                 17.67 seconds (Sampling)
>                 32 seconds (Total)

So MKL cuts sampling time nearly in half!

Same system, same random seed, same stan version (latest commit b63bfa7), both versions single threaded, etc. Compilation takes a bit longer with the Intel compiler (I haven't timed it, but I estimate 2x).

Implementing this is rather easy once you've got MKL installed on your system:
Download and extract a fresh copy of Stan
In your makefile change CC = g++ to CC = icc
Add the MKL path to makefile (e.g. MKLROOT = /apps/intel/2013/mkl)
Add the following to makefile's CFLAGS: -I $(MKLROOT)/include and -DEIGEN_USE_MKL_ALL
Link to your MKL library by adding to your makefile's LDLIBS
The exact implementation will depend on your system. Use the MKL link line advisor <http://software.intel.com/en-us/articles/intel-mkl-link-line-advisor/> for help.
e.g. in my case: -L$(MKLROOT)/lib/intel64 -lmkl_intel_lp64 -lmkl_core -lmkl_sequential -lpthread -lm
Compile your model as usual
e.g. make src/models/speed/logistic/logistic
Note: make sure to do the above changes before compiling for the first time - otherwise Stan will be compiled with g++ and you won't see any performance gains
p.s. Devs - is there anyway to force stan to recompile? (short of deleting all the .cpp files I suppose)
I've also attached an example makefile here (just remove .txt extension) in case the above isn't clear. I hope others find this useful!

Best,
Kyle

messages.body_plain:
I'm also a little unclear on what the problem is.

Are you asking whether we can do cut like in BUGS?
The closest we can come is using the generated quantities
block to generate new variables based on fitted values.
It uses the parameters in each sample, so propagates that
uncertainty.

For example,

   data {
     int N;
     real y[N];
     int N_sim;
   }
   parameters {
     real mu;
     real<lower=0> sigma;
   model {
     y ~ normal(mu,sigma);
   }
   generated quantities {
     real y_sim[N_sim];
     for (n in 1:N_sim)
       y_sim[n] ~ normal_rng(mu,sigma);
   }

This fits the parameters mu and sigma based on the data
y, then generates M new variates y_sim.  There's no feedback
from the generated quantities to the model.  If you instead
declared y_sim as a parameter and included

    y_sim ~ normal(mu,sigma);

in the model, then you do joint inference for (mu,sigma,y_sim).
In this case, I think the answers should be equivalent other than
that generated_quantities will be more efficient --- it shouldn't change
your inferences for mu and sigma.

You can't do anything with the posterior means directly in
Stan, because you can't express it as a log probability function.
You could, though, generate a fit, take the posterior means,
then plug that back in somewhere else.

Maybe if you wrote down a sketch of the BUGS model for what you're
trying to do, it would be easier for us to understand exactly
what you're trying to do.

- Bob

Yes, I used -O3 for both icc and g++.

In one of Ben's comments on another thread it sounded to me like he had tried using icc for compiling but hadn't linked MKL to Eigen. I found that simply using icc alone gave little to no performance improvements - it was the recompiling of Stan+Eigen with the -DEIGEN_USE_MKL_ALL flag that drastically improved performance.

More info on Eigen+MKL here: http://eigen.tuxfamily.org/dox/TopicUsingIntelMKL.html

> Warning
> Be aware that Intel® MKL is a proprietary software. It is the responsibility of the users to buy MKL licenses for their products. Moreover, the license of the user product has to allow linking to proprietary software that excludes any unmodified versions of the GPL.

And yes, please feel free to use those instructions any way you'd like.

messages.body_plain:
So I ran several tests of 400k iterations of Ben's modified logistic model to determine what factors made a difference.

Turns out that the compiler used to compile stan and eigen the first time has no effect. Similarly whether or not the -DEIGEN_USE_MKL flag is set has no effect. The only differences were due to using icc vs g++ when compiling the model itself:

Stan+Eigen compiler Stan+Eigen MKL flag Model compiler Model MKL flag Time (s)
icc yes icc yes 47
icc yes icc no 47
icc no icc yes 47
icc no icc no 46
g++ NA g++ NA 86
g++ NA icc yes 48
g++ NA icc no 47
icc yes g++ NA 87
icc no g++ NA 88

I'm surprised by this. I guess the difference I noticed when setting the flag for eigen before was attributable to something else (e.g. I didn't do the timing very formally then and it was nearly a half hour apart, so perhaps there were other processes utilizing the CPU that I didn't realize).

So using icc for model compilation seems to be the key. That doesn't seem to mesh with Ben's experience, however, so maybe there's something else at play here. Probably worth testing on someone else's machine to see if it holds up.

messages.body_plain:
One data point: I'm pretty sure my undergrad stats textbook said it was okay to use a Gaussian whenever lambda exceeded 5 (admittedly this book, was far too fond of Gaussian approximations).  There may also be a continuity correction that can make it even closer.

I don't know if Kéry and Royle would agree with me, but my feeling is this: ecology is often quite messy.  If lambda is mostly in the tens or hundreds, and this is the most egregious approximation they're making, they're in fabulous shape. Finding a closed-form version would be nice, but it probably wouldn't change the inferences too much.

If they're dealing with a species whose local abundance tends to be lower than that, then it could be worth the effort to find a closed-form alternative.

Dave

On Sunday, January 12, 2014 5:21:17 AM UTC-8, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> We've been talking to some ecologists about fitting
> an N-mixture model:
>
>    http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.0006-341X.2004.00142.x/abstract
>
> The model's discussed in this presentation by Marc Kéry:
>
>    http://www.mbr-pwrc.usgs.gov/workshops/BaysianPop2013/Nmix_intro_Euring_2013.pdf
>
> If Stan had discrete parameters, the model would be:
>
> data {
>    int<lower=0> R;
>    int<lower=0> T;
>    int<lower=0> y[R,T];
> }
> parameters {
>    int<lower=0> N[R];
>    real<lower=0> lambda;
>    real<lower=0,upper=1> p;
> }
> model {
>    lambda ~ ... some positive prior ...
>    p ~ uniform(0,1);
>    for (r in 1:R) {
>      N[r] ~ poisson(lambda);
>      for (t in 1:T) {
>        y[r,t] ~ binomial(N[r], p);
>      }
>    }
> }
>
> I can't figure out how to implement this, the obvious two approaches
> being:
>
>    1.  marginalize out the discrete parameter N, or
>
>    2.  somehow convert the poisson(lambda) to continuous.
>
> For small N, we could do (1) by marginalizing out N by brute force.
>
> For large N, we could use normals to approximate the Poisson and binomial,
> replacing
>
>    poisson(lambda)   with  normal(lambda,lambda)
>
> and replacing
>
>    binomial(N[r],p)  with  normal(N[r] * p, sqrt(N[r] * p * (1 - p))).
>
> I don't have a good sense of how large N would have to be before
> this would be reasonable.
>
> What would make me really happy is if there was a closed form for (1).
> The relevant joint that needs to be marginalized is for non-negative
> integer N and array of non-negative integers y,
>
>    p(N,y|lambda,p) = poisson(N|lambda) * PROD_t binomial(y[t]|N,p)
>
> which leads to an infinite sum for N = 0 to N = infinity:
>
>    p(y|lambda,p) = SUM_N [ poisson(N|lambda) * PROD_t binomial(y[t]|N,p) ]
>
> which I don't know how to solve.
>
> - Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: n-mixture model in Stan? [marginalizing
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Re: n-mixture model in Stan? [marginalizing
messages.body_plain:
The N-mixture model is quite popular in ecology for point counts (bird surveys), aerial surveys, camera traps, etc. From my experience I would say that N tend to be low generally ranging from 0 to 20's for point counts and camera traps. Numbers might be higher for large airscale surveys but I'm pretty sure that numbers in the 100's are quite rare.

I also agree that ecology can be quite messy. That means that pure N-mitxture model are rather rare and ecologists often have to deal with zero-dispersion and zero-inflation when trying to fit those models.

Chris
-------------

On Monday, January 13, 2014 6:46:57 AM UTC-5, Kyle Foreman wrote:
> On Monday, January 13, 2014 9:27:14 AM UTC, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> > I'm guessing the reason why you are seeing different results than I did a few months back is that g++ 4.4.x dates back to 2009 -- 2010. I guess GNU or Red Hat did bugfix releases up until 2012, but I was testing with g++ 4.7.x I think. I'll have to do the comparisons again (also with clang++) soon.
>
> Wow, I hadn't realized 4.4.7 was that old - good to know.

You generally want to use whatever is the most recent compiler you can get a hold of. For this example, doing

./logistic method=sample num_samples=100000 num_warmup=100000 thin=1000 data file=logistic.data.R random seed=1 output refresh=200001 > time.txt

after utilizing various compilers (libstan was compiled from git SHA 09fbc64 once with g++-4.8) yields

COMPILER     WARMUP SAMPLING TOTAL
llvm-g++-4.2 12.02  15.46    27.48
g++-4.4      9.38   12.11    21.49
g++-4.5      9.41   12.19    21.60
g++-4.6      9.03   11.56    20.59
g++-4.7      9.09   11.77    20.86
g++-4.8      9.21   11.81    21.02
g++-4.9 (RC) 9.36   12.09    21.45
clang++-3.4  8.51   10.99    19.50
icpc (13.x)  7.91   10.23    18.14

So, icpc does the best here (Debian, i7), although it was not nearly as stark a difference as what you saw (RHEL). Unfortunately, we see bigger differences across compilers on complicated (typically multivariate) models than in a simple logistic GLM.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Handling Uncertainty/Measurement Error in Stan
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Handling Uncertainty/Measurement Error in Stan
messages.body_plain:
Thanks for the reply Bob. I hadn't used BUGS before using Stan and had just coded my own Gibbs samplers, so I thought this would be easier to attach what I've been working on (I have it set up so the un-rar'ed folder is in C). I also sketched a Gibbs sampler of what I'm trying to do below, more or less. The S_test_stan.r file is the main file. It calls the S_gen_data.r file to create the data and then fits some Stan models.

The key line is 60:
y_sim_index_cutdown <- colMeans(aperm(y_sim_index, c(2, 1, 3)))
In the previous section, I fit the Stan model cross-sectionally as I described above. The y_sim_index variable is the array containing all these results. Thus, this line is like taking the posterior mean in each period (which is what you seem to recommend). I then use these means in subsequent analysis, treating them as though they are observed data.

In a Gibbs sampler, I could just use the y_sim_index posterior samples directly in the next stage of the analysis. For instance, the following sequence I give a headline of "Fit Simple Hierarchical Model with Index as Regressor" in the code regresses the y_bottom variable against the respective index (calculated by that line 60 above). In a Gibbs sampler, in an iteration I can use the y_sim_index in the next line (see sketch). It seems like the impression I'm getting is that Stan requires the formula for the distribution. I'm wondering if that's the case or if there's any way to use simulated variables at all the way I would with Gibbs sampling.

I'm essentially throwing away all the rest of the information about the uncertainty in these means. I considered that I could calculate the covariance in each time period and assume that the measurement error is multivariate normal. I'm worried that this might be slow (I can't even get the multivariate normal-inverse Wishart distribution to work properly), but it seems possible. For this type of data, multivariate normal seems like a good assumption, but it may not always make sense.

Gibbs sketch:

for i in 1:(n_burn+n_gibbs) {
  #cross-sectional estimation
  for j in 1:n_j {
    for t in 1:T {
      estimate x[t, j], the mean in each time period t for group j of variable y
      simulate x[t, j]
    }
  }
  # time-series estimation
  for n in 1:N {
    for equation: y[n] ~ N(beta_y[n] * x[index[n]], sigma[n]^0.5)
    estimate beta_y[n]
    simulate beta_y[n]
    estimate sigma[n]
    simulate sigma[n]
    Note the x's are all from the cross-sectional step above. They change with each Gibbs iteration.
  }

  if i>n_burn {
    save relevant variables

  }
}

On Saturday, January 11, 2014 3:28:17 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> I'm also a little unclear on what the problem is.
>
> Are you asking whether we can do cut like in BUGS?
> The closest we can come is using the generated quantities
> block to generate new variables based on fitted values.
> It uses the parameters in each sample, so propagates that
> uncertainty.
>
> For example,
>
>    data {
>      int N;
>      real y[N];
>      int N_sim;
>    }
>    parameters {
>      real mu;
>      real<lower=0> sigma;
>    model {
>      y ~ normal(mu,sigma);
>    }
>    generated quantities {
>      real y_sim[N_sim];
>      for (n in 1:N_sim)
>        y_sim[n] ~ normal_rng(mu,sigma);
>    }
>
> This fits the parameters mu and sigma based on the data
> y, then generates M new variates y_sim.  There's no feedback
> from the generated quantities to the model.  If you instead
> declared y_sim as a parameter and included
>
>     y_sim ~ normal(mu,sigma);
>
> in the model, then you do joint inference for (mu,sigma,y_sim).
> In this case, I think the answers should be equivalent other than
> that generated_quantities will be more efficient --- it shouldn't change
> your inferences for mu and sigma.
>
> You can't do anything with the posterior means directly in
> Stan, because you can't express it as a log probability function.
> You could, though, generate a fit, take the posterior means,
> then plug that back in somewhere else.
>
> Maybe if you wrote down a sketch of the BUGS model for what you're
> trying to do, it would be easier for us to understand exactly
> what you're trying to do.
>
> - Bob
>
> On 1/11/14, 12:27 AM, John Hall wrote:
> > That's precisely what I'm doing. I'm generating fake data and fitting a model and checking to see if it reconstructs the
> > parameters...What I'm saying is that I'm getting some output from Stan (using the fake data) that's a distribution for
> > some parameters and can I use that distribution (and others) in Stan in another separate Stan estimation/fit (again
> > where the data was fake). In a Gibbs sampling approach, I can just add extra steps to each iteration that use the fake data.
> >
> > More detail that may not be all that necessary:
> > I'm testing fitting some finance asset pricing models with Stan, particularly for use in portfolio management. There's a
> > few papers out there that fit traditional asset pricing models with a hierarchical Bayesian approach, but they focus on
> > the means and variances. The important thing for portfolio management is not just the means and variances, but also the
> > correlations between different securities. Factor models are a common approach to dealing with the large number of
> > correlations to be estimated.
> >
> > If I fit a hierarchical model of the form:
> >
> > y ~ N(a[s], sigma^2) where s is an indicator for industry and sigma is an idiosyncratic variance
> >
> > then it will ignore the correlations. Alternately, a common factor model like:
> >
> > y ~ N(a[s] + b * x_mkt, sigma^2) where x_mkt is the return on the market
> >
> > is essentially using the aggregate to predict the underlying, which you have criticized on your blog. I can reformulate
> > this in terms of a structured multivariate normal distribution, but it doesn't easily scale for more sophisticated
> > distributions that are common in finance.
> >
> > So my first step is to fit a cross-sectional factor model or fundamental factor model (it's from an old paper by Barr
> > Rosenberg), which is a regression cross-sectionally in each period of time using the parameters of some factors. You do
> > that each period in time and then the coefficients to that regression would be like the returns to different factors.
> > You can then forecast the returns and use the factor return forecasts to generate forecasts for the stocks. So for

messages.body_plain:
Yes, Stan requires you to write down the full probability
function as does any kind of full Bayesian modeling.

Your algorithm sketch doesn't look like a Gibbs sampler to me.
If you have N parameters theta[1],...,theta[N], and full probability
function p(theta[1],...,theta[N]),  then Gibbs initializes theta, then
does

for (i in 1:I)
   for (n in 1:N)
     sample theta[n] from p(theta[n] | theta[1],..,theta[n-1],theta[n+1],...,theta[N])

I don't understand your estimate/simulate notation.

The short answer is that you can't mix simulation and sampling
in Stan.  You can sample and do simulations based on the samples,
but you can't then feed the simulations back into the sampler in any way.

- Bob

What email address should I send the model/data to?

I originally had this model running in RStan since it allows me to save only some of the parameters as samples using pars=c(lorum, ipsum, etc.) (is this possible in CmdStan too?)

I just ran the model in CmdStan, and noticed the same phenomenon, of incessant "the current Metropolis proposal is about to be rejected" warnings during warm up and sampling; however, when I took a look at the traceplot, the model appears to function fine, moving into the correct (according to the simulated data) posterior region, and mixing.

What is notable is that the tree depth is low, max=3, sometimes = -1 .

What exactly triggers the "the current Metropolis proposal is about to be rejected" warnings?

 At first, I had thought that the warning was only thrown when the proposed parameter state got rejected after failing to pass a constraint check. Ie. the sample after rejecting a parameter state at iteration X, is identical to the parameter state at X-1. From the last run of this model, it looks the simulation at a given iteration X might attempt to go out to 4 steps, for example, but at step 4 violate a constraint, this triggers the warning; however, the exported parameter state (the sample) is the parameter state at step 3 of iteration X, rather than previous iteration's (X-1) parameter state.

Looking at the Cmd prompt, a warning was issued for every warm-up sample from sample to sample 200. However, after saving warm-up and looking at the samples, only the first 3 proposals and about 3 others spread over the next 190 samples were actually rejected.

Could it just be that Stan 2.1.0 is more generous than Stan 2.0.1 about when it throws the "the current Metropolis proposal is about to be rejected" warnings?

On 1/14/14, 3:02 AM, John Hall wrote:
> For the Gibbs thing, I was just summarizing how I write the program to do the Gibbs sampling more than anything. I
> typically would write seperate functions for estimating the distribution for a parameter and simulating from that
> distribution. It's the same thing as what you're talking about though, just as separate steps.

You can do that in Stan using the generated quantities block.
The parameters are declared as parameters, the model is in
the model, then the quantities to generate conditional on
the parameters are declared and defined in the generated quantities
block.

This is one of the reasons we built the generated quantities --- to
generate predictive quantities based on the parameters.

If you do Gibbs, you have to have the joint probability anyway,
assuming your model's consistent --- the conditionals should
be conditionals of a joint probability.  Technically, all you
need is something proportional to the posterior p(parameters|data),
which itself is proportional to the joint p(parameters,alpha) by
Bayes's rule.  Sorry if this is all obvious.

- Bob

>
>     I don't understand your estimate/simulate notation.
>
>     The short answer is that you can't mix simulation and sampling
>     in Stan.  You can sample and do simulations based on the samples,

>
>     - Bob

On 1/14/14, 6:40 AM, Cody Ross wrote:
> What email address should I send the model/data to?

You can send to me:  ca...@alias-i.com

> I originally had this model running in RStan since it allows me to save only some of the parameters as samples using
> pars=c(lorum, ipsum, etc.) (is this possible in CmdStan too?)
>
> I just ran the model in CmdStan, and noticed the same phenomenon, of incessant "the current Metropolis proposal is about
> to be rejected" warnings during warm up and sampling; however, when I took a look at the traceplot, the model appears to
> function fine, moving into the correct (according to the simulated data) posterior region, and mixing.
>
> What is notable is that the tree depth is low, max=3, sometimes = -1 .

That's fine depending on the model.  Some models only need tree depth of 1.

> What exactly triggers the "the current Metropolis proposal is about to be rejected" warnings?

>   At first, I had thought that the warning was only thrown when the proposed parameter state got rejected after failing
> to pass a constraint check.

That's correct.  But we do multiple proposals along the path
of the simulated Hamiltonian.

> Ie. the sample after rejecting a parameter state at iteration X, is identical to the
> parameter state at X-1.

Not quite.  We can still sample if we move and then get into
a bad space.

The cause is almost always one of arithmetic underflow, overflow or
parameters defined without the proper constraints so that the support
of the probability function defined in the model doesn't match the
constraints.

> From the last run of this model, it looks the simulation at a given iteration X might attempt to
> go out to 4 steps, for example, but at step 4 violate a constraint, this triggers the warning; however, the exported
> parameter state (the sample) is the parameter state at step 3 of iteration X, rather than previous iteration's (X-1)
> parameter state.

Right --- the -1 is the only time the first step gets rejected.

> Looking at the Cmd prompt, a warning was issued for every warm-up sample from sample to sample 200. However, after
> saving warm-up and looking at the samples, only the first 3 proposals and about 3 others spread over the next 190
> samples were actually rejected.
>
> Could it just be that Stan 2.1.0 is more generous than Stan 2.0.1 about when it throws the "the current Metropolis
> proposal is about to be rejected" warnings?

It's not more generous on error checking, but it tries to adapt to a
smaller step size with more rejections due to the plain-old Metropolis/slice
condition.  One of the reasons we made this change is that it's more
robust.  So if you're in an area of high curvature, a big step (which is
a linear approximation of the posterior based on the gradient) can be
rejected whereas two smaller steps won't be rejected.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Hi all.  We have a new Stan postdoc position that we are looking to fill right away!  It's a unique opportunity for someone to be working on the forefront of statistical modeling, computation, and political science.  We're looking to develop Monte Carlo EP and all sorts of other cool things, in the context of a live application.

The ideal candidate would probably be a student in CS or machine learning or maybe statistics who is a strong C++ programmer and also interested in applied Bayesian modeling.  But I think computational skills will be crucial.  If you know of any students or recent graduates who would fit this description, please let me know, also please pass this around widely:
http://andrewgelman.com/2014/01/15/postdoc-involving-pathbreaking-work-mrp-stan-2014-election/

Thanks much.
See you
Andrew

---

Postdoc involving pathbreaking work in MRP, Stan, and the 2014 election!

We’re working with polling company YouGov to track public opinion, state-by-state and district-by-district, during the 2014 campaign. We’ll be using multilevel regression and poststratification, and implementing it in Stan, and developing the necessary new parts of Stan to get this running scalably and efficiently. And we’ll be making the most detailed, up-to-date election forecasts.

What you’ll be doing if you join us as a postdoc:
- You’ll be in the midst of the most advanced polling team anywhere;
- You’ll be doing cutting-edge statistical research on MRP with deep interactions;
- You’ll be doing basic research in statistical computing, developing fast and scalable deterministic and stochastic algorithms for fitting multilevel models;
- You’ll be working inside Stan, the most advanced general computational framework for Bayesian analysis.
We’re doing research, not just implementing existing methods.

What we need:
- Stats knowledge. You should know your way around Bayesian data analysis;
- Serious computing skills. You should be a skilled C++ programmer;
- Interest in the application area. You should care about public opinion, and it should be important to you that our forecasts are good. When our estimates of opinion for some group in the population don’t make sense, you should notice and be bothered by it.

We have a great team with diverse skills (computing, statistics, political science) that plays nicely together and from whom you can learn a lot. Also lots of opportunity to collaborate with researchers in many different quantitative disciplines through Columbia’s Applied Statistics Center.

The position is a 2-year postdoc, funded by Yougov and situated in the Applied Statistics Center at Columbia University.

messages.body_plain:
This is a messy intersection of Windows, which doesn't have
good C++ tools, and R, which doesn't allow packages to easily
control configuration.

What you need to do is edit a file named "Makevars.win" or
"Makevars", which you will find either here:

   R_HOME/.R/Makevars.win

or if that doesn't exist, in

   R_HOME/.R/Makevars

where "R_HOME" is the directory into which R is installed.

You need to edit that file and remove the "-g" line from the compiler
configuration.

You also want to make sure it specifies "-O3" (that's a capital "O",
not a zero) and not "-O3".  If you can find the Makevars file and
would like more help, just send us the contents of the Makevars file
and we can show you what it should look like.  The problem is that
different R packages mess with it, so we can't know what it's going
to look like for users.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
On 1/15/14, 10:55 PM, Jarrett Barber wrote:
> I have a simulator (of tree growth) written in C++ whose returned value I'd like
 > to use as the mean of a Gaussian specification in Stan.  The simulator has
 > about 30 parameters plus various other inputs.  All parameters spaces are subsets
 > of the reals.  I'm hoping that I can simply modify mymodel.cpp, generated by Stan,
 > in the (hopefully) obvious place(s), then link/compile as usual, letting Stan do
 > the rest, e.g., gradients, etc.

I think Daniel's writing some general instructions for people who want to do this.

You have to:

1.  Make sure you declare the parameters with appropriate constraints.  Stan assumes
the support of the log probability function matches the declared constraints on
parameters.  Then you leave the parameter transforms in place.

2.  In general, you have to code a templated version of your function, with different
template parameters for each argument.  You can get by leaving the data or transformed
data variables as doubles.  You can test independently of the model by making sure
you can instantiate the arguments that will be parameters, transformed parameters, or
local variables with stan::agrad::var.  This will also let you test the gradients, and
it's a good idea to test vs. a finite-difference implementation.

Then you have to call our built-in functions rather than the built-in C++ library functions
to make sure auto-diff will work.  But the compiler will let you know where you need to
do that.

If you send us the signature of your function, I can show you what the signature needs
to look like.

An alternative is to add your new function to Stan directly.  This is cleaner,
but we don't yet have a way to make it easy to extend, so you have to modify our
source and compile with that.  There are some sketchy instructions on how to do this
here:

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/wiki/Contributing-New-Functions-to-Stan

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] DLM for Proportions/Multinomial Model
messages.body_plain:
I'll leave the statistical modeling advice to others, but
I'd like to point out that your model isn't quite correct as formulated.
The problem is that you need to add the Jacobian of the inverse
logit transform to the total log probability.

That'd be

   for (k in 1:K) {
     logit(props[t, k]) ~ normal(logit(props[t - 1, k]), tau); // Gaussian on logit scale

     increment_log_prob(log(inv_logit(props[t,k])) + log1m(inv_logit(props[t,k])));
   }

Here the Jacobian adjustment is the log of the derivative of the
inverse transform,

   log | d/dp inv_logit(p) |

     = log( inv_logit(p) * (1 - inv_logit(p) )

     = log(inv_logit(p)) + log1m(inv_logit(p))

where p = props[t,k].  We discuss the Jacobian for the logit in the
section of the manual on constraints and transforms (near the end).

A more typical formulation I've seen is to parameterize props itself on the
logit scale (i.e., unconstrained vector[K] here), and then use softmax
to transform that to the parameter to plug into the multinomial.  Then you
don't need to fiddle with Jacobians.

BUT, and this is a big but for now, our current softmax implementation has a memory
leak.  If your system's small, it probably won't matter.
We fixed it on the 2.1.1 hotfix branch on GitHub, but we haven't released the
code with the fix yet, as we had the same kind of memory leak in a few other
functions that we're going to fix.  In fact, I'm doing that in the other window
I have open now :-)

You could also speed the model up a bit by vectorizing the call to normal, but I'd
wait until the model's all working to try that.

- Bob

Bob:

Thank you.  That was the secret of success, although it took forever to find the .R directory (it was not in the directory where the R program and subdirectories were stored).  Not only did the program install, but I also could get the schools example to work which I could not do last time.

What people have to do is (1) find the .R  directory (which could be in their Documents directory and not in the directory where the R code is), (2) remove the '-g' directive from the first line, and (3) change the 'O0' to 'O3'.  Simple addition to the code, but will cause many Windows users of STAN to sing your praise.

Larry

messages.subject: PyStan running old models
messages.subject_clean: PyStan running old models
messages.body_plain:
I've noticed that PyStan doesn't actually update the model if the code changes unless you restart the Python interpreter. I'm midway through debugging that, but wanted to give a heads-up: if you're having inexplicable problems with a model, try restarting.

A demonstration (I'm actually using ipython, though):

>>> import pystan
>>> m_y = pystan.StanModel(model_code='parameters {real y;} model {y ~ normal(0,1);}')
>>> m_y.optimizing()['par']['y']
array(0.0) # success.
>>> m_z = pystan.StanModel(model_code='parameters {real z;} model {z ~ normal(0,1);}')
>>> m_z.optimizing()['par']['z']
KeyError # because it's actually running m_y!
>>> m_z = pystan.StanModel(model_code='parameters {real z;} model {z ~ normal(0,1);}', model_name='m_z')
>>> m_z.optimizing()['par']['z']
array(0.0) # success.

I've also noticed that if you pickle the StanModel object and reload it in a new session, it correctly runs the new model.

The different models are indeed using new Python module names (there was a tiny bug in the case of loading model code from a a file that had previously made it re-use the same module name. The probably more common case of passing the code as a string gets that tricky detail correct. I'll submit a PR shortly):

>>> [k for k in sys.modules.keys() if 'stanfit' in k]
['stanfit4anon_model_08e08668c8f51816387d4a09ca3747a7',
 'stanfit4anon_model_1079b7dbebb119312268da41f2eee749',
 'stanfit4m_z_32c35ac5f3514fe587f3e01fda9796b0']

What I suspect is going on is that while the Python module is fine, the exported symbols from the C++ code itself are already in the process and so aren't reloaded. They're namespaced under the model name, which would explain why changing the model name makes it work. I'm a bit perplexed why the tests pass, though, since not all of them set model_name. I'm not certain I've run the full testsuite on my toolchain, though.

I'll probably make the interim patch of appending a hash of the model code to the C++ model name. But I suspect the issue could be avoided entirely if the model C++ functions didn't end up exported. And maybe it's just a quirk of my toolchain (clang++ 5, see below) that makes this happen at all. How does RStan handle this?

-Ken

PS:

[GCC 4.2.1 Compatible Apple LLVM 5.0 (clang-500.2.79)], Cython 0.19.2

messages.body_plain:
Sorry --- I just realized I gave you the Jacobian the wrong way around.
I'm used to going from unconstrained parameters to parameters,
which involves the inverse logit.  You're going the other way,
so you need to increment with the log absolute derivative of
the logits, not the inverse logits, that is:

    log | d/dp logit(p) |

     = log | d/dp log(p/(1-p)) |

     = log | d/dp log(p) - d/dp log(1-p) |

     = log | 1/p  + 1/(1-p) |

     = log ( 1/(p * (1-p)) )

     = - log (p * (1 - p))

     = -[log(p) + log(1-p)]

     = -[log(p) + log1m(p)]

I'd check my work on that derivative, too.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Hi Bob,

Thanks for the correction. Your math is correct. The updated code is:

    int<lower=1> T; // number of time periods
    int<lower=1> K; // number of categories
    int<lower=0> counts[T, K];
}
parameters {
    simplex[K] props[T]; // period-specific category proportions
    real<lower=0> tau; // innovation standard deviation
}
transformed parameters {
    vector[K] logit_props[T]; // logit of proportions
    for (t in 1:T) {
        for (k in 1:K) {
            logit_props[t, k] <- logit(props[t, k]);
            // Adjust for logit tranform by incrementing the log probability

            // by the log of the derivative of the logit function
            increment_log_prob(-(log(props[t, k]) + log1m(props[t, k])));

        }
    }
}
model {
    for (t in 1:T) {
        if (t > 1) {
            logit_props[t] ~ normal(logit_props[t - 1], tau);
        }

        counts[t] ~ multinomial(props[t]);
    }
}

Devin

messages.body_plain:
I came across some confusing behavior in initialization (CmdStan 2.1.0, OSX 10.7.5, g++-4.2).

Using the example bernoulli model from the manual (in src/models/basic_estimators)

> ./bernoulli sample save_warmup=1 data file=bernoulli.data.R
Produces a random initial value for theta as expected by the default init=2

> ./bernoulli sample save_warmup=1 init=0 data file=bernoulli.data.R
Results in the initial value for theta = 0.5. Shouldn't this be zero?

> ./bernoulli sample save_warmup=1 init=init.R data file=bernoulli.data.R
where init.R is a dump file with theta <- 0 produces the message "Rejecting user-specified initialization because of vanishing density." I guess this happens when an init exactly equals a bound? This call also returns an exit value of 0. Maybe it should return a more informative exit value, like when a initial value exceeds a bound. Changing init.R to theta <- 0.75 works and produces an expected initial value of 0.75.

It got even stranger when I tested a model with a vector parameter. I tried a very simple regression (files attached) with the following:

> ./mlr sample save_warmup=1 init=0 data file=data.R
which fails to produce initial values equal to zero.

> ./mlr sample save_warmup=1 init=init.R data file=data.R
also usually does not produce the correct initial values. Close but not quite. I say usually because I've found that when sampling from more than one chain, I occasionally get a chain with exactly the correct initial conditions, for all parameters.

I'm assuming the first row of samples in the csv files represent the initial conditions. Is this correct?

Thanks for any insights,
-b

>     ./bernoulli sample save_warmup=1 data file=bernoulli.data.R
>
> Produces a random initial value for theta as expected by the default init=2
>
>     ./bernoulli sample save_warmup=1 init=0 data file=bernoulli.data.R
>
> Results in the initial value for theta = 0.5. Shouldn't this be zero?

0.5 is correct.  It's 0 on the *unconstrained* scale, which is then
inverse-logit transformed to (0,1) resulting in 0.5.
The [-2,2] uniform init is also on the unconstrained scale.
The reason we do this is that we're then guaranteed to get
a valid initialization point if the model's parameters are declared
with appropriate constraints (so support is over all valid variables).

The init files, on the other hand, are on the constrained scale,
and it's up to the user to make sure they satisfy the constraints.

>     ./bernoulli sample save_warmup=1 init=init.R data file=bernoulli.data.R
>
> where init.R is a dump file with theta <- 0 produces the message "Rejecting user-specified initialization because of
> vanishing density." I guess this happens when an init exactly equals a bound? This call also returns an exit value of 0.
> Maybe it should return a more informative exit value, like when a initial value exceeds a bound. Changing init.R to
> theta <- 0.75 works and produces an expected initial value of 0.75.
>
> It got even stranger when I tested a model with a vector parameter. I tried a very simple regression (files attached)
> with the following:
>
>     ./mlr sample save_warmup=1 init=0 data file=data.R
>
> which fails to produce initial values equal to zero.
>
>     ./mlr sample save_warmup=1 init=init.R data file=data.R
>
> also usually does not produce the correct initial values. Close but not quite. I say usually because I've found that
> when sampling from more than one chain, I occasionally get a chain with exactly the correct initial conditions, for all
> parameters.

> I'm assuming the first row of samples in the csv files represent the initial conditions. Is this correct?

Yes, that's supposed to happen if save_warmup=1.

You've definitely tickled a bug here.  If I do this:

   ~/temp2/lau$ ./mlr sample save_warmup=1 init=init.R data file=data.R

it saves the initialization as the first sample, whereas if I do this:

   ./mlr sample num_samples=100 num_warmup=100 save_warmup=1 init=init.R data file=data.R

it saves 200 iteration values, but the first one's not the initialization.

- Bob

On 1/19/14, 3:02 AM, Steve wrote:
> Just to clarify - the initial values in the init.R file are in fact used as the initial values on the constrained scale,
> and the first values saved are the 2nd set of values in the chain?

Right, but the "2nd set of values" notion is a bit subtle because
there's an adaptation step at the get go that looks for a suitable
step size to make progress.

The first phase of adaptation (after finding a workable step size)
then uses that initial step size with a unit mass matrix
(same step size in every dimension) in an attempt to find the high
mass volume of the posterior.

The second phase of adaptation then alternatively looks for a step
size that leads to the right rejection rate (set at 0.8 in Stan 2.1.0
byd efault) and estimates the mass matrix (effectively
the scale of each parameter in the default setting, which is a diagonal
mass matrix).

The third and final phase of adaptation then fine tunes the step size
with the final estimate of the mass matrix from the second adaptation phase.

The length of all of these phases is tunable in Stan 2.1.0, but it's
probably easier to just run for enough iterations that the chains
start mixing well after adaptation.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Initialization not working as expected
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Initialization not working as expected
messages.body_plain:
We took the discussion up on the dev list.

The current state of Stan is that the first line output
if save_warmup=1 is the first iteration *after* the
inits.  It may be close to the inits if the sampler didn't
move far or exactly the inits if the first move was rejected.

We're going to fix this in a future release so that we
always save the init value as the first iteration.  This will
mainly be useful for random inits, because there's no way to
recover the initialized values otherwise.

- Bob

messages.subject: PyStan traceplot and other issues
messages.subject_clean: PyStan traceplot and other issues
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I just started working with PyStan, as I plan to slowly move my workload over from R to Python as much as possible. One of the big barriers to this was Python's relatively nascient statistical abilities, but PyStan removes that barrier almost entirely, so thanks!

I have two questions:
1) Is it possible in Python to see a traceplot of just one parameter? If I have a fitted object, I can see a traceplot of all parameters using fit.traceplot(). However, this is incredibly cumbersome if you have lots of parameters (including things like predicted values). In R, I can use a command traceplot(posteriors, pars = 'beta') to see a traceplot of JUST beta, but this capability is missing so far as I know. Is this something that can be added to PyStan or am I just doing it wrong? I can do it myself using the following lines:

# traceplot plots for each parameter
beta = fit.extract(permuted=True)['beta']
# stan_args gives one list per chain
n_chains = len(fit.stan_args)

# assumes that the beta array is just one chain tacked onto the end of another
bSplit = np.array_split(beta, n_chains)

# plot
for i in range(n_chains):
    py.plot(bSplit[i])
py.show()

but I'd prefer a parameter argument like in R.

2) This issue is a little more quirky than anything. I can run PyStan fine most times. My code runs fine from the Terminal and as well as the interactive interpreter in Spyder (an IDE). But when I try to run it in an interactive interpreter in PyCharm (a better IDE), the model appears to compile in to C++ just fine but then spits about an error message for what appears to be at every iteration of the model (10,000 or so)

Process PoolWorker-5827:
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/System/Library/Frameworks/Python.framework/Versions/2.7/lib/python2.7/multiprocessing/process.py", line 249, in _bootstrap
    sys.stdin.close()
AttributeError: StdIn instance has no attribute 'close'

I don't know what this means, and it appears to be fairly specific to PyCharm. But I just wanted to report it so that you all are aware that PyStan may not work in some interactive interpreters.

Thanks!

Nate

I did the centering this way because I was trying to get mean population beta parameters (Beta_mu) and the above are the group level betas centered at zero. I know I had a prior of zero to begin with but often one groups' parameters might get stuck far from zero and switch with the population beta parameters.

> Another approach I've used for this in large IRT models that

Yes, the model eventually converges to a reasonable estimate but it can take many hours, and it gets around that point before warmup ends. When printing the diagnostic file, adaption ends at 100 rows. I've initialized the chains to start at several different reasonable points (this was necessary, otherwise auto initialization fails). Some chains get stuck and some don't.

> to the complex model you posted?  That should let you both
> assess whether the model's getting reasonable results and
> as you add more complexity, put your finger on where the poor

I've had less issues when only estimating a varying slope and intercept for each group. Once I start adding more varying effects for each group things start to slow down.

On 1/20/14, 3:59 PM, Joseph Burling wrote:
>
> First of all, thank you for the quick and thorough response.
>
>
>     I don't understand the model's parameterization as is, but
>     maybe someone else will have a clue.  In particular, I'm not
>     sure what's going on with all the centering you're doing,
>     such as
>
>         mu_d[k] <- row(beta_dyad_raw, k) - mean(beta_dyad_raw[k]);
>
>         mu_o[k] <- row(beta_obj_raw, k) - mean(beta_obj_raw[k]);
>
>         epsilon_i <- epsilon_raw_adj - mean(epsilon_raw_adj);
>
>
>
> I did the centering this way because I was trying to get mean population beta parameters (Beta_mu) and the above are the
> group level betas centered at zero. I know I had a prior of zero to begin with but often one groups' parameters might
> get stuck far from zero and switch with the population beta parameters.

The real problem with this kind of centering is that the model
winds up being unidentified on the unconstrained scale (the centered
parameters are identified, but not the parameters being sampled, which are just
the transforms of the variables defined in the parameters block).

Andrew recommended the approach you took for BUGS in his regression book
with Jennifer, but it's problematic for Stan because the adaptation
and sampling happens on the unconstrained scale.

>     Another approach I've used for this in large IRT models that
>     aren't inherently identified is to give the epsilon_raw_adj
>     a prior centered at 0 (the uniform does this, but it doesn't favor
>     a centered result).
>
>     Does the model at least converge to a reasonable estimate?
>     And does it converge to the same place from multiple starting
>     points?  If so, does it converge well before the warmup phase
>     is over?  Adaptation needs to spend some time after convergence
>     before it can estimate the scales properly.
>
>
>
> Yes, the model eventually converges to a reasonable estimate but it can take many hours, and it gets around that point
> before warmup ends. When printing the diagnostic file, adaption ends at 100 rows. I've initialized the chains to start
> at several different reasonable points (this was necessary, otherwise auto initialization fails). Some chains get stuck
> and some don't.

You really want to get to a reasonable point about halfway through adaptation.
That'll make sampling go much faster by allowing better adaptation.

Getting stuck is usually because of the requirement for detailed balance
in the sampler.  If you jump to an unlikely place (or start there), it's
hard to get out again.

>     Is there any way to start with a simpler model and work up
>     to the complex model you posted?  That should let you both
>     assess whether the model's getting reasonable results and
>     as you add more complexity, put your finger on where the poor
>     mixing arises.
>
>
> I've had less issues when only estimating a varying slope and intercept for each group. Once I start adding more varying
> effects for each group things start to slow down.
>
>     If there are only a few hundred parameters, you could also
>     try a dense mass matrix --- it could be that there's not a reasonable
>     way to scale all the parameters without a rotation that makes sense.
>
>     You only have uniform-in-an-interval priors on many of
>     the parameters --- is the range reasonable given what you know
>     about the problem?  Adding something more peaked in the way of
>     priors can help with mixing.  Also, initialization (assuming
>     you don't initialize yourself) will be centered at the center
>     of the intervals specified as constraints.
>
>
> I've fit a similar model with the lme4 package in order to obtain wide, reasonable constraints. A lot of the uniform
> priors with the constraints are used for a truncated half cauchy. If I were to use something more peaked, do you mean
> something like a beta and reparameterizing the cauchy differently like so, tan(pi()/2 * beta) ? Or did you have
> something else in mind.

We're going to be implementing something like blme in Stan this
year.  We're having trouble finding time to do it, but it's one
of our higher priorities.

>     If you hit the maximum tree depth, that can be for two reasons.
>     One is that you just turned the step size down so low due to
>     jitter that it goes out to the max depth without making a U-turn.
>     The other is that you really need a small step size because of
>     high curvature in the posterior or because you're way out in
>     a tail and have to go a long way before turning around.
>
>     To make the model more efficient, I'd suggest not making a diagonal
>     matrix S_d, but doing the scaling in a loop that's *outside* the
>     multi_normal_cholesky loop.
>
>
> Sorry, can you elaborate a little further on this?

Sure.  Rather than this:

   S_d <- diag_matrix(sigma_dyad);
   L_d <- cholesky_decompose(Rho_dyad);

   for (j in 1:J) {
     col(beta_dyad_raw, j) ~ multi_normal_cholesky(mu_zeros, S_d * L_d);
   }

it'd be better to do this:

   L_d <- cholesky_decompose(Rho_dyad);
   for (i in 1:cols(L_d))
     for (j in i:cols(L_d))
       L_d[i,j] <- L_d[i,j] * sigma_dyad[i];

   for (j in 1:J) {

     col(beta_dyad_raw, j) ~ multi_normal_cholesky(mu_zeros, L_d);
   }

You should check my algebra --- I'm not very good at matrices.

The loop saves a bunch of multiplies over the S_d * L_d, and they're
only done once.

An intermediate solution would be to assign (S_d * L_d) to a temporary
matrix variable outside of the loop.

>
>     Another efficiency issue is in the exp for lambda.  This can
>     be problematic numerically, and we provide an alternative.
>     Instead of
>
>         lambda <- Exposure .* exp(X * Beta_mu + Z_dyad * Beta_dyad + Z_obj * Beta_object + epsilon_i);
>
>     and then
>
>         poisson_log(Pixels[n], lambda[n]))
>
>     you can set
>
>         lambda <- log(Exposure) + X * ....
>
>     and then use:
>
>         poisson_log_log(Pixels[n], lambda[n])
>
>     The possion_log distribution takes its parameter on the log scale and does
>     the exponentiation implicitly inside, which is both more efficient and
>     more arithmetically stable.
>
>
> Thanks again, I'll try this out along with some of the other suggestions you've made. I really appreciate the help.

Hopefully someone like Michael or Matt or Andrew who understand the
parameterizations and their effects better than me will have other
suggestions.

As Andrew likes to point out, hard questions on mailing lists
get fewer answers because they take a lot longer for the devs to
figure out what's going on.

So if you can break the reparameterization down into a simple question,
you might have more luck getting an answer.

- Bob

Which of these are inputs and which are outputs?  And are the double* and int* arrays
or just single values?   And is the gparms struct just another bunch of double values?

This old-school C is very underspecified at the function level!

There is no notion of struct in Stan, so you'd have to pass in std::vector containers
with the values for sparms elements and for gparms elements and then create
the structs internally.

Then, sparm is going to have to be generalized so that all of the double
values are stan::agrad::var values.  And then any function that operates
on them is going to have to be generalized so that it deals with var
values appropriately.  We probably have most of the functions you need,
but if your C++ function is complicated, it's going to be a lot of work.

You can look at any of the built-in matrix functions in
stan/agrad/rev/matrix, though it'd probably be easiest to
start with stan/agrad/rev/functions, which just take
single inputs.

You can either template out the arguments or write them
for stan::agrad::var.  Either way, the inputs should be
constant references, either "const T&" or "const stan::agrad::var&".

The Stan language itself doesn't have any way of
taking mutable arguments that are set, so everything
has to be packed into a vector return.

Eventually, we will probably add R-style-lists/C-style-structs,
but it's not on our short-term to-do list (meaning it's
unlikely to be done in 2014).

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Sorry if this is somewhat off-topic. I am using Stan via RStan, and I
was wondering about the most convenient way to do posterior predictive
checks (eg the Gelman et al papers).

I have tried the following:

1. Generated quantities in Stan.

pro: easy to code, can usually copy-paste code from the model block with
little modification. if I am just looking at a few generated quantities
that I know in advance, this looks like the best way.

con: if I don't know what I am looking for, I either recompile and rerun
the model (relatively slow), or simulate _all_ the parameters and save
them (can be a huge blob in memory, but works OK for smaller models).

2. Simulation in R.

pro: also easy to code. flexible enough for experimentation with various
checks.

con: I have yet to find a clean, concise idiom for this. Loops are
messy, especially if the model itself has nested loops.

I have looked at the rv library [1] I did not find it convenient. Maybe
I am using it the wrong way?

[1] http://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/rv/

I was wondering if users of Stan on this list could share their way of
doing posterior predictive checks, possibly with example code. I am sure
I have a lot to learn that could simplify my work.

Best,

Tamas

Absolutely on topic.

> I have tried the following:
>
> 1. Generated quantities in Stan.
>
> pro: easy to code, can usually copy-paste code from the model block with
> little modification. if I am just looking at a few generated quantities

> con: I have yet to find a clean, concise idiom for this. Loops are
> messy, especially if the model itself has nested loops.

That's also a nice summary of the pros and cons.

The other two pros for doing it in Stan are (a) that there's no confusion
about parameterizations since our _rng functions and sampling
probability functions have the same parameterizations, and (b) it works
cross-platform (CmdStan, RStan, PyStan).

The third option would be to swap around the parameters and
generated quantities block.  The pro is that it's the easiest of
all the options, but the con is that you don't get independent
samples, just MCMC samples.  I'm about to drop the following into
the next version of the manual on just this topic:

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/485?source=cc#issuecomment-32600765

And I also plan to summarize the points you made (you'll see I added
them to the issue comment linked above).

- Bob

Thanks.

I don't think that it is possible to automate the generation of
posterior simulations (eg in a hierarchical model, maybe I just want to
simulate from a given level), so I would not insist on Stan being able
to do this by swapping parameters and data.

I am in favor of functional approaches, so ideally, I would prefer an R
function with the following syntax:

data_for_stan <- list(N_observations=nrow(something),...)
fit <- stan(...)
posterior <- extract(fit,permuted=TRUE)

map_data_frame(posterior,
               function(mu,sigma,...) {
                 ## simulate data
                 ...
                 ## summarize
                 list(p1=my_favorite_statistic(...),...)
               })

Ideally, map_data_frame would do the "right thing": slice up arrays
along the first dimension (so it can deal with a 3-dimensional array in
the data frame that is a simulated matrix, etc), call a function
matching the names to arguments, and then pack up the result as another
data_frame.

One could use such a function in two stages, too: first simulate, save
that, then calculate statistics on it.

I just don't know enough R wizardry to implement this. My main problem
is that AFAIK R does not allow vectors to have array elements, so
sub-arrays need to be extracted, then repacked.

Best,

Tamas

Hopefully Ben can jump in with some insight here.
Some comments below.

On 1/21/14, 3:42 AM, Nathan Lemoine wrote:
> I'm having trouble running a toy examples for multivariate regression. This stan code is:
>
> stanMod = """
> data{
>      int<lower = 0> N;
>      int<lower = 0> K;
>
>      vector[K] Y[N];
>      vector[N] D;
>
>      cov_matrix[K] R;
> }
>
> parameters{
>      vector[K] a;
>      vector[K] b;
>
>      cov_matrix[K] Omega;
> }
>
> transformed parameters{
>      vector[K] mu[N];
>
>      for(k in 1:K){
>          for(i in 1:N){
>              mu[i, k] <- a[k] + b[k] * D[i];
>          }
>      }
> }
>
> model{
>      for(i in 1:N){
>          Y[i] ~ multi_normal(mu[i], Omega);
>      }
>
>      Omega ~ inv_wishart(K+1, R);
> }
> """

We're no longer very keen on the inverse Wishart priors.
See this paper by Ben Goodrich et al.:

http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/unpublished/Visualization.pdf

But the model should still work.

>
> I get this warning:
>
> /Informational Message: The current Metropolis proposal is about to be rejected becuase of the following issue:/
> /Error in function stan::prob::inv_wishart_log(N4stan5agrad3varE): WW is not positive definite (7.3809879583185371e+71:0)./
> /If this warning occurs sporadically, such as for highly constrained variable types like covariance matrices, then the
> sampler is fine,/
> /but if this warning occurs often then your model may be either severely ill-conditioned or misspecified./

For what it's worth, that's *not* an error message.  We just
don't know how to make that point any clearer to users.  We don't
want to get rid of it as it's helpful, but we may have to in order
to stop freaking our users out about it.

The dump of the value is a mess here --- we really need to fix
that.  But that 7e71 seems to indicate that you're getting
huge values in the covariance matrix.

The key issue is:   does the error persist in most iterations?  If
so, there's a problem.

I think we need to lower our tolerance for positive definiteness
somehow.  We're using the Eigen built-ins to do this, and they're
very picky about what counts as positive definite.

> I'm not sure what I'm doing wrong, if this is the right way to parameterize it. This model works in JAGS so I thought
> I'd try porting it over to STAN. I've read other threads that suggest the problem is in the Omega (in particular the
> inv_wishart coming too close to not being positive definite for the covariance matrix). I've tried numerous things, such
> as changing Omega from a covariance matrix to a regular matrix (relaxing the requirement of positive definiteness I
> think).

No, you need to declare Omega as a covariance matrix.  In general,
the constraints on a parameter need to match its support in the model.

This error's coming from the multivariate normal distribution, not
from the parameter itself.

The model runs, but the chains do not converge at all. I've tried removing the multivariate response and
> changing the model to:
>
> for(i in 1:N){
>          for(k in 1:K){
>              Y[i, k] ~ normal(mu[i], stdev[k]);
>          }
>      }
>
> I still get an error message:
>

> /Informational Message: The current Metropolis proposal is about to be rejected becuase of the following issue:/
> /Error in function stan::prob::normal_log(N4stan5agrad3varE): Scale parameter is -3.364634555144618:0, but must be > 0!/
> /If this warning occurs sporadically, such as for highly constrained variable types like covariance matrices, then the
> sampler is fine,/
> /but if this warning occurs often then your model may be either severely ill-conditioned or misspecified./

>
> but the model runs and the chains do converge. I'm not crazy about this because a) I still get error messages,

See above.

b) I'm
> not modeling the covariance between response variables, which is preferable,

Right --- this one's the deal breaker.

> and c) the parameter estimates are just too
> similar (almost identical) for a[1]:a[2] and b[1]:b[2], so I'm not sure I trust it.

I'd recommend simulating data from the model and seeing
if you can recover the parameters.

> I've tried reparameterizing to the Cholesky decomposition as in the manual, but most examples I've found are for
> multivariate normal of parameters, not a response, and I'm pretty sure I did it wrong.

You can use the Cholesky decomposition on parameters.
It's just going in as an argument to the multivariate normal.

> Am I screwing something up?

Not that I can see from the model, but I don't know what your data
are like.  If the covariance really does involve terms on the scale of
7e71, there may be a problem with the data.

- Bob

Let me just say that I agree this would be a good idea.  I've long felt that it would be good to have a general template for posterior checking.  It should be are easy to check a model as to fit it.  I also think that there should be a way to automate the graphics (for example, histogram to show the distribution of a 1-D test statistic, scatterplot to show the distribution of a 2-D test statistic, parallel coordinate plots for 3 or more dimensions.
