On Jan 21, 2014, at 1:25 PM, Tamas Papp wrote:

>
> On Tue, Jan 21 2014, ca...@alias-i.com wrote:
>
>> On 1/21/14, 1:01 PM, Tamas Papp wrote:
>>> Hi,
>>>
>>> Sorry if this is somewhat off-topic.I am using Stan via RStan, and I
>>> was wondering about the most convenient way to do posterior predictive
>>> checks (eg the Gelman et al papers).
>>
>> Absolutely on topic.
>>
>>> I have tried the following:
>>>
>>> 1. Generated quantities in Stan.
>>>
>>> pro: easy to code, can usually copy-paste code from the model block with
>>> little modification. if I am just looking at a few generated quantities
>>> that I know in advance, this looks like the best way.
>>>
>>> con: if I don't know what I am looking for, I either recompile and rerun
>>> the model (relatively slow), or simulate _all_ the parameters and save
>>> them (can be a huge blob in memory, but works OK for smaller models).
>>>
>>> 2. Simulation in R.
>>>
>>> pro: also easy to code. flexible enough for experimentation with various
>>> checks.
>>>
>>> con: I have yet to find a clean, concise idiom for this. Loops are
>>> messy, especially if the model itself has nested loops.
>>
>> That's also a nice summary of the pros and cons.
>>
>> The other two pros for doing it in Stan are (a) that there's no confusion
>> about parameterizations since our _rng functions and sampling
>> probability functions have the same parameterizations, and (b) it works
>> cross-platform (CmdStan, RStan, PyStan).
>>
>> The third option would be to swap around the parameters and
>> generated quantities block.  The pro is that it's the easiest of
>> all the options, but the con is that you don't get independent
>> samples, just MCMC samples.  I'm about to drop the following into
>> the next version of the manual on just this topic:
>>
>> https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/485?source=cc#issuecomment-32600765
>>
>> And I also plan to summarize the points you made (you'll see I added
>> them to the issue comment linked above).
>
> Thanks.
>
> I don't think that it is possible to automate the generation of
> posterior simulations (eg in a hierarchical model, maybe I just want to
> simulate from a given level), so I would not insist on Stan being able
> to do this by swapping parameters and data.
>
> I am in favor of functional approaches, so ideally, I would prefer an R
> function with the following syntax:
>
> data_for_stan <- list(N_observations=nrow(something),...)
> fit <- stan(...)
> posterior <- extract(fit,permuted=TRUE)
>
> map_data_frame(posterior,
>               function(mu,sigma,...) {
>                 ## simulate data
>                 ...
>                 ## summarize
>                 list(p1=my_favorite_statistic(...),...)
>               })
>
> Ideally, map_data_frame would do the "right thing": slice up arrays
> along the first dimension (so it can deal with a 3-dimensional array in
> the data frame that is a simulated matrix, etc), call a function
> matching the names to arguments, and then pack up the result as another
> data_frame.
>
> One could use such a function in two stages, too: first simulate, save
> that, then calculate statistics on it.
>
> I just don't know enough R wizardry to implement this. My main problem
> is that AFAIK R does not allow vectors to have array elements, so
> sub-arrays need to be extracted, then repacked.
>
> Best,
>
> Tamas

messages.body_plain:
We expect to get these warnings, especially with highly
constrained models.  We can't seem to formulate text that
doesn't lead to these kinds of exchanges on the mailing list,
so I think it's probably best if we just get rid of them.

As warning message itself says, if they do not persist
they are not a problem.  In particular they do not affect
the detailed balance of the sampler --- they are just
indicators that there's a Metropolis rejection due to
constraint violations, which is itself due to discretization
of the Hamiltonian dynamics and limited floating-point
precision.

I think the large covariances are coming from the initializations.
I saw them in the simulation, too.  Even with a perfect
correlation, at convergencye, you'd only expect the posterior covariance
to be somewhere near the larger variance of the two variables.

- Bob

Hi Bob,

Thanks for the rewrite.

I'm implementing your rewrite now, which seems a more elegant way to the same end, so I do appreciate it.  It is still on the slow side however still - in spite of your elegance here.

The difficulty is, unfortunately, both in mixing and slow sampling.  I expected the mixing, which is the same in WINBUGS, just a lot of parameters with high auto-correlation.  However, slow sampling is what really concerns me in order to make running this kind of model viable.  My understanding is, to compensate for the proliferation of parameters in these types of models, I'll need to compensate with a larger burnin and sample (which seems to be a hallmark of most IRT models I've tried to run).

Thanks again.  I'll keep plugging/experimenting with different things.  I've tried to "vectorize" the response data to no avail thus far, and perhaps "categorical logit" may help me here?

Best,
Jason

On Tuesday, January 21, 2014 9:07:14 AM UTC-6, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>
>
> On 1/21/14, 3:33 PM, Jason Engle wrote:
>
> > I'm trying to translate a Nominal Response model (Bock 1972) from a working BUGS code that runs interminably slowly.
> > I've tried STAN with the same code, but the performance fares equally as poorly, if not worse,
>
> Is it mixing slowly or just running slowly per iteration?
> Speeding up the implementation won't help with the mixing.
> Often poor mixing arises because a model's not well identified.
>
> What you want to compare is time per effective sample, not
> time per iteration.   The number of effective samples you get out
> in the end is all that matters in terms of posterior inference.
> The residual error in estimating posterior means is reported
> as MCMC std error in Stan output, and that's just (estimated)
> posterior variance divided by the sqrt of the number of effective
> samples.
>
> > which leads me to suspect
> > I'm doing something suboptimal in the world of STAN, but have had no luck in figuring it out over the course of a day of
> > putzing.
>
> > My primary thought is that (from forums and such):
> >
> > resp[k,j]'~categorical(p[j,k]);
> >
> > should be done all at once as vectors.  That's fine, but I run across an error when I form it as resp'<-categorical(p):
> >
> > no matches for function name="transpose"
> >      arg 0 type=int[2]
> > available function signatures for transpose:
> > 0.  transpose(vector) : row vector
> > 1.  transpose(row vector) : vector
> > 2.  transpose(matrix) : matrix
> > expression is ill formed
>
> Stan's strongly typed and each function is very picky about
> the type of arguments it works on.  Your variable "resp"
> is a 2D integer array (i.e., int[2]), whereas the transpose
> operator (') only applies to vectors, row vectors, or matrices.
>
> I rewrote the model for you more efficiently.  To understand
> the changes, note that if x is a matrix then x[n] is a row
> vector, and look up the definition of categorical_logit, which
> will lead you to softmax.  You were implementing softmax yourself
> in code.  But using the correct parameterization of categorical
> will be much faster.  Also note that I vectorized the prior for z.
>
> And please check my work on the transforms
> to make sure that both I did it right and you understand what I did.
> (We should have a version of categorical_logit that takes a row vector
> as a parameter, and then you wouldn't need that final transposition.)
>
> You could definite temporaries for the argument to categorical_logit,
> but it's not necessary in Stan.
>
> - Bob
>
> data {
>    int N;
>    int T;
>    int NC;
>    int resp[T,N];
>    matrix[T,NC] lam;
> }
> parameters {
>    real theta[N];
>    real thetaN[T];
>    matrix[T,NC] z;
> }
> model {
>    theta ~ normal(0,1);
>    thetaN ~ normal(0,1);
>
>    for (t in 1:T)
>      z[t] ~ normal(0,1);
>
>    for (n in 1:N)
>      for (t in 1:T)
>        resp[t,n] ~ categorical_logit((z[t]
>                                       + lam[t] * fabs(theta[n] - thetaN[t]))');
> }
>
>

messages.body_plain:
I just came across this post and answer after searching through the STAN manual for info. I thought such an option might have been implemented for command line STAN since it appears to be implemented in RSTAN as the "schools" example seems to show - or am I misinterpreting this example?

For example, if we want to sample more iterations, we can proceed as follows.
fit2 <- stan(fit = fit1, data = schools_dat, iter = 10000, chains = 4)

On Tuesday, November 27, 2012 11:12:44 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> On 11/27/12 10:29 PM, Jeffrey Arnold wrote:
> > Sorry for resurrecting an old thread.  This question is probably due to my fuzzy understanding of HMC + NUTS.  My
> > understanding is that the warmup stage calculates the step_size and the step_size multipliers. Would it make sense to
> > allow for initial values of the step_size and the individual parameter step size multipliers? Or to allow for specifying
> > fixed step size multipliers,  something equivalent to the option --equal_step_sizes, but using an arbitrary mass
> > matrix?  "--epsilon=e --step_size_multipliers=1,1.5,2,0.5"?
>
> Absolutely.  It's on our to-do list.
>
> I'm not sure a command-line list is the way to go.  Some models
> have thousands of params and most OS-es put some kind of limit
> on the size of the command-line text.  So we probably want a file
> format.
>
> Technically, the current NUTS-II implementation in Stan uses
> varying step sizes per dimension, not a mass matrix.  Radford
> Neal discusses this in his MCMC handbook paper on HMC in section
> 5.4.2.4 <http://5.4.2.4>:
>
> http://www.mcmchandbook.net/HandbookChapter5.pdf
>
> A Columbia Stats Dept. grad student, Yuanjun Guo, is working on
> generalizing the adaptation from varying step sizes to full
> mass matrices.  At that point, the command-line's not going
> to be very workable for input.  And then we'll probably want
> to look at some low-rank approximations.
>
> We're also looking into doing Riemann Manifold HMC with
> a diagonal mass matrix, which would be fairly easy to
> compute (it needs third-order derivatives, but we could
> add that capability), and would completely get around
> trying to estimate a fixed mass matrix, which we know
> doesn't work well for distributions whose posterior
> covariance is position dependent.
>
> - Bob
>
> >
> >
> > On Sunday, November 18, 2012 5:06:52 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> >
> >
> >
> >
> >     On 11/18/12 4:47 PM, John Aponte wrote:
> >      > Is there any way to save the state of the simulations, to inspect the chains and later on continue without the
> >     need to
> >      > restart the simulations from the begining??
> >
> >     I'm afraid not.
> >
> >     There are two very different restart scenarios:
> >
> >         (a) the sampler hasn't converged
> >
> >         (b) the sampler has converged, but you need
> >             more effectife samples.
> >
> >     In the case of (a), we usually don't want to start
> >     where we left off, but rather let adaptation run
> >     long.  And that requires starting where adaptation
> >     left off, not at the last sample.
> >
> >     In case (b), it makes sense to restart from where you
> >     left off using the adaptation from the first run.
> >
> >     You lose at most a factor of two from starting again
> >     if you are doubling input sizes each time:
> >
> >         1K, 2K, 4K, 8K, 16K
> >
> >     vs. the number of samples if using restart:
> >
> >         1K, 1K, 2K, 4K, 8K
> >
> >     So it hasn't been a big priority for us compared to things
> >     like adding discrete samples and vectorizing auto dif
> >     calculations and making multivariate models more efficient.
> >
> >     The information on the adaptation is available as
> >     a comment in the command line version of Stan -- I don't
> >     know if it's available through RStan (yet).  But there's
> >     no good way yet to restart Stan in the post-adaptation phase
> >     with adaptation values from a previous run.
> >
> >     - Bob
> >
> >
> >
> > --
> >
> >

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] creating user defined (normal mean) function in C++
messages.body_plain:
This helps!  Thanks.

Alas, my tree growth function calls other user-written C functions, which call other user-written C functions…most of which make heavy use of gsl C library functions.  Instead of templafying “everything”, I am hoping to create a sort of wrapper for my “main” tree growth function, so that the wrapper assigns the values of stan::agrad::var typed parameters to standard types that subsequent functions can operate on without (much) further generalization.  Does this sound reasonably doable to you?

Best,

Jarrett

On Tuesday, January 21, 2014 1:52:36 PM UTC-7, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> Here’s an example.  Consider the function
>
> double f(double x1, double x2, double y1, double y2) {
>   double x_sum = x1 * x1 + x2 * x2;
>   double y_sum = y1 * y2;
>   return x_sum / y_sum;
> }
>
> where x1, x2 are parameters and y1, y2 are data.  You want to template the function as
>
> template <typename T>
> T f(T x1, T x2, double y1, double y2) {
>   T x_sum = x1 * x1 + x2 * x2;
>   double y_sum = y1 * y2;
>   return x_sum / y_sum;
> }
>
> Because *, +, and / are all defined for our autodiff variables you can then call
>
> double out = f<double>(x1, x2, y1, y2) [ calls regular version of code ]
> stan::a grad::var out = f<stan::agrad::var>(x1, x2, y1, y2) [ calls autodiff version ]
>
> You just have to be careful that you don’t use any functions or operations in the definition f
> that aren’t defined for out autodiff variables.
>
> On Jan 21, 2014, at 8:17 PM, Jarrett Barber <jarrett...@asu.edu> wrote:
>
> > To check my understanding so far:
> >
> > In short: template my functions and template my parameter arguments or, alternatively,  “classify” my parameters according to the stan::agrad::var hierarchy.  Other, non-parameter arguments (function data inputs or function outputs, even by reference) do not need to be generalized, correct? Parameters, other inputs and outputs should be done via std::vector that Stan creates when translating from Stan to C++, correct?
> >
> > Without a firmer grasp of these details, I would prefer to be as Stan-independent as possible to allow for running of my growth model outside of Stan, so this makes me want to choose _not_ to use the stan::agrad::var hierarchy but to use instead the template mechanism.
> >
> > Does this make sense?
> >
> > Best,
> >
> > Jarrett

messages.body_plain:
You either have to be able to template everything
else out or you have to be able to calculate
derivatives with respect to the parameters.  If you
can calculate derivatives, it's actually not that hard
to interface with the derivative code.  But presumably
that won't be easy if it's a nest of C calls.

Stan's not really defined to let you plug in arbitrary
functions.  Some other packages, such as emcee in Python
(which I haven't used) are better positioned to let you plug
in arbitrary probability functions.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Save the state of the simulations to inspect the chains and continue the simulations?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Save the state of the simulations to inspect the chains and continue the simulations?
messages.body_plain:
Using a previous fit just saves the compiled model.

It starts warmup again from scratch, so has to go through adaptation
of step size and mass matrix again.

RStan is nice in that it'll let you put a bunch of fit objects
together into a new one.

What we need is something that will save the state of adaptation
and let it be read back in again so we can keep running from where
we left off.  There's no way to read it back in at the moment,
and in CmdStan, the output is only in the form of comments in the
output csv file.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Andrew's always hung up the lexicon, even though
I'm the linguist in the group.

We haven't had any problem getting IRT models to mix
and sample well, even at large scale.

The best thing you can do if the model's not well
identified (often the problem with correlated parameters)
is come up with some kind of reparameterization that is
well identified.  But keep in mind it has to be well
identified on the unconstrained scale for really
optimal behavior, though you can often get better mixing
in practice if you just define some transformed parameters
or generated quantities of interest that are identified.

Our multivariate distributions like categorical_logit
aren't vectorized, so you're not going to have luck
there.  The categorical_logit will should make things a lot
faster compared to your computing softmax yourself in
Stan code --- it precomputes all the derivatives rather
than figuring them all out with the chain rule at run time.
The other vectorization shouldn't make much of a difference
other than simplifying the code.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] recommended workflow for posterior predictive checks (maybe in R/Rstan)
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] recommended workflow for posterior predictive checks (maybe in R/Rstan)
messages.body_plain:
Hi Andrew,

For graphical posterior predictive checks, I am using something like
this (uses libraries lattice and latticeExtra, does not handle 3d but
that would be easy to add):

--8<---------------cut here---------------start------------->8---
comparisonplot <- function(xdata, xpred, main="Posterior predictive check", sub=NULL, ...) {
  ## Return a trellis plot for graphical posterior predictive
  ## checks. Type is automatically selected based on the dimensions of
  ## xdata. For stochastic predicted data, uses hexbin plots, with a
  ## LOESS smoother line.
  range <- extendrange(c(xdata,xpred),f=0.05)
  if (is.null(sub))
    sub <- sprintf("P(data <= predicted)=%.2f", mean(xdata <= xpred))
  if (length(xdata)==1) {
    histogram(xpred,
              main=main,
              sub=sub,
              panel=function(...) {
                panel.histogram(...)
                panel.abline(v=xdata,col="black",lty=2,lwd=2)
                panel.abline(v=mean(xpred),col="red",lty=2,lwd=2)
              },
              xlim=range,
              ...)
  } else if (length(xpred)==length(xdata)) {
    hexbinplot(xpred ~ xdata,
               main=main,
               sub=sub,
               panel=function(...) {
                 panel.hexbinplot(...)
                 panel.abline(a=0,b=1)
                 panel.loess(...,col="red",lty=2,lwd=2)
               },
               xlim=range, ylim=range, aspect="iso")
  } else {
    stop("possible dimension mismatch")
  }
}
--8<---------------cut here---------------end--------------->8---

Example:

--8<---------------cut here---------------start------------->8---
comparisonplot(0,rnorm(100,mean=-3))
comparisonplot(rnorm(100),rnorm(100,mean=-1))
--8<---------------cut here---------------end--------------->8---

Obviously, it can be made much fancier (automatic variable names etc).

Best,

Tamas

I also think that there should be a way to automate the graphics (for example, histogram to show the distribution of a 1-D test statistic, scatterplot to show the distribution of a 2-D test statistic, parallel coordinate plots for 3 or more dimensions.

>> On Tue, Jan 21 2014, ca...@alias-i.com wrote:
>>
>>> On 1/21/14, 1:01 PM, Tamas Papp wrote:
>>>> Hi,
>>>>
>>>> Sorry if this is somewhat off-topic.I am using Stan via RStan, and I
>>>> was wondering about the most convenient way to do posterior predictive
>>>> checks (eg the Gelman et al papers).
>>>
>>> Absolutely on topic.
>>>
>>>> I have tried the following:
>>>>
>>>> 1. Generated quantities in Stan.
>>>>
>>>> pro: easy to code, can usually copy-paste code from the model block with
>>>> little modification. if I am just looking at a few generated quantities
>>>> that I know in advance, this looks like the best way.
>>>>
>>>> con: if I don't know what I am looking for, I either recompile and rerun
>>>> the model (relatively slow), or simulate _all_ the parameters and save
>>>> them (can be a huge blob in memory, but works OK for smaller models).
>>>>
>>>> 2. Simulation in R.
>>>>
>>>> pro: also easy to code. flexible enough for experimentation with various
>>>> checks.
>>>>
>>>> con: I have yet to find a clean, concise idiom for this. Loops are
>>>> messy, especially if the model itself has nested loops.
>>>
>>> That's also a nice summary of the pros and cons.
>>>
>>> The other two pros for doing it in Stan are (a) that there's no confusion
>>> about parameterizations since our _rng functions and sampling
>>> probability functions have the same parameterizations, and (b) it works
>>> cross-platform (CmdStan, RStan, PyStan).
>>>
>>> The third option would be to swap around the parameters and
>>> generated quantities block.  The pro is that it's the easiest of
>>> all the options, but the con is that you don't get independent
>>> samples, just MCMC samples.  I'm about to drop the following into
>>> the next version of the manual on just this topic:
>>>
>>> https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/485?source=cc#issuecomment-32600765
>>>
>>> And I also plan to summarize the points you made (you'll see I added
>>> them to the issue comment linked above).
>>
>> Thanks.
>>
>> I don't think that it is possible to automate the generation of
>> posterior simulations (eg in a hierarchical model, maybe I just want to
>> simulate from a given level), so I would not insist on Stan being able
>> to do this by swapping parameters and data.
>>
>> I am in favor of functional approaches, so ideally, I would prefer an R
>> function with the following syntax:
>>
>> data_for_stan <- list(N_observations=nrow(something),...)
>> fit <- stan(...)
>> posterior <- extract(fit,permuted=TRUE)
>>
>> map_data_frame(posterior,
>>               function(mu,sigma,...) {
>>                 ## simulate data
>>                 ...
>>                 ## summarize
>>                 list(p1=my_favorite_statistic(...),...)
>>               })
>>
>> Ideally, map_data_frame would do the "right thing": slice up arrays
>> along the first dimension (so it can deal with a 3-dimensional array in
>> the data frame that is a simulated matrix, etc), call a function
>> matching the names to arguments, and then pack up the result as another
>> data_frame.
>>
>> One could use such a function in two stages, too: first simulate, save
>> that, then calculate statistics on it.
>>
>> I just don't know enough R wizardry to implement this. My main problem
>> is that AFAIK R does not allow vectors to have array elements, so
>> sub-arrays need to be extracted, then repacked.
>>
>> Best,
>>
>> Tamas

messages.body_plain:
Hi

I am working on a problem where the model with which I'm trying perform inference is very complicated. In brief, the model describes the spatial variation of a measurable quantity over three (though possibly more) dimensions, and the model itself can be though of as being piecewise, with very many pieces. While I think Stan has the necessary functions and control structures to implement the model, the model file would be quite horrific to read. That is, of course, unless it's possible to define functions within the Stan language; from reading the manual, it doesn't seem like this is possible (am I wrong?).

What options are available to me if I want to use Stan? Can I define my own functions within the Stan language? Can I do so (sanely) by writing some kind of extension in C++?

Thanks in advance,

— Chris

messages.body_plain:
There's been a lot of discussion on this list recently about
what you need to do to interface a C++ function to Stan.

Short answer:  If you can write a C++ function where parameters
are instantiated as stan::agrad::var and data as double/int
depending on type, then you can interface pretty easily.

This means all routines acting on parameters need to also be
defined for stan::agrad::var.  You can use our stan::math and
stan::agrad and stan::prob libs, but it's usually a lot of work.

- Bob

>>>>
>>>>> I have tried the following:
>>>>>
>>>>> 1. Generated quantities in Stan.
>>>>>

messages.body_plain:
After looking at some of the function definitions in the C++ (Stan) source code, and recalling the introductory discussion in the Stan Manual about analytic derivatives, I now understand the main reason for templating (analytic derivatives).  It seems silly now that I could have somehow (implicitly) considered that numerical differentiation could be used and still result in the speediness of Stan.

It does appear that the Stan C++ library does provide all of the functions that I will need to revise my (my colleague's really) tree growth model code.  Encouraging.  But, after my realization of analytic derivatives, I began to think of the chain rule, which, in my case, quickly reminded me that one of the output quantities in my growth model is defined implicitly as the result of a root-finding routine: find the tree radius such that an expression of tree size (allometry) equals an expression of carbon allocation, else risk getting a grossly misproportioned and dysfunctional tree.  Of course, these size and allocation expressions are functions of parameters to be sampled.  (I intend that the tree radius provided by my model to be essentially the mean of a normal distribution specified in Stan language, hence the connection to gradients of the log-posterior.)  More precisely, I have functions f(radius, parameters) and g(radius, parameters), and radius is defined implicitly as the solution to f(radius, parameters) = g(radius, parameters), and f and g are otherwise fairly simple.

Differentiation (wrt parameters) for my implicitly defined tree radius is no problem on paper (Implicit Function Theorem) (I haven't actually done this yet, but I expect this to be no problem, on paper, because my equations are relatively simple.)  But, my lack of experience in C++/Stan innards leaves me wondering: will I be able to exploit a relatively high-level solution using templates, as we have been discussing, or do I have to dig down and "calculate derivatives" and "interface with the derivative code" as Bob suggests?

Anyway, responses are appreciated.  I hope someone finds this discussion at least mildly interesting and useful.

BTW, have been using my own MH MCMC routine for sampling a small subset of parameters, but I anticipate problems in the future as I try to sample a larger number of parameters, use larger data sets, and make model extensions.  I think HMC might be one way to help with anticipated problems, and I think Stan might save me from reinventing the wheel.

Best,

Jarrett

messages.body_plain:
There are several ways you can identify a model like this.
But they'll all be pretty ugly to code in Stan as is.

What we really need is a mean_zero vector data type (a K-vector
gets K-1 free parameters).  And a first_element_zero vector data type
(also K-1 free params).  In the meantime...

One approach is to define each row as a scaled and offset
simplex:

parameters {
   simplex[NC] z_raw[T];
   real<lower=0> z_scale[T];
   ...
}
transformed parameters {
   matrix[T,NC] z;
   ...

   for (t in 1:T)

     z[t] <- z_scale[t] * (z_raw[t] - 1.0 / T);

   ...
}

This lets the z be anything but insures each z[t] sums to 0.
You then want to define priors on the z_raw (perhaps uniform)
and on the z_scale (whatever makes sense).

The other standard approach is to fix one of the values in each
row, such as z[t,1] == 0.  To do this, you need to define (NC-1)-vectors
that are free, then put them back together in z.  Not very pretty.
And also asymmetric in terms of the priors.

To constrain the sign of just one entry in an M-vector, you have
to define it like this:

parameters {
   vector[M-1] a2_M;
   real<lower=0> a1;
}
transformed parameters {
   vector[M] a;
   a[1] <- a1;
   for (m in 2:M)
     a[m] <- a2_M[m-1];
}

File this under "stupid Stan tricks" :-)

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Implementing complicated models (defining custom functions?)
messages.body_plain:
Hi Chris,

The short answer is that no, you can't define custom functions easily in Stan.  If you're willing to hack the C++ (as Bob alluded to) you can add your own functions that way.  At a really high level, how to do this is described here: https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/wiki/Contributing-New-Functions-to-Stan  If you only wanted the function for yourself (i.e., not planning to submit it to the main repository), you can skip all the testing.

What you seemed mostly to be asking about was a way, in a Stan model file, to define a new function in the Stan modelling language.  This is not possible right now but is something we've talked about adding since Stan was first released.

That said, if you're willing to use the C preprocessor yourself, there is a way you can do this in your own.  Basically, use C preprocessor macros in a file, lets say called foo.stancp

#define FOOFUNC(a,sigma) a ~ normal(0,sigma)

model {
  FOOFUNC(x,sigma1);
  FOOFUNC(y,sigma1+sigma2);
...
}

and then, when you're building the model using CmdStan, call:

> cpp foo.stancp foo.stan
> stanc foo.stan

Where the first call uses the C preprocessor on it's own.  If you're using RStan or PyStan this is still possible, but would be a little more complicated.

Cheers,
Marcus

Bob,
I've been having this warning since transitioning to the latest version of Stan. Maybe not necessarily removing it, but having different levels of warnings displayed might be helpful (like Matlab's fmincon has a display variable that you can adjust to display increasing levels of details about an optimization).

Anyway, I had been using the following code (based on a thread from January of last year):

//For testing, I had set S_prior to the identity matrix, V_prior to S_prior times 100, and nu_prior to N.
data {
  int<lower=0> N; //# of variables
  int<lower=0> T; //# of observations
  vector[N] y[T]; //data, formatted as NxT
  vector[N] mu_prior;  //prior on mean
  cov_matrix[N] V_prior; //prior uncertainty on mean
  cov_matrix[N] S_prior; //prior on covariance
  int<lower=0> nu_prior; //prior degrees of freedom for covariance
}
transformed data {
  matrix[N, N] L_V_prior; //Haven't had any luck getting cholesky_factor_cov[N] working
  matrix[N, N] L_S_prior;
  matrix[N, N] inv_L_S_prior;
  int<lower=0> nu_post;

  L_V_prior <- cholesky_decompose(V_prior);
  L_S_prior <- cholesky_decompose(S_prior);
  inv_L_S_prior <- inverse(L_S_prior);
  nu_post <- T + nu_prior;
}
parameters {
  vector[N] mu;
  cov_matrix[N] sigma;
}
transformed parameters {
  matrix[N, N] L_sigma;

  sigma ~ inv_wishart(nu_post, inv_L_S_prior' * inv_L_S_prior);
  for (t in 1:T) {
    y[t] ~ multi_normal_cholesky(mu, L_sigma);
  }
}

You suggest not using the inverse Wishart, but still using the Cholesky. I was able to change the end to

  vector[N] mu;
  cov_matrix[N] inv_sigma;
}
transformed parameters {
  matrix[N, N] L_inv_sigma;
  L_inv_sigma <- cholesky_decompose(inv_sigma);
}
model {
  mu ~ multi_normal_cholesky(mu_prior, L_V_prior);
  inv_sigma ~ wishart(nu_post, L_S_prior * L_S_prior');
  for (t in 1:T) {
    y[t] ~ multi_normal_prec(mu, L_inv_sigma * L_inv_sigma');
  }
}

and get approximately what I was getting with the original code (I had also tried with just inv_sigma in the multi_normal_prec statement). However, this version is pretty slow since it's using multi_normal_prec instead of multi_normal_cholesky. I wasn't able to get multi_normal_cholesky working when converting inv_sigma back to sigma and then L_sigma.

Any tips? Or general best practices advice for this type of model?

messages.body_plain:
There's also the post processing trick, which goes as follows:

Suppose you have parameters theta_1,…,theta_J whose overall level is nonidentified jointly with some other parameter.  For example, there is a term in the model, mu + theta_j, and the likelihood is unchanged if you add a const to mu and subtract that const from the vector theta.

You get identification in two steps:
(1) Assign weak priors to the theta_j's, just so they have a proper posterior.  For example, independent normal priors with mean 0 and scale 10.
(2) Create derived parameters:
mu.adj <- mu + mean(theta)
theta.adj_j <- theta_j - mean(theta).
You run the HMC on (mu,theta), but you save and monitor convergence of (mu.adj, theta.adj).
This is what we call the additive redundant parameterization in the ARM book.

Ideally this could be done in a more automatic way (I think this might be what Bob is saying when he is talking about a mean_zero vector data type). As it is, it's a bit of a hack because you have to define these additive parameters manually.  But it can work.

> (also K-1 free params).  In the meantime...

> One approach is to define each row as a scaled and offset
> simplex:
>
> parameters {
>  simplex[NC] z_raw[T];
>  real<lower=0> z_scale[T];
>  ...
> }

>  matrix[T,NC] z;
>  ...

>    z[t] <- z_scale[t] * (z_raw[t] - 1.0 / T);
>
>  ...

>

Continued thanks to Bob and Michael for kindly guiding me toward to a solution.

I’m trying to reconcile Michael’s comments, “It is possible to automatically differentiate these kinds of solutions, by either explicitly differentiating the root finder or appealing to the things like the Implicit Function Theorem” with, in an earlier post, “It is possible but would require adding a new var implementation which requires a much deeper understanding of the inner workings of the autodiff code.”  (Perhaps I mistakenly conflate these 2 posts.)

Selfishly assuming that I’m only looking for a solution to my particular problem at the moment, I may use implicit differentiation to get the derivative of my implicit function.  A more careful (considering existence, multiple implicit functions, etc.) approach for more a more general solution of cases with implicit functions may have to appeal to the Implicit Function Theorem (or related), along with a much more ambitious code effort.  But I think I may get by for now with the derivative obtained by implicit differentiation for my particular case.

So, I have (“…explicitly…”, as I take Michael to mean) the analytic derivative in hand.  Then, I must implement “…via a new var implementation…then implement the chainable method in the corresponding vari”.  Once I do this, then, as Michael says, I can “…automatically differentiate…”.  Yes?

Am I missing a possibly more “automatic”, high-level approach that doesn’t require entering the innards of var and vari and the chainable method?

And, yes, I do anticipate huge differences going forward (and Stan's cool), hence my persistence in spite of revealing my neophyte level of C++ know-how. (I can see the power of generalization, but I’m still devising my coup.)

I’ll keep in mind Bob’s suggestion about finite differences.

Somewhat gropingly,

Jarrett

smaller dimension as we do for simplices and covariance matrices.  Actually, if all you
need is for the sum to be zero then why not just use a simplex (n variables constrained
to sum to 1) and then subtract one?

> So, I have (“…explicitly…”, as I take Michael to mean) the analytic derivative in hand.  Then, I must implement “…via a new var implementation…then implement the chainable method in the corresponding vari”.  Once I do this, then, as Michael says, I can “…automatically differentiate…”.  Yes?

Correct, not that it’s an easy task — it took me a while to get my head around our implementation in order to do things like this myself.  We can help you through it if you want to push forward.

Autodiff really just computes the chain rule automatically — it has no idea how to compute partial derivatives, so what our autodiff library does is define partial derivatives for most of the useful functions out there.  If you want to add a new function then you have to tell Stan its partials.

You need to subtract 1 total, so to do that symmetrically, you'd subtract 1.0 / N
from each of the N entries.  (Be sure not to use 1/N, as that'll round to 0
given the way integer arithmetic works.)

>>>>>          >>     time per iteration.   The number of effective samples you get out

But if you subtract 1.0/N from each, they won't all be positive.  You need
to then scale by a positive-constrained variable to get an arbitrary vector that
sums to 1.  So to get a transformed parameter theta that sums to 1 in a way
that's well identified, you can do this:

parameters {
   simplex[N] theta_raw;
   real<lower=0> theta_scale;
   ...
}
transformed parameters {
   vector[N] theta;
   theta <- theta_scale * (theta_raw - 1.0 / N);
   ...

I'm having a deja vu moment, having just written this in response
to another message today or yesterday.

You then need a prior on theta_scale.

I'm still a little confused here, because this doesn't seem
over-parameterized, yet there are N free parameters, whereas
a vector that sums to 0 should really only have (N-1) free
parameters.  Am I missing something here?

- Bob

Congratuatlions, it's the 2^9-th issue :-)

> Anyway, I had been using the following code (based on a thread from January of last year):

> data {

>    matrix[N, N] L_S_prior;

>    int<lower=0> nu_post;

>    L_V_prior <- cholesky_decompose(V_prior);
>    L_S_prior <- cholesky_decompose(S_prior);
>    inv_L_S_prior <- inverse(L_S_prior);
>    nu_post <- T + nu_prior;
> }
> parameters {
>    vector[N] mu;
>    cov_matrix[N] sigma;
> }
> transformed parameters {
>    matrix[N, N] L_sigma;
>    L_sigma <- cholesky_decompose(sigma);
> }
> model {
>    mu ~ multi_normal_cholesky(mu_prior, L_V_prior);
>    sigma ~ inv_wishart(nu_post, inv_L_S_prior' * inv_L_S_prior);
>    for (t in 1:T) {
>      y[t] ~ multi_normal_cholesky(mu, L_sigma);
>    }
> }
>
> You suggest not using the inverse Wishart, but still using the Cholesky. I was able to change the end to
>
> parameters {
>    vector[N] mu;
>    cov_matrix[N] inv_sigma;
> }
> transformed parameters {
>    matrix[N, N] L_inv_sigma;
>    L_inv_sigma <- cholesky_decompose(inv_sigma);
> }
> model {
>    mu ~ multi_normal_cholesky(mu_prior, L_V_prior);
>    inv_sigma ~ wishart(nu_post, L_S_prior * L_S_prior');
>    for (t in 1:T) {
>      y[t] ~ multi_normal_prec(mu, L_inv_sigma * L_inv_sigma');
>    }
> }
>
> and get approximately what I was getting with the original code (I had also tried with just inv_sigma in the
> multi_normal_prec statement). However, this version is pretty slow since it's using multi_normal_prec instead of
> multi_normal_cholesky. I wasn't able to get multi_normal_cholesky working when converting inv_sigma back to sigma and
> then L_sigma.
>
> Any tips? Or general best practices advice for this type of model?

We keep improving the way we handle this, but we're not quite
to where we want to be yet.

I'd recommend scaling a correlation matrix.  Give the correlation_matrix
an lkj_correlation prior, see the doc.  Then you can use the same
kind of priors you'd use for any scale parameter for the scales.

We're about to roll out 2.2.0 (I think we're bypassing 2.1.1), and
it has diag_pre_multiply and diag_post_multiply
functions which can be used to neatly scale.

So it'd be:

parameters {
   corr_matrix[N] Omega;
   vector<lower=0> sigma;
}
transformed parameters {
   cholesky_factor_cov[N] L;
   L <- cholesky_decompose(Omega);
   for (i in 1:N)
     for (j in 1:i)
       L[i,j] <- L[i,j] * sigma[i];
}
model {
    Omega ~ lkj_corr(nu);  // nu controls concentration around unit
    sigma ~ ... whatever you like for scales ...;
    ...

I'll drop a section on this into the next manual
release.

We're going to introduce a correlation matrix Cholesky
factor type which should be more efficient, but have the
same effect as the above.

For a discussion and a link to Ben's paper, see

   http://andrewgelman.com/2012/08/30/visualizing-distributions-of-covariance-matrices/

- Bob

Thanks for the quick reply. I remember something like that in the manual; I'll give that a try when I have some time. The only thing I'm not sure on with this approach is if there will ever be a meaningful correlation between the sigmas when you do it that way (assume for instance you use a inverse gamma). If you do the estimation with the inverse Wishart, it might be that if you plot the posterior for two variances they are correlated. I have actually tried something similar in a Gibbs sampling approach but since each inverse gamma draw was independent it took out the correlations in the variances.

Also, if you're going to recommend working with the correlation matrices, it seems like a next step would be to consider working with copulas. If the multivariate dependence were set up with copulas (even a normal copula), then it presumably would be easier to switch from normal marginals to a t marginal, or assume a constant dependence with stochastic volatility.

On a separate note (not to bog you guys down with too many issues), while the extract function can allow you to only select certain outputs, my understanding is that the stan function simulates every parameter and transformed parameter (and generated quantities) from a .stan file. However, I may not always need to output all the transformed parameters (and generated quantities). In the above example, I may not really need to output the simulated stochastic volatility of each series in each point in time. As the number of variables or length of the series increases, it may cause memory issues on less powerful machines. Similarly, it might be convenient if you could input the output of a previous stan function call and then output whichever other transformed parameters or generated quantities you may need. In that example, it would be like fitting the model with one stan call and outputting only some of the parameters, then calling the stan function again to calculate the posterior predictive given the previous call. This way you wouldn't calculate the generated quantities unless you need them and you don't have to rely on separate stan files (one with generated quantities, one without) when testing.

> The only thing I'm not sure on with this approach is if there will ever be a meaningful correlation between the sigmas
> when you do it that way (assume for instance you use a inverse gamma). If you do the estimation with the inverse
> Wishart, it might be that if you plot the posterior for two variances they are correlated. I have actually tried
> something similar in a Gibbs sampling approach but since each inverse gamma draw was independent it took out the
> correlations in the variances.

That's really two issues.

1.  The LKJ prior still allows correlations.  You can
make it uniform on the correlation matrix.  Or you
can create a prior with more probability mass around
the identity correlation matrix.

2.  Gibbs sampling has a lot of trouble with the multivariate
priors because of the correlations --- it basically takes
forever to converge to the correct posterior.  You'll find HMC
does much better with this.

> Also, if you're going to recommend working with the correlation matrices, it seems like a next step would be to consider
> working with copulas. If the multivariate dependence were set up with copulas (even a normal copula), then it presumably
> would be easier to switch from normal marginals to a t marginal, or assume a constant dependence with stochastic volatility.

I've heard of copulas, but don't understand them.  Is there
a simple reference for the constraints on parameters and densities
involved?  If it's a fixed number of parameters --- that is, it's
not a non-parametric method like Dirichlet processes --- then we
should be able to code it in Stan.  Either in the Stan modeling
language or in the underlying C++ --- the latter is more efficient
and stable.

> On a separate note (not to bog you guys down with too many issues), while the extract function can allow you to only
> select certain outputs, my understanding is that the stan function simulates every parameter and transformed parameter
> (and generated quantities) from a .stan file. However, I may not always need to output all the transformed parameters
> (and generated quantities). In the above example, I may not really need to output the simulated stochastic volatility of
> each series in each point in time. As the number of variables or length of the series increases, it may cause memory
> issues on less powerful machines.

You can write the output to files so you won't blow out during sampling,
but then the posterior analysis can be a problem.

That's already on our to-do list.  It's not an immediate priority,
but we'll get to it eventually.

It's similar to the BUGS/JAGS monitor specification.

> Similarly, it might be convenient if you could input the output of a previous stan
> function call and then output whichever other transformed parameters or generated quantities you may need.

That's another very good idea.  It would force us to modularize the generated
model code a bit to support it, but the underlying code generator
is already modularized that way.

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/513

We've also been thinking about issues like that in order to do posterior
predictive checks more seamlessly.

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Trouble with Multivariate Regression
messages.body_plain:
Here are some references (the first is a more gentle introduction, the file is below the cached heading):
http://citeseerx.ist.psu.edu/viewdoc/summary?doi=10.1.1.160.8266
Nelson's "An Introduction to Copulas" is a popular reference that you could find at an academic library
http://arxiv.org/abs/1112.4204

Copulas are the multivariate dependence in a joint distribution. Sklar's theorem is the most important result, which says that any joint distribution can be expressed as some univariate distributions times the copula. The benefit of this approach is that you can model the univariate marginal distributions separately from the multivariate dependence. As such, copula estimation often requires the inverse pdf for the marginals, which might be one barrier to implementing them in Stan presently (I didn't see inverse pdfs in the manual).

I used student t marginals and a normal copula as a good example above of why copulas are helpful. Basically, if you were to instead fit a multivariate student t distribution, then you effectively assume the degrees of freedom parameter is the same across every variable. The student t + normal copula would often be fit by first fitting each of the variables with a student t distribution with each having its own degrees of freedom. Then you would create a new multivariate variable applying the appropriate student t inverse pdf to each variable. This puts each variable between 0 and 1. To fit the normal copula to this, I might apply a standard normal cdf to that and estimate the resulting correlation matrix.

Hi Bob (and all),

Just an update. The workaround:

parameters {
   simplex[N] theta_raw;
   real<lower=0> theta_scale;
   ...
}
transformed parameters {
   vector[N] theta;
   theta <- theta_scale * (theta_raw - 1.0 / N);
   ...

it works.

That is, it (a) accomplishes sampling speed that this model was unable to attain in BUGS and (b) ceases to reverse scale intermittently.

Yet, exactly as it does in BUGS, the samples meander.  The parameters are plausible after a hefty sample, but, as I understand, it may require a much larger sample to produce a high enough "effective sample".  Being able to be confident of convergence may be another matter as well.  Maybe the correlation of "z" may not be something that's easily overcome.

As for setting multiple category (NC-1) vectors and sett the first of the series to "0", I have not been successful - but given the volume of code, it may be my own error.  "Warmup" seems to sample correctly, and then when it gets to "sampling", it samples the same values over and over.

So, I'll keep working that option as well intermittently.

Again, thanks.  All this is not to say that this isn't possible.  By all accounts it should be with some coaxing.

Best,
Jason

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] lognormal clarification
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] lognormal clarification
messages.body_plain:
On 1/25/14, 2:51 AM, Devin Caughey wrote:
> Hello all,
>
> I have a quick clarification question. The manual's discussion of changes of variables and manually adjusting the log
> probability uses the example of a log normal distribution parameterized as log(y) ~ normal(mu, sigma). However, a
> footnote on pg. 149 recommends using the lognormal probability function instead, as in: y ~ lognormal(mu, sigma). Is it
> also necessary to increment the log probability manually when using the lognormal function?

No.  The only time you need to do a Jacobian adjustment
is when the left-hand side of a "~" involves parameters to which
you've applied a non-linear change of variables.

If y is a parameter or transformed parameter or local variable that
depends on a parameter, then you need it with

  log(y) ~ normal(mu, sigma);

If y is just data or transformed data, you don't need the adjustment.

Also, you never need an adjustment with

   y ~ lognormal(mu,sigma);

if y is a parameter.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] help with identifying centered parameterization
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] help with identifying centered parameterization
messages.body_plain:
> Could someone who understands identification a bit better
> than me help out in figuring out which of the two proposals
> below lead to an identified parameterization of a centered
> vector on the unconstrained scale?

Neither and both?  The problem is that there are an infinite number of
ways to map between the unconstrained space and the constrained space.
More formally, the unconstrained space is an affine subspace of the
constrained space, i.e. the unconstrained space decomposes into
an origin and a plane.

Now given any transformation we can always rotate and scale to obtain a new,
equally valid transformation.  Moreover there will be combinatorial symmetry
in decided which unconstrained point is interpreted as the “origin”.

> Proposal A:
>
>  parameters {
>    simplex[K] beta_ratios;
>    real<lower=0> beta_scale;
>    ...
>  transformed parameters {
>    vector[K] beta;
>    ...
>    beta <- beta_scale * (beta_ratios - (1.0 / K));

First thing, the simplex won’t work here because it assumes n _positive_ variables
that sum to 1, not n unconstrained variables.

Second thing, the beta_scale is not necessary.  It just indexes many of the possible
transformations you could have (by the scaling noted above) but should not be
interpreted as a parameter.  In other words, beta_scale is a constant.

> Proposal B:
>
> parameters {
>    vector[K-1] beta_prefix;
>    ...
>  }
>  transformed parameters {
>    vector[K] beta;
>    ...
>    for (k in 1:(K-1))
>      beta[k] <- beta_prefix[k];
>    beta[K] <- - sum(beta_prefix);

>    …

The problem here is not that the transformation is invalid, but rather a uniform distribution
on the unconstrained space is not a uniform distribution on the constrained space, and
vice-versa.

Unfortunately there’s no way to define a truly symmetric transformation — one of the
constrained variables will always have to be the origin which will distinguish it from
the others.  You can try to marginalize over all the possible assignments, but then
you have to deal with the Jacobian being a sum of terms (that you would have to
compute before taking the log).  Not fun.

Anyways, it’s easy to go from constrained to unconstrained, but trying to go from
unconstrained to constrained will always break the symmetry.  As far as I can tell.

The (beta_ratios - 1.0 / K) is constrained to have absolute values

In this particular case, we're going to put a prior on the parameters, not
on the transformed parameters.  That's what I meant by it being a bit odd
because of the asymmetry.

>
> Unfortunately there’s no way to define a truly symmetric transformation — one of the
> constrained variables will always have to be the origin which will distinguish it from
> the others.  You can try to marginalize over all the possible assignments, but then
> you have to deal with the Jacobian being a sum of terms (that you would have to
> compute before taking the log).  Not fun.
>
> Anyways, it’s easy to go from constrained to unconstrained, but trying to go from
> unconstrained to constrained will always break the symmetry.  As far as I can tell.

I think that's right unless we want to apply the Jacobian adjustment.
Then we could put the prior on beta and we'd be back to what I meant
by symmetric in that you could put a prior on each of the beta[k] for
k in 1:K.

messages.body_plain:
> By identified here, I really just meant are there different
> values of the parameters that lead to the same transformed parameter
> vector?

Yes, I know.  Let me try again.

In general we have a constrained space, C, and an unconstrained space, U.
Now in many cases there is a canonical isomorphism between C and U,
for example with the simplex.

In this case, however, there is no canonical transformation; rather there is
an infinite family of equivalent transformations.  Pick any one and you can map
the constrained space to an unconstrained space where the system is
identified.

With beta_scale you’re trying to parameterize the transformations — but
you don’t need to do that.  You only need to pick out one of them.

> Although the simplex is constrained to positive
> values that sums to 1, (beta_ratios - 1.0 / K) is
> a set of values that sums to 0 and whose absolute
> values sum to 1.  It's only going to be non-negative
> in the symmetric case.
>
> For example, if you look at the simplex (0.3, 0.7),
> then (0.3, 0.7) - 0.5 = (-0.2, 0.2).

Yes, they can be negative but only so much.  The resulting beta have
support on (-1/K, infinity), not (-infinty, infinity).

> In this particular case, we're going to put a prior on the parameters, not
> on the transformed parameters.  That's what I meant by it being a bit odd
> because of the asymmetry.

Right.  But because there’s no canonical transformation between the
constrained and unconstrained space this may not be the best idea.
Unless you’re careful to define an asymmetric prior so that the resulting
prior on the constrained scale is symmetric.

>> Neither and both?  The problem is that there are an infinite number of
>> ways to map between the unconstrained space and the constrained space.
>> More formally, the unconstrained space is an affine subspace of the
>> constrained space, i.e. the unconstrained space decomposes into
>> an origin and a plane.
>>
>> Now given any transformation we can always rotate and scale to obtain a new,
>> equally valid transformation.  Moreover there will be combinatorial symmetry
>> in decided which unconstrained point is interpreted as the “origin”.
>
> By identified here, I really just meant are there different
> values of the parameters that lead to the same transformed parameter
> vector?
>
> If you are building something like an IRT model and require one
> set of coefficients to have mean 0, it identifies the model as a whole.
>
>>> Proposal A:
>>>
>>>  parameters {
>>>    simplex[K] beta_ratios;
>>>    real<lower=0> beta_scale;
>>>    ...
>>>  transformed parameters {
>>>    vector[K] beta;
>>>    ...
>>>    beta <- beta_scale * (beta_ratios - (1.0 / K));
>>
>> First thing, the simplex won’t work here because it assumes n _positive_ variables
>> that sum to 1, not n unconstrained variables.
>
> Maybe I wasn't clear on the goal here, which is to
> define a vector beta of unconstrained values that
> sums to 0.
>
> Although the simplex is constrained to positive
> values that sums to 1, (beta_ratios - 1.0 / K) is
> a set of values that sums to 0 and whose absolute
> values sum to 1.  It's only going to be non-negative
> in the symmetric case.
>
> For example, if you look at the simplex (0.3, 0.7),
> then (0.3, 0.7) - 0.5 = (-0.2, 0.2).
>
>> Second thing, the beta_scale is not necessary.  It just indexes many of the possible
>> transformations you could have (by the scaling noted above) but should not be
>> interpreted as a parameter.  In other words, beta_scale is a constant.
>
> The (beta_ratios - 1.0 / K) is constrained to have absolute values
> sum to 1.  By scaling by beta_scale, the absolute value sums to
> beta_scale.
>
> Isn't the result that beta can be any vector that sums to 0?
>
>>> Proposal B:
>>>
>>> parameters {
>>>    vector[K-1] beta_prefix;
>>>    ...
>>>  }
>>>  transformed parameters {
>>>    vector[K] beta;
>>>    ...
>>>    for (k in 1:(K-1))
>>>      beta[k] <- beta_prefix[k];
>>>    beta[K] <- - sum(beta_prefix);
>>>    …
>>
>> The problem here is not that the transformation is invalid, but rather a uniform distribution
>> on the unconstrained space is not a uniform distribution on the constrained space, and
>> vice-versa.
>
> In this particular case, we're going to put a prior on the parameters, not
> on the transformed parameters.  That's what I meant by it being a bit odd
> because of the asymmetry.
>
>>
>> Unfortunately there’s no way to define a truly symmetric transformation — one of the
>> constrained variables will always have to be the origin which will distinguish it from
>> the others.  You can try to marginalize over all the possible assignments, but then
>> you have to deal with the Jacobian being a sum of terms (that you would have to
>> compute before taking the log).  Not fun.
>>
>> Anyways, it’s easy to go from constrained to unconstrained, but trying to go from
>> unconstrained to constrained will always break the symmetry.  As far as I can tell.
>
> I think that's right unless we want to apply the Jacobian adjustment.
> Then we could put the prior on beta and we'd be back to what I meant
> by symmetric in that you could put a prior on each of the beta[k] for
> k in 1:K.
>
> - Bob

Now I have to figure out what a canonical isomorphism is.  The quick
Wikipedia lookup's less than helpful:

   http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canonical

   Canonical homomorphism, canonical isomorphism: an homomorphism that is uniquely defined by its main property, for
   example, the canonical homomorphism of the integers into the rational numbers, the canonical homomorphism of a vector
   space onto the quotient by a subspace. More precisely, a canonical morphism or canonical homomorphism is a morphism
   whose existence and unicity are provided by a universal property.

This is a bit more useful:

   http://www.quora.com/Mathematics/What-is-a-canonical-isomorphism

but it's going to take some thought on my part.  Ah, the education continues.

> In this case, however, there is no canonical transformation; rather there is
> an infinite family of equivalent transformations.  Pick any one and you can map
> the constrained space to an unconstrained space where the system is
> identified.
>
> With beta_scale you’re trying to parameterize the transformations — but
> you don’t need to do that.  You only need to pick out one of them.

I think we'll have to take this up at the next meeting
when there's more bandwidth!  I don't even see how
(0,inf) <--> (-inf,inf) has a canonical transform.  There
are lots of continuous monotonic functions that map one to
the other.  For example, log and log^3 both map
(0,inf) to (-inf,inf).

>> Although the simplex is constrained to positive
>> values that sums to 1, (beta_ratios - 1.0 / K) is
>> a set of values that sums to 0 and whose absolute
>> values sum to 1.  It's only going to be non-negative
>> in the symmetric case.

>> then (0.3, 0.7) - 0.5 = (-0.2, 0.2).

> support on (-1/K, infinity), not (-infinty, infinity).

They can only be -1/K negative, whereas they can be up to
(1 - 1/K) positive.  But the final values aren't constrained
at all, at least independently.

If the simplex is (0.3,0.7) and beta_scale = 1e6, then
you get (-2e5,2e5) out.

Going the other way, I'm stuck on the algebra in trying to
solve

   Given K-vector beta such that

     sum(beta) = 0,

   solve for beta_simplex and beta_scale such that

     beta = (beta_simplex - 1/K) * beta_scale
     sum(beta_simplex) = 1
     beta_simplex[k] > 0
     beta_scale > 0

I don't think there's going to be a unique solution because there
are too many free variables in beta_simplex and beta_scale compared
to beta.

>> In this particular case, we're going to put a prior on the parameters, not
>> on the transformed parameters.  That's what I meant by it being a bit odd
>> because of the asymmetry.

underlying values --- the last one gets constrained so that the sum

We really do want to discuss parameterizations of multi-logit and multi-probit,

to the users (and to me!).

messages.body_plain:
> Now I have to figure out what a canonical isomorphism is.

Sorry I just meant a natural one.  For example, the tangent space and cotangent
space on a manifold have a canonical isomorphism because they are dual to
each other.  You can define many more, but that’s the only one that arises
naturally from the underlying geometric structure.

> I think we'll have to take this up at the next meeting
> when there's more bandwidth!  I don't even see how
> (0,inf) <--> (-inf,inf) has a canonical transform.  There
> are lots of continuous monotonic functions that map one to
> the other.  For example, log and log^3 both map
> (0,inf) to (-inf,inf).

You’re right — you need to impose additional assumptions to make log natural.
A better example is the logit — logit(ax + b) works just as well as logit(x).  In
fact, this provides a nice parallel to this case.

For a multivariate system we should be able to choose any logit( a^{T} X b + c),
where a and b are vectors, X a matrix, and c a scalar (i.e. you can rotate,
translate, and then scale the argument).  Now a, b, and c aren’t parameters
but rather constants that determine the mapping and its inverse.  Same thing
happens here — you can always rotate and scale the unconstrained space
relative to the constrained space.

> I don't think there's going to be a unique solution because there
> are too many free variables in beta_simplex and beta_scale compared
> to beta.

Yeah, this is where specifying the transformation is really important.  Some of the
constants cancel out in the constrained -> unconstrained mapping but matter
for the inverse.

> I'm probably missing something else here, because this seems like the same problem
> as for the simplex itself.  The simplex has K values, but only (K-1)
> underlying values --- the last one gets constrained so that the sum
> is 1.

The simplex is different because of the positivity constraint.  This limits the potential
transformations — you no longer have translation or rotation invariance — I think you
still have scale invariance but it always cancels out.  The lack of rotational invariance is
the biggest feature because it prevents the permutation symmetries we see here.

> We really do want to discuss parameterizations of multi-logit and multi-probit,
> because they bring up the same issues and we should be making recommendations
> to the users (and to me!).

See the discussion above — lots of ways to do it, no natural way.  The logit/probit case
is nice because the rotation/scaling/translation have intuitive meaning or can be
absorbed into existing parameters.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Andrew and everyone,

On the topic of posterior preditive checks without loops: I wrote up a
small set of functions for mapping posteriors functionally:

https://gist.github.com/tpapp/8650643

Examples are at the end. To take a well-known example from the BDA
appendix,

theta_rep <- array (NA, c(n_sims, J))
y_rep <- array (NA, c(n_sims, J))
for (s in 1:n_sims){
  theta_rep[s,] <- rnorm (J, schools_sim$mu[s], schools_sim$tau[s])
  y_rep[s,] <- rnorm (J, theta_rep[s,], sigma)
}

would be something like

theta_and_y <- map_subarrays(school_sim,
  function(mu, tau, sigma) {
    theta_rep <- rnorm(J, mu, tau)
    list(theta_rep=theta_rep,
         y_rep=rnorm(J, theta_rep, sigma))
  })

The good news is that this does what I want, and the syntax works great,
simplifying loops (or nested loops) considerably.

The bad news is that it is painfully slow for nontrivial examples. This
comes from the management of list labels, if I understand
correctly. Currently, it is so slow as to be unusable.

If you know any R wizards, maybe they can speed it up a bit. I asked on
the R-devel mailing list, where the message was not approved ("please
ask on R-help") and then didn't get the kind of help I was looking for
on R-help. So I am back to loops, ugly as they are, I don't want to
waste too much time on this now.

Also, aaply from the plyr libray works for with a little tweaking
(cbinding arrays together, destructuring, applying the function, etc),
but that's not much nicer than loops.

Best,

Tamas

messages.body_plain:
I think I've stumbled across what I needed, albeit it's a little slow. A simple set of code is below (using just one index). This approach can be used for hierarchical models when you want to be able to model some kind of systematic factor and exposures to such a factor. My example was meant for an asset pricing model (in finance) that estimates a bottom-up market factor instead of using the observed market returns.

I generated some x's that are effectively the cross-sectional mean in each period of the y's. I then regress each of the y's against x. Importantly, I do this in two separate steps to ensure the x's will be tied down.

When I was originally trying to get this to work in one Stan file, I had tried this format, but crucially without the first y statement (which I can seem to only be able to do in the loop). This led to there being too many parameters. While the x's in that method may have been correlated with the original data used to generate the data, they had significantly different means (perhaps even different signs) and variances. This led to the beta_x's and mu_y's being way off what is sensible, even if they would produce the correct posterior predictive distributions. Including the first y statement ties everything down.

data {
  int<lower=0> N;
  int<lower=0> T;
  vector[T] y[N];
}

parameters {
  real mu_x;
  real<lower=0> var_x;
  vector[T] x;
  real beta_x[N];
  real mu_y;
  real<lower=0> var_y;
}
transformed parameters {
  real<lower=0> std_x;
  real<lower=0> std_y;

  std_x <- sqrt(var_x);
  std_y <- sqrt(var_y);
}
model {
  mu_x ~ normal(0, 100);
  var_x ~ inv_gamma(0.001, 0.001);
  x ~ normal(mu_x, std_x);
  beta_x ~ normal(0, 100);
  var_y ~ inv_gamma(0.001, 0.001);
  mu_y ~ normal(0, 100);

  for (n in 1:N) {
    y[n] ~ normal(x, std_y);
    y[n] ~ normal(mu_y + beta_x[n] * x, std_y);

  }
}

Just to clarify with respect to the variances/standard deviations, you just recommend removing the inv_gamma statements from the model statement without making any changes to the parameters. I didn't notice a speed up doing that, but I'll take your word for it that I should do it. And I'll read your 2006 paper to try to figure out why.

I can put some more information on the mean, but for a simple test I just felt like putting something there that might work on any type of data. In a more complicated version I would include the prior in the data step to allow for better customization.

messages.body_plain:
Hi, my suggestion is not so much for speed as for stability.  With some data, the gamma prior can lead to unstable results.  It can also be a very strong prior, dominating the data.  We discuss in the 2006 paper and also in BDA.

On Jan 27, 2014, at 7:49 PM, John Hall wrote:

> Just to clarify with respect to the variances/standard deviations, you just recommend removing the inv_gamma statements from the model statement without making any changes to the parameters. I didn't notice a speed up doing that, but I'll take your word for it that I should do it. And I'll read your 2006 paper to try to figure out why.
>
> I can put some more information on the mean, but for a simple test I just felt like putting something there that might work on any type of data. In a more complicated version I would include the prior in the data step to allow for better customization.
>
> On Monday, January 27, 2014 1:06:07 PM UTC-5, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> > As Bob would say, Andrew doesn't like those inv_gamma(0.001, 0.001) priors.  Really, you have no reason to touch those variances at all.  The sd's are just fine to work with on their own.  Andrew also doesn't like normal(0,100), as he thinks it's better to put in some weak prior information to control the scale of a problem.
> >
> > On Jan 27, 2014, at 5:41 PM, John Hall wrote:
> >
> > > I think I've stumbled across what I needed, albeit it's a little slow. A simple set of code is below (using just one index). This approach can be used for hierarchical models when you want to be able to model some kind of systematic factor and exposures to such a factor. My example was meant for an asset pricing model (in finance) that estimates a bottom-up market factor instead of using the observed market returns.
> > >
> > > I generated some x's that are effectively the cross-sectional mean in each period of the y's. I then regress each of the y's against x. Importantly, I do this in two separate steps to ensure the x's will be tied down.
> > >
> > > When I was originally trying to get this to work in one Stan file, I had tried this format, but crucially without the first y statement (which I can seem to only be able to do in the loop). This led to there being too many parameters. While the x's in that method may have been correlated with the original data used to generate the data, they had significantly different means (perhaps even different signs) and variances. This led to the beta_x's and mu_y's being way off what is sensible, even if they would produce the correct posterior predictive distributions. Including the first y statement ties everything down.
> > >
> > > data {
> > >   int<lower=0> N;
> > >   int<lower=0> T;
> > >   vector[T] y[N];
> > > }
> > >
> > > parameters {
> > >   real mu_x;
> > >   real<lower=0> var_x;
> > >   vector[T] x;
> > >   real beta_x[N];
> > >   real mu_y;
> > >   real<lower=0> var_y;
> > > }
> > > transformed parameters {
> > >   real<lower=0> std_x;
> > >   real<lower=0> std_y;
> > >
> > >   std_x <- sqrt(var_x);
> > >   std_y <- sqrt(var_y);
> > > }
> > > model {
> > >   mu_x ~ normal(0, 100);
> > >   var_x ~ inv_gamma(0.001, 0.001);
> > >   x ~ normal(mu_x, std_x);
> > >   beta_x ~ normal(0, 100);
> > >   var_y ~ inv_gamma(0.001, 0.001);
> > >   mu_y ~ normal(0, 100);
> > >
> > >   for (n in 1:N) {
> > >     y[n] ~ normal(x, std_y);
> > >     y[n] ~ normal(mu_y + beta_x[n] * x, std_y);
> > >   }
> > > }
> > >
> > >
> > > On Tuesday, January 14, 2014 5:07:02 AM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > > > On 1/14/14, 3:02 AM, John Hall wrote:
> > > > > For the Gibbs thing, I was just summarizing how I write the program to do the Gibbs sampling more than anything. I
> > > > > typically would write seperate functions for estimating the distribution for a parameter and simulating from that
> > > > > distribution. It's the same thing as what you're talking about though, just as separate steps.
> > > >
> > > > You can do that in Stan using the generated quantities block.
> > > > The parameters are declared as parameters, the model is in
> > > > the model, then the quantities to generate conditional on
> > > > the parameters are declared and defined in the generated quantities
> > > > block.
> > > >
> > > > This is one of the reasons we built the generated quantities --- to
> > > > generate predictive quantities based on the parameters.
> > > >
> > > > If you do Gibbs, you have to have the joint probability anyway,
> > > > assuming your model's consistent --- the conditionals should
> > > > be conditionals of a joint probability.  Technically, all you
> > > > need is something proportional to the posterior p(parameters|data),
> > > > which itself is proportional to the joint p(parameters,alpha) by
> > > > Bayes's rule.  Sorry if this is all obvious.
> > > >
> > > > - Bob

> > > > >      >      Note the x's are all from the cross-sectional step above. They change with each Gibbs iteration.

On 1/27/14, 5:41 PM, John Hall wrote:
> I think I've stumbled across what I needed, albeit it's a little slow. A simple set of code is below (using just one
> index). This approach can be used for hierarchical models when you want to be able to model some kind of systematic
> factor and exposures to such a factor. My example was meant for an asset pricing model (in finance) that estimates a
> bottom-up market factor instead of using the observed market returns.
>
> I generated some x's that are effectively the cross-sectional mean in each period of the y's. I then regress each of the
> y's against x. Importantly, I do this in two separate steps to ensure the x's will be tied down.
>
> When I was originally trying to get this to work in one Stan file, I had tried this format, but crucially without the
> first y statement (which I can seem to only be able to do in the loop).

Yes, we only vectorize one-dimensional arrays.  We're going
to add higher dimensional ones in the future, with the same
requirements on matching shapes as we have now.

> This led to there being too many parameters.
> While the x's in that method may have been correlated with the original data used to generate the data, they had
> significantly different means (perhaps even different signs) and variances. This led to the beta_x's and mu_y's being
> way off what is sensible, even if they would produce the correct posterior predictive distributions. Including the first
> y statement ties everything down.

 >    for (n in 1:N) {

 >      y[n] ~ normal(x, std_y);
 >      y[n] ~ normal(mu_y + beta_x[n] * x, std_y);
 >    }

What this is doing is saying that

    p(y[n,k] | x, std_y, mu_y, beta_x[n], x[k])

      = normal(y[n,k] | x[k], std_y) * normal(y[n,k] | mu_y + beta_x[n] * x[k], std_y)

Is that really what you wanted to do?

- Bob

>
> data {
>    int<lower=0> N;
>    int<lower=0> T;
>    vector[T] y[N];
> }
>
> parameters {
>    real mu_x;
>    real<lower=0> var_x;
>    vector[T] x;
>    real beta_x[N];
>    real mu_y;
>    real<lower=0> var_y;
> }
> transformed parameters {
>    real<lower=0> std_x;
>    real<lower=0> std_y;
>
>    std_x <- sqrt(var_x);
>    std_y <- sqrt(var_y);
> }
> model {
>    mu_x ~ normal(0, 100);
>    var_x ~ inv_gamma(0.001, 0.001);
>    x ~ normal(mu_x, std_x);
>    beta_x ~ normal(0, 100);
>    var_y ~ inv_gamma(0.001, 0.001);
>    mu_y ~ normal(0, 100);
>

>    for (n in 1:N) {

>      y[n] ~ normal(x, std_y);
>      y[n] ~ normal(mu_y + beta_x[n] * x, std_y);
>    }
> }
>
>
> On Tuesday, January 14, 2014 5:07:02 AM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>

>     On 1/14/14, 3:02 AM, John Hall wrote:
>      > For the Gibbs thing, I was just summarizing how I write the program to do the Gibbs sampling more than anything. I
>      > typically would write seperate functions for estimating the distribution for a parameter and simulating from that
>      > distribution. It's the same thing as what you're talking about though, just as separate steps.
>
>     You can do that in Stan using the generated quantities block.
>     The parameters are declared as parameters, the model is in
>     the model, then the quantities to generate conditional on
>     the parameters are declared and defined in the generated quantities
>     block.
>
>     This is one of the reasons we built the generated quantities --- to
>     generate predictive quantities based on the parameters.
>
>     If you do Gibbs, you have to have the joint probability anyway,
>     assuming your model's consistent --- the conditionals should
>     be conditionals of a joint probability.  Technically, all you
>     need is something proportional to the posterior p(parameters|data),
>     which itself is proportional to the joint p(parameters,alpha) by
>     Bayes's rule.  Sorry if this is all obvious.
>
>     - Bob
>
>      > On Monday, January 13, 2014 7:15:01 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>      >
>      >     Yes, Stan requires you to write down the full probability
>      >     function as does any kind of full Bayesian modeling.
>      >
>      >     Your algorithm sketch doesn't look like a Gibbs sampler to me.
>      >     If you have N parameters theta[1],...,theta[N], and full probability
>      >     function p(theta[1],...,theta[N]),  then Gibbs initializes theta, then
>      >     does
>      >
>      >     for (i in 1:I)
>      >         for (n in 1:N)
>      >           sample theta[n] from p(theta[n] | theta[1],..,theta[n-1],theta[n+1],...,theta[N])
>      >
>      >     I don't understand your estimate/simulate notation.
>      >
>      >     The short answer is that you can't mix simulation and sampling
>      >     in Stan.  You can sample and do simulations based on the samples,
>      >     but you can't then feed the simulations back into the sampler in any way.
>      >
>      >     - Bob

>      >      >     Maybe if you wrote down a sketch of the BUGS model for what you're
