messages.body_plain:
Bob,
I can't say that if I wrote down what I thought I was trying to do (at least a simple version of what I'm trying to do), I would have that written down, but that's probably because I am self-taught on Bayesian statistics (my MA degree did not cover the subject one iota). Nevertheless, it's the first thing I've done that's giving me the correct results using one Stan file, which makes it feel right.

If you recall above, I had wanted to cross-sectionally estimate some means in each period in one Stan file and then pass the distribution of those means to another Stan fit statement. This approach seems to ensure that this takes place since it constrains the x's with respect to the y's. For instance, had I just fit
p(y[n,k] | x, std_y, mu_y, beta_x[n], x[k])=normal(y[n,k] | mu_y + beta_x[n] * x[k], std_y)
then there are too many parameters in mu_y + beta_x[n] * x[k]. If there's a better way to get the same results without this approach, I'm all ears.

On Monday, January 27, 2014 1:59:54 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>
>
> On 1/27/14, 5:41 PM, John Hall wrote:
> > I think I've stumbled across what I needed, albeit it's a little slow. A simple set of code is below (using just one
> > index). This approach can be used for hierarchical models when you want to be able to model some kind of systematic
> > factor and exposures to such a factor. My example was meant for an asset pricing model (in finance) that estimates a
> > bottom-up market factor instead of using the observed market returns.
> >
> > I generated some x's that are effectively the cross-sectional mean in each period of the y's. I then regress each of the
> > y's against x. Importantly, I do this in two separate steps to ensure the x's will be tied down.
> >
> > When I was originally trying to get this to work in one Stan file, I had tried this format, but crucially without the
> > first y statement (which I can seem to only be able to do in the loop).
>
> Yes, we only vectorize one-dimensional arrays.  We're going
> to add higher dimensional ones in the future, with the same
> requirements on matching shapes as we have now.
>
> > This led to there being too many parameters.
> > While the x's in that method may have been correlated with the original data used to generate the data, they had
> > significantly different means (perhaps even different signs) and variances. This led to the beta_x's and mu_y's being
> > way off what is sensible, even if they would produce the correct posterior predictive distributions. Including the first
> > y statement ties everything down.
>
>
>
>  >    for (n in 1:N) {
>  >      y[n] ~ normal(x, std_y);
>  >      y[n] ~ normal(mu_y + beta_x[n] * x, std_y);
>  >    }
>
>
> What this is doing is saying that
>
>     p(y[n,k] | x, std_y, mu_y, beta_x[n], x[k])
>
>       = normal(y[n,k] | x[k], std_y) * normal(y[n,k] | mu_y + beta_x[n] * x[k], std_y)
>
> Is that really what you wanted to do?
>
> - Bob
>
> >
> > data {
> >    int<lower=0> N;
> >    int<lower=0> T;
> >    vector[T] y[N];
> > }
> >
> > parameters {
> >    real mu_x;
> >    real<lower=0> var_x;
> >    vector[T] x;
> >    real beta_x[N];
> >    real mu_y;
> >    real<lower=0> var_y;
> > }
> > transformed parameters {
> >    real<lower=0> std_x;
> >    real<lower=0> std_y;
> >
> >    std_x <- sqrt(var_x);
> >    std_y <- sqrt(var_y);
> > }
> > model {
> >    mu_x ~ normal(0, 100);
> >    var_x ~ inv_gamma(0.001, 0.001);
> >    x ~ normal(mu_x, std_x);
> >    beta_x ~ normal(0, 100);
> >    var_y ~ inv_gamma(0.001, 0.001);
> >    mu_y ~ normal(0, 100);
> >
> >    for (n in 1:N) {
> >      y[n] ~ normal(x, std_y);
> >      y[n] ~ normal(mu_y + beta_x[n] * x, std_y);
> >    }
> > }
> >
> >
> > On Tuesday, January 14, 2014 5:07:02 AM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> >
> >     On 1/14/14, 3:02 AM, John Hall wrote:
> >      > For the Gibbs thing, I was just summarizing how I write the program to do the Gibbs sampling more than anything. I
> >      > typically would write seperate functions for estimating the distribution for a parameter and simulating from that
> >      > distribution. It's the same thing as what you're talking about though, just as separate steps.
> >
> >     You can do that in Stan using the generated quantities block.
> >     The parameters are declared as parameters, the model is in
> >     the model, then the quantities to generate conditional on
> >     the parameters are declared and defined in the generated quantities
> >     block.
> >
> >     This is one of the reasons we built the generated quantities --- to
> >     generate predictive quantities based on the parameters.
> >
> >     If you do Gibbs, you have to have the joint probability anyway,
> >     assuming your model's consistent --- the conditionals should
> >     be conditionals of a joint probability.  Technically, all you
> >     need is something proportional to the posterior p(parameters|data),
> >     which itself is proportional to the joint p(parameters,alpha) by
> >     Bayes's rule.  Sorry if this is all obvious.
> >
> >     - Bob
> >
> >      > On Monday, January 13, 2014 7:15:01 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> >      >
> >      >     Yes, Stan requires you to write down the full probability
> >      >     function as does any kind of full Bayesian modeling.
> >      >
> >      >     Your algorithm sketch doesn't look like a Gibbs sampler to me.
> >      >     If you have N parameters theta[1],...,theta[N], and full probability
> >      >     function p(theta[1],...,theta[N]),  then Gibbs initializes theta, then
> >      >     does
> >      >
> >      >     for (i in 1:I)
> >      >         for (n in 1:N)
> >      >           sample theta[n] from p(theta[n] | theta[1],..,theta[n-1],theta[n+1],...,theta[N])
> >      >
> >      >     I don't understand your estimate/simulate notation.
> >      >
> >      >     The short answer is that you can't mix simulation and sampling
> >      >     in Stan.  You can sample and do simulations based on the samples,
> >      >     but you can't then feed the simulations back into the sampler in any way.
> >      >
> >      >     - Bob
> >      >
> >      >
> >      >
> >      >
> >      >
> >      >     On 1/14/14, 12:39 AM, John Hall wrote:
> >      >      > Thanks for the reply Bob. I hadn't used BUGS before using Stan and had just coded my own Gibbs samplers, so I
> >      >     thought
> >      >      > this would be easier to attach what I've been working on (I have it set up so the un-rar'ed folder is in
> >     C). I also
> >      >      > sketched a Gibbs sampler of what I'm trying to do below, more or less. The S_test_stan.r file is the main
> >     file.
> >      >     It calls
> >      >      > the S_gen_data.r file to create the data and then fits some Stan models.
> >      >      >
> >      >      > The key line is 60:
> >      >      > y_sim_index_cutdown <- colMeans(aperm(y_sim_index, c(2, 1, 3)))
> >      >      > In the previous section, I fit the Stan model cross-sectionally as I described above. The y_sim_index
> >     variable is
> >      >     the
> >      >      > array containing all these results. Thus, this line is like taking the posterior mean in each period
> >     (which is
> >      >     what you
> >      >      > seem to recommend). I then use these means in subsequent analysis, treating them as though they are
> >     observed data.
> >      >      >
> >      >      > In a Gibbs sampler, I could just use the y_sim_index posterior samples directly in the next stage of the
> >      >     analysis. For
> >      >      > instance, the following sequence I give a headline of "Fit Simple Hierarchical Model with Index as
> >     Regressor" in the
> >      >      > code regresses the y_bottom variable against the respective index (calculated by that line 60 above). In a
> >     Gibbs
> >      >      > sampler, in an iteration I can use the y_sim_index in the next line (see sketch). It seems like the
> >     impression I'm
> >      >      > getting is that Stan requires the formula for the distribution. I'm wondering if that's the case or if
> >     there's
> >      >     any way
> >      >      > to use simulated variables at all the way I would with Gibbs sampling.
> >      >      >
> >      >      > I'm essentially throwing away all the rest of the information about the uncertainty in these means. I
> >     considered
> >      >     that I
> >      >      > could calculate the covariance in each time period and assume that the measurement error is multivariate
> >     normal. I'm
> >      >      > worried that this might be slow (I can't even get the multivariate normal-inverse Wishart distribution to

> >      >      > properly), but it seems possible. For this type of data, multivariate normal seems like a good assumption,

> >      >     may
> >      >      > not always make sense.
> >      >      >
> >      >      > Gibbs sketch:
> >      >      >
> >      >      > for i in 1:(n_burn+n_gibbs) {
> >      >      >    #cross-sectional estimation
> >      >      >    for j in 1:n_j {

> >      >      >    }
> >      >      >    # time-series estimation

> >      >      >      for equation: y[n] ~ N(beta_y[n] * x[index[n]], sigma[n]^0.5)

> >      >      >      estimate sigma[n]
> >      >      >      simulate sigma[n]
> >      >      >      Note the x's are all from the cross-sectional step above. They change with each Gibbs iteration.
> >      >      >    }
> >      >      >

> >      >      >    }
> >      >      > }
> >      >      >
> >      >      >
> >      >      > On Saturday, January 11, 2014 3:28:17 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> >      >      >
> >      >      >     I'm also a little unclear on what the problem is.
> >      >      >
> >      >      >     Are you asking whether we can do cut like in BUGS?
> >      >      >     The closest we can come is using the generated quantities

> >     returns in
> >      >     each
> >      >      >      > iteration and can just add extra steps to perform any additional analysis. I'm just not sure if I
> >     can do

> >      >      >      >
> >      >      >      > On Friday, January 10, 2014 4:21:22 PM UTC-5, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> >      >      >      >
> >      >      >      >     Hi, I don't quite understand the question, but I think the way to go is to just fully specify the

messages.body_plain:
Maybe someone else will know a simpler or more standard
way to achieve the same effect as

 >    for (n in 1:N) {
 >      y[n] ~ normal(x, std_y);
 >      y[n] ~ normal(mu_y + beta_x[n] * x, std_y);
 >    }

Looking more closely at your model, I think the real issue you're
having is that beta_x[n] and x are both parameters, which introduces
a serious non-identifiability issue.  You can multiply beta_x[n] by K and
multiply x by 1/K and you get the same answer.

The weak priors you have on the components aren't going to be enough
to pull them into line.  The fact that x has a hierarchical prior is
just going to push the problem up to mu_x and make it worse as far
as fitting goes.

Adding the second sampling distribution is going to pull x[k] back
toward the mean of the y[,k], providing a kind of identifiability.

- Bob

messages.subject: Stan wish list for Bayesian demography
messages.subject_clean: Stan wish list for Bayesian demography
messages.body_plain:
Hi Stanners!

One of my research interests is in Bayesian models for population
demography. By that I mean population demographic models that take
uncertainties in the parameter estimates into account, and provide
uncertainties for the model outputs (population growth rate etc.), using
a Bayesian approach. The key reference here is Poole, D. & Raftery, A.
E. Inference for deterministic simulation models: The Bayesian melding
approach Journal of the American Statistical Association, 2000, 95,
1244-1255.

Poole and Raftery use the SIR algorithm to compute posterior densities
for model outputs, however I think it would be EXTREMELY cool to
implement Poole and Raftery's approach in Stan. These population models
are matrix models, which are asymmetric. Analysing the models amounts to
an eigenanalysis of this population projection matrix. Consequently, I
need to be able to calculate eigenvalues and eigenvectors for asymmetric
matrices. Could this functionality be added to Stan?

Another feature of the Poole and Raftery approach is that there are TWO
priors on each input and output of the model (this avoids the Borel
paradox). One is the usual subjective prior. The other is the prior
induced on the outputs by the priors on the model inputs. This prior is
obtained by sampling from the input priors and then running them through
the matrix model. Then follows logarithmic pooling of the two priors to
produce a single prior for each output, and then usual Bayesian
inference can be conducted. I'm not sure how to do this in Stan, but I
am willing to try. If anyone has any ideas on how to do it, I'm all ears!

On a lighter note, you can buy Stan Ulam shirts on the Internet!!
http://www.zazzle.com/ulam_fermiac_tee_shirts-235971823213376354

Cheers,

Simon.

--
Simon Blomberg, BSc (Hons), PhD, MAppStat, AStat.
Senior Lecturer and Consultant Statistician
School of Biological Sciences
The University of Queensland
St. Lucia Queensland 4072
Australia
T: +61 7 3365 2506
email: S.Blomberg1_at_uq.edu.au <http://S.Blomberg1_at_uq.edu.au>
http://www.evolutionarystatistics.org

Policies:
1.  I will NOT analyse your data for you.
2.  Your deadline is your problem.

Statistics is the grammar of science - Karl Pearson.

Yes, it'd be pretty easy --- there are asymmetric algorithms in the
Eigen package we use.  Unless we could work out some analytic
gradients, it'd be relatively slow.  How big are the matrices
that need to be decomposed?

There's no way to do any kind of across-iteration inference in
Stan.  But if it can be expressed as a density, we could do it.

If by putting two priors, you just mean you want to have

    theta ~ foo(...);
    theta ~ bar(...);

with the interpretation

    p(theta|..., ...) = foo(theta|...) * bar(theta|...)

you can just write it as above.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
On Mon, Jan 27 2014, ca...@alias-i.com wrote:

> So what's the motivation for the function over using loops?
> I, at least, find the loops so much easier to understand.

In general, I like functional solutions: that means that I don't have to
create the array (or other structure) I use or collecting the results,
and I don't need to keep track of a loop index variable. Loops are OK
for a single level, but nested loops can become error-prone very
quickly.

But my main language is Common Lisp, so I guess I prefer more functional
approaches simply because of habit (and, also, I tend to use R as if it
was a recalcitrant Lisp with a thin layer of infix syntax upon it).

Meanwhile, Hadley Wickham, the author of various great R packages for
working with data (including plyr), kindly suggested some other
approaches which are more idiomatic in R. I will experiment with these
and report back to the list.

>> Which is OK-ish, but for a few parallel chains etc this
>> becomes too long.
>
> We definitely don't need 1K iterations for posterior predictive checks!
> I'd say you'd be good with 50 (or even fewer) for most purposes.

Then I am confused, I was under the impression that one calculates a
replication for each posterior draw.

Best,

Tamas

I understand that tastes in programming style do vary. And the functional
approach is both loved and hated by R users I've talked to.  I don't
understand R's functional programming styles, which is why I find the loops
easier to comprehend.  I do love functional languages in general --- I spent
years working on typed higher-order lambda calculus and domain theory;  it's
just R I find opaque.

>>> Which is OK-ish, but for a few parallel chains etc this
>>> becomes too long.
>>
>> We definitely don't need 1K iterations for posterior predictive checks!
>> I'd say you'd be good with 50 (or even fewer) for most purposes.
>
> Then I am confused, I was under the impression that one calculates a
> replication for each posterior draw.

No reason you have to do it for each posterior draw.  Also, no reason
to have 1000 posterior draws for most examples.  The default number of
iterations is going to change in the near future to something more
reasonable like 200.

What you should is decide how much accuracy you need in the posterior quantities
of interest, such as parameter means or intervals.  Then figure out how many
effective samples you need to get it, then only draw that many samples.

Same for posterior predictive checks.

- Bob

either, other than for generated quantities.

you're trying to do better than me.  I was lost at "generating

it that means it's not a parametric density, but just a bunch

> easier to comprehend.  I do love functional languages in general --- I spent
> years working on typed higher-order lambda calculus and domain theory;  it's
> just R I find opaque.

I am coming to the same conclusion --- even if base R could accommodate
a functional style, many functions, especially in libraries, rely on
resolving variables on a dynamically created environment (eg columns of
a data frame). Also, generic (non-homogenous) vectors/arrays are
cumbersome and not supported. So maybe I will have to change my style
when I program in R. OTOH, it is hard to miss similarities between Common
Lisp and R: eg the S4 classes, etc.

>> Then I am confused, I was under the impression that one calculates a
>> replication for each posterior draw.
>
> No reason you have to do it for each posterior draw.  Also, no reason
> to have 1000 posterior draws for most examples.  The default number of
> iterations is going to change in the near future to something more
> reasonable like 200.
>
> What you should is decide how much accuracy you need in the posterior quantities
> of interest, such as parameter means or intervals.  Then figure out how many
> effective samples you need to get it, then only draw that many samples.
>
> Same for posterior predictive checks.

I guess my habit of drawing many chains, each with at least 2000-5000
iterations, comes from the days when I used inefficient samplers (which
I usually programmed myself). Indeed Stan is much more efficient so I
will have to adjust.

Best,

Tamas

Hi!

The outputs from cmd-line stan can become quite large for complex models. Hence the desire to compress these files with bzip2 (which saves 70% of the file size). But the

read_comments

If I pass a list of *.csv.bz2 files to read_stan_csv, the r-function read.csv will not complain at all to read in the compressed csv file, but the read_comments function which is internal to rstan does not like the compressed file. Thanks for considering this feature, which would help to work many of us to work more efficiently.

Best regards,

Sebastian

messages.body_plain:
Compression of some form is a good option to add, but in general our file sizes are going to be overly large so long as we're outputting text.  A double precision floating point number takes around 20 bytes to represent in a CSV (counting spaces, commas, decimals, signs, etc). Cheers,
Marcus

messages.subject: confidence intervals on parameters differ between STAN and JAGS?
messages.subject_clean: confidence intervals on parameters differ between STAN and JAGS?
messages.body_plain:
Super quick question:

I'm playing with the radon data (the group-level predictor example). I fit the STAN model using the example code posted online. Then, I redid the model to be more similar to the BUGS code, where the intercepts are a function of county-level uranium (as an aside, is STAN like lmer in that it figures out when a predictor is on the group level? In the example code online, the county-level uranium looks like it's at the individual level but STAN seems to figure out that it's at the county level). The STAN output matches lmer almost exactly, and both STAN variants give nearly identical parameter estimates (0.7 +/- 0.1) and confidence intervals (0.1 - 0.9) for the group-level coefficient (g1), although estimates of the county-level intercepts differ between models (but they're being modeled differently, so I expect that).

Then I ran the model in JAGS using the code from ARM (Chapter 12, pg. 361).

However, the JAGS model estimates the group-level coefficient g1 less precisely (although g0 seems to be similar), with a mean of 0.65 +/- 0.22 and a confidence interval of 0.21 - 1.1. I looked through the manual and the previous posts to see if this had come up, but I couldn't find anything. I did notice that JAGS and STAN estimate the county-level intercepts similarly (when running comparable models, albeit JAGS is again more imprecise), just the county-level regression coefficient differs.

My super quick question is: is it normal or to be expected that STAN gives more precise than JAGS/BUGS due to its different sampling algorithm? I was pretty surprised that JAGS was so imprecise for that parameter.

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am building a model that combines a IRT model - to measure the latent trait outcome variable - and a set of varying intercept predictors (much like the election88 example). The idea is for something like a structural equation model.

I began by building and testing each model separately (using an additive scale as the outcome variable for the multilevel model). So far so good. However, I am stumped as to how to combine the two. Specifically, I gather from reading some exchanges on this list that the ability parameter of the IRT model - which I call theta - requires a normal(0, 1) prior to resolve the additive offset identification problem. But theta is is also my outcome variable, so I also want theta to be sampled from a normal(theta_hat, sigma_theta) distribution, where theta_hat is the vector of fitted values from the MLM.

Any suggestions?

messages.body_plain:
> On Jan 28, 2014, at 4:47 PM, Nathan Lemoine <lemoine...@gmail.com <mailto:lemoine...@gmail.com>> wrote:

>> ... as an aside, is STAN like lmer in that it figures out when a predictor is on the group level? In

>> the example code online, the county-level uranium looks like it's at the individual level but STAN seems to figure out
>> that it's at the county level

Are you talking about one of the ARM examples?  If so, which one?
It looks like there are a lot of Radon examples.

To answer your question, Stan only does what's written in the
model --- it doesn't try to get clever and figure out user intent.

I would guess that lmer also only does what's in the model expression,
but I'm not sure about that.

Also, lmer is only approximating the posterior confidence intervals using
curvature at the solution, whereas Stan's estimating the posterior intervals
using sampling.  Quantiles (boundaries of intervals) require more effective samples to
estimate than means or medians, because, for example, the 5% quantile is only based on
the smallest 5% of the samples.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Combining multilevel and item-response models
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Combining multilevel and item-response models
messages.body_plain:
On 1/28/14, 6:00 PM, Christopher Claassen wrote:
>
> Hi all,
>
> I am building a model that combines a IRT model - to measure the latent trait outcome variable - and a set of varying
> intercept predictors (much like the election88 example). The idea is for something like a structural equation model.
>
> I began by building and testing each model separately (using an additive scale as the outcome variable for the
> multilevel model). So far so good. However, I am stumped as to how to combine the two. Specifically, I gather from
> reading some exchanges on this list that the ability parameter of the IRT model - which I call theta - requires a
> normal(0, 1) prior to resolve the additive offset identification problem. But theta is is also my outcome variable, so I
> also want theta to be sampled from a normal(theta_hat, sigma_theta) distribution, where theta_hat is the vector of
> fitted values from the MLM.
>
> Any suggestions?

Funny -- Andrew and I were just discussing this today, so maybe he'll
weigh in if I mess up my recollection of what we discussed.  The main
issue that came up is that normal(0,1) prior is a hack in that it
centers the abilities, but they're not still not identified in the population.
That is, if you add or subtract students, the values will change (though not
in expecation).

The second thing that came up is that by fixing one
of the abilities to 0, you do identify the population in that everyone's
ability is scaled to the student with the ability pinned to 0.  Still not
very nice if you want a more "natural" interpretation of the parameters.  But
the simple fact is that the model's not identified by just

   discrimination[j] * (ability[i] - difficulty[j])

Fixing the prior of ability to normal(0,1) deals with both the
multiplicative and additive non-identifiability.  The choice of 0
and 1 are arbitrary here, but you might as well use those because
they're standard and it works well for Stan's sampling scale and default
inits.

For the additive non-identifiability, you can either pin down
the location of the ability OR the difficulty parameters.  For the
multiplicative identifiability, you need to pin down the scale of
one or the other.

You can also set one of the abilities to 0 or one of the difficulties
to 0, but that's clunky to code.

If you're using a predictor theta_hat, you can avoid using an intercept
term in theta_hat --- if you add an intecept there, it's just another
additive term that's not identified.  It then pushes the problem of
scale identifiability up to the prior on the slopes.

You could also set sigma_theta = 1 to deal with the scale issue, though I've
often found in a hierarchical model having a reasonable prior on sigma_theta
will do exactly the same thing.

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] confidence intervals on parameters differ between STAN and JAGS?
messages.body_plain:
I guess what I meant is that lmer/lme seems to "figure out" that u is a county-level predictor and treats the denominator degrees of freedom accordingly, but I guess this is more related to hypothesis testing than parameter estimates. It just seemed a little odd to me to use u as the full vector where u[i,j] are identical within a county [j], rather than the "traditional" approach of making the intercept a[j] a function of u[j]. I'm not used to thinking about it that way. This stems more from an incomplete understanding of the way the model is structured on my part. I always thought it was necessary to remove the duplicate u[i]'s (within a county), otherwise the parameter might be estimated too precisely (i.e. assuming there are more data points than actually are present).

I guess, pedagogically, it's easier for me to think about the model (using the full u vector) as (a[county[i]] + b2*u[i] ) + b1*x[i], which more clearly shows the intercept varying at the group level (and the effect of u on that intercept).

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Stan wish list for Bayesian demography
messages.body_plain:
Hi, with regard to the last point, you can add more than one prior to a parameter in Stan.  One way to think about this is that each of these "priors" represents a different data source.

On Jan 28, 2014, at 2:46 AM, Simon Blomberg wrote:

> Hi Stanners!
>
> One of my research interests is in Bayesian models for population demography. By that I mean population demographic models that take uncertainties in the parameter estimates into account, and provide uncertainties for the model outputs (population growth rate etc.), using a Bayesian approach. The key reference here is Poole, D. & Raftery, A. E. Inference for deterministic simulation models: The Bayesian melding approach Journal of the American Statistical Association, 2000, 95, 1244-1255.
>
> Poole and Raftery use the SIR algorithm to compute posterior densities for model outputs, however I think it would be EXTREMELY cool to implement Poole and Raftery's approach in Stan. These population models are matrix models, which are asymmetric. Analysing the models amounts to an eigenanalysis of this population projection matrix. Consequently, I need to be able to calculate eigenvalues and eigenvectors for asymmetric matrices. Could this functionality be added to Stan?
>
> Another feature of the Poole and Raftery approach is that there are TWO priors on each input and output of the model (this avoids the Borel paradox). One is the usual subjective prior. The other is the prior induced on the outputs by the priors on the model inputs. This prior is obtained by sampling from the input priors and then running them through the matrix model. Then follows logarithmic pooling of the two priors to produce a single prior for each output, and then usual Bayesian inference can be conducted. I'm not sure how to do this in Stan, but I am willing to try. If anyone has any ideas on how to do it, I'm all ears!

messages.subject: Re: Borel paradox and parameterization [was Re: [stan-users] Stan wish list for Bayesian demography]
messages.subject_clean: Borel paradox and parameterization [was Re: [stan-users] Stan wish list for Bayesian demography]
messages.body_plain:
On Mon, Jan 27, 2014 at 9:01 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> I'm trying to get Michael's attention with the new subject.
> This is much more up his alley than mine.  More below.
>
> On 1/28/14, 2:46 AM, Simon Blomberg wrote:
> > Hi Stanners!
> >
> > One of my research interests is in Bayesian models for population demography. By that I mean population demographic
> > models that take uncertainties in the parameter estimates into account, and provide uncertainties for the model outputs
> > (population growth rate etc.), using a Bayesian approach. The key reference here is Poole, D. & Raftery, A. E. Inference
> > for deterministic simulation models: The Bayesian melding approach Journal of the American Statistical Association,
> > 2000, 95, 1244-1255.
> >
> > Poole and Raftery use the SIR algorithm to compute posterior densities for model outputs, however I think it would be
> > EXTREMELY cool to implement Poole and Raftery's approach in Stan. These population models are matrix models, which are
> > asymmetric. Analysing the models amounts to an eigenanalysis of this population projection matrix. Consequently, I need
> > to be able to calculate eigenvalues and eigenvectors for asymmetric matrices. Could this functionality be added to Stan?
>
> Yes, it'd be pretty easy --- there are asymmetric algorithms in the
> Eigen package we use.  Unless we could work out some analytic
> gradients, it'd be relatively slow.  How big are the matrices
> that need to be decomposed?

Asymmetric eigenanalysis would be a bit harder than just wrapping the write Eigen functions.  The eigenvalues and eigenvectors or an asymmetric matrix can be complex.  We'd either need to support complex numbers or, in a pinch, we could return the real and imaginary parts separately but this would become tedious at best.

Cheers,
Marcus

Hi Andria,

Odd, I can't seem to reproduce this with the current develop branch:

[mbrubake@structure birats]$ ./birats sample num_warmup=20 num_samples=10 save_warmup=1 data file=birats.data.R random seed=4294967295 output file=birats.csv
...
 random
   seed = 4294967295 (Default)
 output
   file = birats.csv
   diagnostic_file =  (Default)
   refresh = 100 (Default)
...

Anyway, you seem to have somehow managed to pick the seed which represents the largest value an unsigned 32-bit integer can take.  I.E., 4294967295 = 2^32 - 1.  This is most likely causing a bug somewhere either in parsing the number or in representing it.  We'll have to take a look, but I suspect that so long as you pick values less than that (or, in the worst case, less than 2^31 - 1 = 2,147,483,647) all will be well!

Cheers,
Marcus

runs.

for i in {1..3}; do

	num_samples=1000 \
	num_warmup=1000 \
	save_warmup=1 \
	thin=1 \
	data file=$1.data.R \
	random seed=100$i \
	output file=$1.out$i.csv refresh=0 \
	id=$i &
done

This works fine if refresh is a positive integer.  I saw some posts wherein refresh=-1, but that didn't work either.

Best,

Jarrett

messages.body_plain:
To get rid of all the output, you'd ned to redirect the
standard output to /dev/null, as in:

$ ./normal sample output > /dev/null
$

Or you can choose a very high refresh rate (greater than num_samples + num_warmup),
but you'll still get the output of the configuration, the first
iteration, first sampling iteration, and last sampling iteration.

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] thinning the result of extract(fit, permuted=TRUE)
messages.body_plain:
Once you're extracting using permuted=TRUE, you should not sample at random or thin by taking every 10th or whatever, you should just take the first few in order from the permuted sample.  Why?  Because the permutation order gets saved, so next time you want to grab them, you'll again get the first 30 or however many draws from this permuted set.

messages.body_plain:
Neat.  Did it work as expected?

Both these models remind me of Blei and Lafferty's dynamic topic models, which are
also time-series multinomials, although modeled quite differently:

   http://www.cs.cmu.edu/~lafferty/pub/dtm.pdf

Instead of modeling the evolution of the parameters for a Dirichlet-Multinomial,
they use a logistic normal that evolves the actual multinomial
parameter on the logit scale.  That's more like your first model.

- Bob

> this is what should happen. (But maybe they're connected with what's going wrong for me in OSX.)
>
> "Informational Message: The current Metropolis proposal is about to be rejected becuase of the following issue:
> Error in function stan::prob::multi_normal_log(N4stan5agrad3varE): Covariance matrixCovariance matrix is not positive
> definite. Covariance matrix(0,0) is 1.0595482065447281e-176:0."

No, that's not going to be be connected with that error.  I'm still
wondering what we should do about the informational message here because
it's really confusing users no matter how much we qualify it.

I'm not sure what's going on here.   We are fixing a problem that
reported similar errors when (log) gamma functions underflowed/overflowed
and we weren't catching the specific type of exception they threw from
the Boost C++ library.

Your Windows environment reports:

   OS: x86_64, mingw32; rstan: 2.1.0; Rcpp: 0.10.6; inline: 0.3.13

so I'm wondering if you're using a 32-bit version of R on Windows?

Can you share the model and data that's causing a problem on OS X?

> P.S. Having recently installed RStan on both OSX and Windows, I'm really impressed with how clear/easy-to-follow the
> installation instructions are for both systems. That was very nice.

Thanks.  We try, but the way R's set up behind the scenes makes it
very fiddly --- there's no way to do a binary install in R (that we
know of, anyway) that doesn't mess with R's global configuration.
Therefore, the install depends on whatever else may have been installed
beforehand and what config those installs may have left behind.  Having
users have to edit global files seems very suboptimal.

And we're always happy to hear where the instructions are confusing
and even happier to field proposed corrections.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
I have a variable that takes on values in the range 1-4.  I was thinking
of modeling this as a beta distribution, but since there are a lot of
cases at the extremes that seems problematic.  I'm not sure the beta
function in stan will even accept such inputs and produce estimates.  I
could fake it by pulling the values in a bit, but I'm not sure that's a
good idea.

I'd appreciate any suggestions on how to fit such outcomes.  I don't
think it's a big deal if the fit doesn't reproduce the detailed features
of the distribution for my purposes, though if this lack of fit leads to
estimation problems that would matter.

"Detailed" features refers to that fact that most of the observations
are exactly integers, and all the values are evenly divisible by 1/3.

My main focus is on how covariates shift the distribution.  One approach
might be to treat the outcome as categorical or ordinal, but that seems
likely to create a lot more parameters.

The distribution also kind of looks like a truncated normal if one uses
1 unit size bins.

If you're curious, here's the basic data:

> table(tfat$FrndPartRace)

                1 1.33333333333333 1.66666666666667                2
              162               55               83              156
2.33333333333333 2.66666666666667                3 3.33333333333333
               71               73               93               19
3.66666666666667                4
                5               29

Thanks.
Ross

messages.subject: Non-uniqueness of eigenvectors and implications for initializing model
messages.subject_clean: Non-uniqueness of eigenvectors and implications for initializing model
messages.body_plain:
I'm working on a model to analyze some ordinal (Likert-scale) survey data and I'm having difficulties creating good initial values, where good means "the joint probability doesn't round down to 0."  At a high level, the model looks something like this:
N = # of individuals
M = # of questions
K = # of levels
z is an M x N array of latent responses (modeled)
zeta is an M-vector giving the prior mean for z[,i] (modeled)
Sigma is an M x M matrix giving the prior covariance for z[,i] (modeled)
cutp is an ordered vector of cutpoints used to translate each z[i,j] into an ordinal response x[i,j] (modeled)
A computational difficulty here is handling the likelihood for an individual's array of ordinal responses x[,i], which is the integral of an M-dimensional multivariate normal density over a rectangular region. The straightforward data augmentation using z doesn't work well (difficult to program in Stan, and very slow mixing), so I'm using a covariance decomposition approach. I end up with something that looks like this:

    xi[j, i] ~ Normal(0, 1)
    z[ , i] ~ MultivariateNormal(zeta + A * xi[ , i], D)

where
D is a diagonal matrix
A is a function of D and the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a matrix R*
R* is a function of D and another matrix R
R + D = Sigma.
This allows me to integrate out the z[,i], giving a likelihood conditional on R, D, and xi that is the product of univariate normal CDFs.

I'm using an R script to generate reasonable initial values for the model variables. To get reasonable values for xi requires reproducing some of the computations used to produce that A matrix, including the computation of eigenvalues and eigenvectors of R*.

There's the rub: I cannot reproduce in R the computation of the A matrix, because the eigendecomposition is not unique. Even if there are no repeated eigenvalues, and you normalize the eigenvectors, and you use a standard ordering of eigenvectors based on the eigenvalues, you can still multiply any subset of the eigenvectors by -1 and get another, equally valid, set of eigenvectors. There's no way I know of to guarantee that I'll get the same set of eigenvectors in R as I get in Stan.

If anyone has any ideas for dealing with this problem, I would be very happy to hear them.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Distribution for modeling a scale
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Distribution for modeling a scale
messages.body_plain:
HI, my quick hack would be to take the logit of the variable after transforming to a 0.5 to 4.5 scale, that is, work with logit((y - 0.5)/4).  This will make it continuous and will spread out the extremes a bit.  Of course it won't give correct predictions but otherwise it could do what you need.
If it works (or if it doesn't), please let me know!
A
